questions.q: Which standard amino acid has no stereocenter at its α-carbon?
o: Alanine
Alanine's α-carbon bears four different groups, including a methyl side chain.
Proline
Proline's α-carbon is chiral; its ring does not create symmetry there.
Glycine
Correct: its side chain is H, so the α-carbon carries two identical H atoms.
Cysteine
Cysteine is chiral; it is just unusual in being R rather than S.
questions.note: Glycine is the only achiral standard amino acid.
questions.x: A stereocenter needs four different substituents. Glycine's side chain is just a hydrogen, so its α-carbon holds two identical H atoms and cannot be chiral. Every other standard amino acid, including proline with its ring, has four distinct groups on the α-carbon.

questions.q: Amino acids incorporated into human proteins by ribosomes have which configuration at the α-carbon?
o: L
Correct: ribosomal protein synthesis uses L-amino acids exclusively.
D
D-amino acids appear in some bacterial cell walls, not in ribosomal human proteins.
A racemic mix of D and L
Translation is stereospecific; tRNA charging selects only one enantiomer.
R in every case
Most L-amino acids are S by CIP rules; L and R are different systems.
questions.note: Trap: D/L (Fischer) is not the same as R/S (CIP).
questions.x: Ribosomal translation uses only L-amino acids because aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and the ribosome are stereospecific. D-amino acids do occur in nature, for example in bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan, but they are made by other enzymes. D/L is a Fischer-projection label that is independent of the CIP R/S system, so L does not mean R.

questions.q: Almost every chiral L-amino acid has S absolute configuration. Which L-amino acid is the exception, with R configuration?
o: Serine
The CH₂OH carbon (O,H,H) ranks below COOH (O,O,O), so L-serine stays S.
Methionine
Its first side-chain atom is carbon (C,H,H), which ranks below COOH, so it is S.
Glycine
Glycine is achiral and has no R/S designation at all.
Cysteine
Correct: the sulfur in CH₂SH outranks the carboxyl carbon by CIP priority, flipping the label to R.
questions.note: Sulfur at the first side-chain atom is what changes the priority order.
questions.x: CIP priority is decided by atomic number at the first point of difference. In cysteine the side chain's first atom set is (S,H,H), and sulfur outranks the carboxyl's (O,O,O), so the side chain becomes priority 2 and the label flips to R. In serine or methionine the carboxyl still outranks the side chain, so those L-amino acids stay S.

questions.q: Which pair of amino acids both carry a negatively charged side chain at physiological pH?
o: Asparagine and glutamine
These are the uncharged amides of Asp and Glu.
Aspartate and glutamate
Correct: both side-chain carboxyls (pKa ≈ 4) are deprotonated at pH 7.4.
Lysine and arginine
These are basic and positively charged at pH 7.4.
Serine and threonine
Their hydroxyls (pKa > 13) are uncharged at physiological pH.
questions.x: A side chain is negatively charged at pH 7.4 only if it has an acidic group with pKa well below 7.4. Aspartate and glutamate carboxyls (pKa ≈ 4) are almost fully deprotonated. Asparagine and glutamine look similar but are amides, which do not ionize, so they are polar and neutral.

questions.q: An enzyme needs a residue that can donate a proton and accept one back near pH 7. Which side chain is best suited?
o: Lysine
Lysine's pKa ≈ 10.5 leaves it almost fully protonated at pH 7.
Histidine
Correct: its imidazole pKa ≈ 6 means both forms exist near neutral pH.
Arginine
Arginine's guanidinium (pKa ≈ 12.5) essentially never deprotonates at pH 7.
Aspartate
Aspartate (pKa ≈ 3.9) is almost fully deprotonated at pH 7.
questions.note: A good acid-base catalyst has a pKa close to the working pH.
questions.x: General acid-base catalysis works best when the catalytic group has a pKa near the operating pH, so substantial amounts of both protonated and deprotonated forms exist. Histidine's imidazole (pKa ≈ 6) fits this. Lys, Arg and Asp have pKa values far from 7, so each is locked almost entirely in one protonation state.

questions.q: Lysine has pKa values of 2.2 (α-COOH), 9.0 (α-NH₃⁺) and 10.5 (side chain). What is its net charge at pH 7.0?
o: This treats the amines as deprotonated, but pH 7 is below both of their pKa values.
This forgets that the side-chain amine is also protonated below pH 10.5.
Correct: both amines are protonated (+2) and the carboxyl is deprotonated (−1).
This treats the α-carboxyl as protonated, but pH 7 is far above its pKa of 2.2.
questions.x: Compare pH with each pKa: a group is mostly protonated when pH < pKa. At pH 7 the carboxyl (pKa 2.2) is COO⁻ (−1), while both amines (pKa 9.0 and 10.5) are NH₃⁺ (+1 each). The net charge is +1; forgetting that the side-chain amine is also protonated gives 0.

questions.q: Glycine has pKa values of 2.3 and 9.7. What is its isoelectric point?
o: Correct: pI = (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 6.0, the average of the two pKa values.
Neutral pH is not automatically the pI; it depends on the pKa values.
The pI lies between the two pKa values, not at the amino group's pKa.
This adds the pKa values instead of averaging them.
questions.x: For an amino acid with no ionizable side chain, the neutral zwitterion exists between pKa1 and pKa2, so pI is their average: (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 6.0. The pI depends on the molecule's pKa values, so it is not automatically 7.

questions.q: Glutamate has pKa values of 2.2 (α-COOH), 4.2 (side chain) and 9.7 (α-NH₃⁺). What is its pI?
o: Correct: average the two pKa values flanking the neutral form: (2.2 + 4.2)/2 = 3.2.
Averaging all three pKa values is not how pI is found.
This uses only the α-groups and ignores the acidic side chain.
This averages the side-chain and amino pKa values, the rule for a basic amino acid.
questions.note: Acidic amino acid: average the two lowest pKa values.
questions.x: The pI is the average of the two pKa values that bracket the net-neutral species. For glutamate, the neutral form exists after the α-COOH loses its proton and before the side-chain COOH does, so pI = (2.2 + 4.2)/2 = 3.2. Averaging the α-groups only ignores the extra acidic group that pulls the pI down.

questions.q: Arginine has pKa values of 2.2 (α-COOH), 9.0 (α-NH₃⁺) and 12.5 (side chain). What is its pI?
o: Averaging the α-group pKa values ignores the basic side chain.
Averaging all three pKa values is not a valid method.
Correct: the neutral form sits between the two highest pKa values: (9.0 + 12.5)/2.
The pI lies between two pKa values, not at one of them.
questions.note: Basic amino acid: average the two highest pKa values.
questions.x: Write the species in order of deprotonation: +2, +1, 0, −1. For arginine the neutral species exists between the α-NH₃⁺ (9.0) and the side chain (12.5), so pI = (9.0 + 12.5)/2 = 10.75. Basic amino acids have high pI values because the extra positive group must be removed before the molecule is neutral.

questions.q: A histidine side chain has pKa 6.0. At pH 7.0, roughly what percentage of these side chains are protonated?
o: A ratio of 100:1 would need pH to be 2 units above the pKa.
Correct: base/acid = 10¹ = 10, so protonated = 1/11 ≈ 9%.
50% protonation happens only when pH equals the pKa.
This flips the ratio; pH above pKa favors the deprotonated form.
questions.note: Each pH unit above the pKa shifts the base:acid ratio tenfold.
questions.x: Henderson-Hasselbalch gives [base]/[acid] = 10^(pH − pKa) = 10¹ = 10 at pH 7.0. So for every 1 protonated imidazole there are 10 neutral ones, and the protonated fraction is 1/11 ≈ 9%. The tempting 91% inverts the ratio; pH above pKa always favors the deprotonated form.

questions.q: A fully protonated amino acid is titrated with NaOH. The curve shows three buffering regions centered at pH 2.2, 9.0 and 10.5. Which amino acid is it?
o: Glutamate
Glutamate's extra pKa is near 4.2, not 10.5.
Histidine
Histidine's extra pKa is near 6.0.
Alanine
Alanine has no ionizable side chain, so it shows only two buffering regions.
Lysine
Correct: an extra pKa near 10.5 matches lysine's ε-amino group.
questions.x: Each buffering plateau on a titration curve marks a pKa. pKa values near 2 and 9 belong to the α-carboxyl and α-amino groups, so the third plateau identifies the side chain. A side-chain pKa near 10.5 is lysine's ε-amino group, whereas glutamate (≈4.2) and histidine (≈6.0) would show plateaus much lower.

questions.q: While titrating glycine with NaOH, the solution passes through the isoelectric point. What is observed at that point?
o: The pH changes sharply with a small amount of added base
Correct: the pI is an equivalence point, where buffering capacity is lowest.
The pH resists change most strongly
Strongest buffering happens at a pKa, not at the pI.
The pH equals the pKa of the amino group
The pI lies halfway between the two pKa values.
Most molecules carry a net charge of +1
At the pI the dominant species is the neutral zwitterion.
questions.note: Flat parts of the curve are pKa values; steep parts are equivalence points.
questions.x: On a titration curve, the flat regions are at pKa values, where a weak acid and its conjugate base buffer each other. The pI of glycine falls at the first equivalence point, where essentially all molecules are zwitterions and little conjugate pair is present to buffer. So the pH jumps steeply there with small additions of base.

questions.q: How many equivalents of OH⁻ must be added to fully protonated glycine to reach its isoelectric point?
o: At 0.5 equivalents pH equals pKa1, which is a buffering region.
Correct: removing the carboxyl proton gives the zwitterion, net charge 0.
At 1.5 equivalents pH equals pKa2 of the amino group.
At 2.0 equivalents glycine is fully deprotonated, net charge −1.
questions.x: Fully protonated glycine (⁺H₃N–CH₂–COOH) has net charge +1. One equivalent of OH⁻ removes the carboxyl proton, giving the zwitterion with net charge 0, which is the pI. Half-integer equivalents (0.5 and 1.5) correspond to the pKa values, the midpoints of the buffering regions.

questions.q: How is a peptide bond formed between two amino acids?
o: Hydrolysis of the carboxyl group by water
Hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds; it does not form them.
Oxidation of two side-chain thiols
That forms a disulfide bond, not a peptide bond.
Condensation of a carboxyl group with an amino group, releasing water
Correct: it is a dehydration reaction that forms an amide.
Esterification between two hydroxyl groups
Peptide bonds are amides made with nitrogen, not esters.
questions.x: A peptide bond is an amide formed by condensation: the carboxyl group of one amino acid joins the amino group of the next and a water molecule is released. Hydrolysis is the reverse reaction, adding water to break the bond. Disulfide bonds and esters are different linkages that do not join backbone residues.

questions.q: Why is rotation about the peptide C–N bond restricted?
o: Bulky side chains physically block the rotation
Side chains are on the α-carbons; the restriction comes from bond electronics.
The bond is a full C=N double bond
It is a resonance hybrid, only partly double, which is why it is shorter than a single bond.
Hydrogen bonds from water lock the bond in place
Solvent does not cause this; the planarity is intrinsic to the amide.
Resonance gives the bond partial double-bond character
Correct: the nitrogen lone pair delocalizes into the carbonyl, keeping the group planar.
questions.x: The amide nitrogen's lone pair delocalizes into the carbonyl, giving the C–N bond about 40% double-bond character. This makes the bond shorter than a C–N single bond and locks the six atoms of the peptide group in a plane. It is not a true double bond, which is why it is described as partial.

questions.q: Which description best fits the geometry of most peptide bonds in proteins?
o: Planar and cis
Cis is uncommon and occurs mostly before proline.
Trans and freely rotating
Partial double-bond character prevents free rotation.
Planar and trans
Correct: trans puts the α-carbons on opposite sides and avoids steric clash.
Nonplanar with tetrahedral nitrogen
The amide nitrogen is sp²-like and planar because of resonance.
questions.x: Resonance makes the peptide group planar, and steric clash between consecutive α-carbons strongly favors the trans arrangement. Cis peptide bonds are rare and occur mainly when the following residue is proline, whose ring makes cis and trans closer in energy. Planarity rules out free rotation and a tetrahedral nitrogen.

questions.q: Backbone conformations are described by the φ and ψ angles. Which bonds do these angles describe?
o: The peptide C–N bond and the C=O bond
Both have double-bond character and do not rotate freely.
N–Cα and Cα–C(carbonyl)
Correct: these single bonds flank the α-carbon and can rotate.
Only bonds within the side chains
Side-chain angles are called χ angles, not φ and ψ.
The disulfide S–S bonds
Disulfides are not part of the backbone.
questions.x: Because the peptide C–N bond is planar and rigid, backbone flexibility comes from the two single bonds on either side of each α-carbon. φ describes rotation about N–Cα and ψ about Cα–C(O). Side-chain rotations are called χ angles, and Ramachandran plots show which φ/ψ combinations are sterically allowed.

questions.q: A peptide sequence written as Met-Gly-Ser by convention means what?
o: Met is at the N-terminus and Ser is at the C-terminus
Correct: sequences are written from N-terminus to C-terminus.
Met is at the C-terminus and Ser is at the N-terminus
This reverses the standard convention.
Gly forms both peptide bonds through its side chain
Peptide bonds are backbone bonds; glycine has no side chain.
The residues can be in any order
Order is the primary structure and defines the peptide.
questions.x: By convention, peptide and protein sequences are written from the free α-amino end (N-terminus) on the left to the free α-carboxyl end (C-terminus) on the right. This matches the direction of ribosomal synthesis. Because sequence order defines primary structure, Met-Gly-Ser and Ser-Gly-Met are different peptides.

questions.q: Complete hydrolysis of a tripeptide into free amino acids uses how many water molecules?
o: One water breaks only one of the two peptide bonds.
Correct: a tripeptide has two peptide bonds, and each needs one water to break.
There are three residues but only two peptide bonds.
This double-counts; each peptide bond uses one water.
questions.note: n residues → n − 1 peptide bonds.
questions.x: A chain of n amino acids is joined by n − 1 peptide bonds, and hydrolysis consumes one water per bond broken. A tripeptide has 2 peptide bonds, so complete hydrolysis uses 2 waters. Counting residues instead of bonds gives the tempting wrong answer of 3.

questions.q: Peptide bond hydrolysis has ΔG < 0, yet proteins persist in neutral water for years without enzymes. Why?
o: Hydrolysis is endergonic at neutral pH
Hydrolysis is exergonic; forming peptide bonds is what needs energy.
Water cannot reach the peptide bond
Backbones on protein surfaces are fully exposed to water.
The activation energy for uncatalyzed hydrolysis is very high
Correct: the reaction is favorable but kinetically very slow.
Peptide bonds re-form spontaneously as fast as they break
Re-formation is unfavorable; it is not a balanced cycle.
questions.note: Thermodynamics says if a reaction can go; kinetics says how fast.
questions.x: ΔG tells whether a reaction is favorable, not how fast it goes. Peptide hydrolysis is exergonic but has a very high activation energy, so without a catalyst the half-life in neutral water is years. Proteases speed the reaction by lowering the activation energy without changing ΔG.

questions.q: Which amino acid has its side chain covalently bonded to its own α-amino nitrogen?
o: Proline
Correct: its side chain loops back to the backbone nitrogen, forming a secondary amine.
Lysine
Lysine's side-chain amine is free at the end of a four-carbon chain.
Histidine
Histidine's imidazole ring is separate from the backbone nitrogen.
Tryptophan
Tryptophan's indole ring hangs off the β-carbon, not the α-nitrogen.
questions.x: Proline's three-carbon side chain bonds back to the α-amino nitrogen, forming a five-membered pyrrolidine ring and making proline a secondary amine. This fixes its φ angle and removes the backbone N–H hydrogen-bond donor, which is why proline disrupts α-helices. Other cyclic side chains like His and Trp are not attached to the backbone nitrogen.

questions.q: Which amino acid has the most hydrophobic side chain?
o: Serine
Serine's hydroxyl makes it polar.
Glutamine
Glutamine has a polar amide side chain.
Aspartate
Aspartate is charged at physiological pH.
Leucine
Correct: its branched alkyl side chain is nonpolar.
questions.x: Hydrophobic side chains are made of hydrocarbon with no polar or ionizable groups. Leucine's branched isobutyl side chain fits this and tends to be buried in protein cores. Serine (hydroxyl), glutamine (amide) and aspartate (charged carboxylate) all interact favorably with water.

questions.q: A protein kinase phosphorylates a side-chain hydroxyl. Which residue could it target?
o: Alanine
Alanine's methyl group has no hydroxyl to accept a phosphate.
Threonine
Correct: Ser, Thr and Tyr have hydroxyls that kinases phosphorylate.
Phenylalanine
Phenylalanine lacks tyrosine's para-hydroxyl group.
Valine
Valine's side chain is purely hydrocarbon.
questions.x: Kinases transfer the γ-phosphate of ATP onto a hydroxyl group, forming a phosphoester. Serine, threonine and tyrosine are the residues with side-chain hydroxyls, so they are the usual targets in eukaryotes. Phenylalanine is the tempting distractor because it resembles tyrosine but lacks the OH.

questions.q: N-linked glycosylation attaches an oligosaccharide to a side-chain nitrogen. Which residue receives it?
o: Serine
Serine is a site for O-linked glycosylation through its hydroxyl.
Asparagine
Correct: N-linked sugars attach to the amide nitrogen of Asn.
Glutamate
Glutamate's side chain is a carboxylate, not a nitrogen.
Lysine
Lysine is not the acceptor in N-linked glycosylation.
questions.x: N-linked glycosylation, which begins in the rough ER, attaches an oligosaccharide to the side-chain amide nitrogen of asparagine, typically in an Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequence. O-linked glycosylation, by contrast, attaches sugars to the hydroxyl oxygen of serine or threonine, mostly in the Golgi. Matching the linkage atom (N vs O) to the residue is the key.

questions.q: Protein concentration is often estimated from absorbance at 280 nm. Which side chain contributes most to this absorbance?
o: Histidine
Imidazole absorbs very little at 280 nm.
Leucine
Aliphatic side chains do not absorb in this range.
Serine
Serine has no conjugated system that absorbs UV light.
Tryptophan
Correct: its indole ring absorbs strongly near 280 nm.
questions.note: Trp and Tyr cause the A280 signal.
questions.x: Absorbance at 280 nm comes mainly from aromatic side chains with extended conjugated π systems. Tryptophan's indole absorbs most strongly, followed by tyrosine; phenylalanine contributes little. Histidine's imidazole and aliphatic or hydroxyl side chains absorb negligibly at this wavelength.

questions.q: In a folded protein at pH 7, a lysine side chain sits next to a glutamate side chain. What interaction do they most likely form?
o: A salt bridge
Correct: positively charged NH₃⁺ and negatively charged COO⁻ attract each other.
A disulfide bond
Only cysteine thiols form disulfide bonds.
A hydrophobic interaction
Both side chains are charged, not nonpolar.
A peptide bond
Peptide bonds join backbone groups during translation, not side chains.
questions.x: At pH 7 lysine's side chain is NH₃⁺ and glutamate's is COO⁻, so the two attract electrostatically, forming a salt bridge (ionic bond). Disulfide bonds require two cysteines, and hydrophobic interactions require nonpolar groups. Peptide bonds join only backbone carboxyl and amino groups.

questions.q: Which point mutation is most conservative, least likely to alter protein structure?
o: Leucine → aspartate
This puts a charged residue where a nonpolar one was.
Glycine → tryptophan
This swaps the smallest side chain for the bulkiest one.
Leucine → isoleucine
Correct: both are branched, nonpolar side chains of similar size.
Lysine → glutamate
This reverses the side-chain charge from + to −.
questions.x: A conservative substitution swaps a residue for one with similar size, shape and chemistry, so folding and interactions are barely changed. Leucine and isoleucine are isomeric, branched and nonpolar. Changes that alter charge, polarity or size dramatically, like Leu→Asp or Gly→Trp, are much more likely to disrupt structure.

questions.q: In sickle-cell hemoglobin, a surface glutamate in β-globin is replaced by valine. Why does deoxyhemoglobin S polymerize?
o: The valine forms disulfide bonds between hemoglobin molecules
Valine has no thiol and cannot form disulfides.
The mutation oxidizes heme iron to Fe³⁺
The substitution does not change the iron's oxidation state.
The mutation prevents α and β chains from assembling
HbS still forms α₂β₂ tetramers.
The valine creates a hydrophobic surface patch that binds a pocket on neighboring hemoglobins
Correct: a sticky nonpolar contact drives fiber formation in the deoxy state.
questions.x: The Glu6→Val substitution replaces a charged surface residue with a hydrophobic one. In deoxyhemoglobin S, this valine fits into a complementary hydrophobic pocket on a neighboring tetramer, so molecules stick together into long fibers that deform red cells. The tetramer still assembles and the iron stays Fe²⁺; the defect is an abnormal intermolecular contact.

questions.q: A mixture of Asp (pI 2.8), Gly (pI 6.0) and Lys (pI 9.7) is electrophoresed at pH 6.0. Which moves toward the anode?
o: Glycine
At its pI glycine has no net charge and stays near the origin.
Lysine
Lysine is positive at pH 6.0 and moves toward the cathode.
Aspartate
Correct: pH 6.0 is above Asp's pI, so it is negative and moves toward the + electrode.
None of them; all are zwitterions
Only glycine is net neutral at this pH.
questions.note: pH > pI → negative; pH < pI → positive.
questions.x: A molecule's net charge depends on pH relative to its pI: pH above pI makes it negative, pH below pI makes it positive. At pH 6.0 aspartate (pI 2.8) is negative and migrates to the anode (+), lysine (pI 9.7) is positive and moves to the cathode, and glycine at its pI stays put.

questions.q: In isoelectric focusing, a protein with pI 5.5 is loaded where the gel pH is 8. How does it move?
o: Toward the cathode, stopping where pH = 5.5
A negatively charged protein moves away from the cathode.
Toward the anode, stopping where pH = 5.5
Correct: it is negative at pH 8 and moves toward lower pH until its net charge is zero.
Toward the anode until it reaches the end of the gel
It stops once the local pH equals its pI and its charge is zero.
It stays at the loading point
It carries net negative charge at pH 8, so it migrates.
questions.x: In isoelectric focusing a stable pH gradient runs from low pH at the anode to high pH at the cathode. A protein at pH 8 with pI 5.5 is negatively charged, so it moves toward the anode into progressively lower pH. As it reaches pH 5.5 its net charge becomes zero and it stops, focusing there rather than running off the gel.

questions.q: Estimate the net charge of the tripeptide Lys-Glu-His at pH 7.0 (side-chain pKa values: Lys 10.5, Glu 4.2, His 6.0).
o: This forgets the protonated N-terminal amino group.
Correct: N-terminus +1, Lys +1, Glu −1, C-terminus −1, His mostly neutral.
Counting His as protonated is wrong; pH 7 is above its pKa of 6.
This ignores the two negative charges from Glu and the C-terminus.
questions.note: Remember the termini when counting charges in a peptide.
questions.x: Count every ionizable group, including the termini. At pH 7 the N-terminal amine (pKa ≈ 8) and Lys (10.5) are protonated, +2; the C-terminal carboxyl and Glu (4.2) are deprotonated, −2. His (6.0) is only about 9% protonated, so it contributes nearly 0 and the net charge is about 0.

questions.q: What is the net charge of the tripeptide Gly-Lys-Asp at pH 1?
o: At pH 1 the carboxyl groups are protonated and carry no negative charge.
This misses that the Lys side chain is also protonated.
Correct: at pH 1 the N-terminus and Lys are +1 each, and both carboxyls are neutral COOH.
Asp's carboxyl becomes neutral, not positive, when protonated.
questions.x: At pH 1, which is below every carboxyl pKa, the C-terminal and Asp carboxyls are mostly protonated COOH and carry no charge. Both amines, the N-terminus and the Lys side chain, are protonated NH₃⁺. The net charge is therefore +2; protonating a carboxyl makes it neutral, not positive.

questions.q: Which amino acid has a thioether (C–S–C) side chain?
o: Methionine
Correct: its side chain is CH₂CH₂–S–CH₃.
Cysteine
Cysteine has a thiol (–SH), not a thioether.
Serine
Serine has a hydroxyl and no sulfur.
Threonine
Threonine has a hydroxyl and no sulfur.
questions.x: A thioether has sulfur bonded to two carbons. Methionine's side chain, CH₂CH₂–S–CH₃, fits this description, while cysteine has a terminal thiol (–SH) that can be oxidized to form disulfide bonds. Methionine therefore cannot form disulfides.

questions.q: Which amino acid is polar but uncharged at physiological pH?
o: Glutamate
Glutamate is negatively charged at pH 7.4.
Isoleucine
Isoleucine is nonpolar.
Glutamine
Correct: its amide side chain is polar and does not ionize.
Lysine
Lysine is positively charged at pH 7.4.
questions.x: Glutamine's side-chain amide is polar and can hydrogen-bond, but amides do not ionize in the physiological pH range. Glutamate and lysine are polar too, but they are charged at pH 7.4. Isoleucine is nonpolar.

questions.q: An aspartate side chain has pKa 3.9. At pH 4.9, what is the ratio of deprotonated to protonated side chains?
o: Correct: pH − pKa = 1, so [A⁻]/[HA] = 10¹.
This reverses the ratio; pH above pKa favors the base.
A 1 : 1 ratio happens only at pH = pKa.
That would need pH to be 2 units above the pKa.
questions.x: Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). With pH − pKa = 4.9 − 3.9 = 1, the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] = 10. When pH is above pKa the deprotonated form dominates, so the reversed 1:10 is wrong.

questions.q: Which form of alanine is most abundant in water at pH 7?
o: H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COOH
The uncharged form is negligible at any pH in water.
⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COOH
The cationic form dominates only below pH ≈ 2.
H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻
The anionic form dominates only above pH ≈ 9.7.
⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻
Correct: at neutral pH the amino group is protonated and the carboxyl is deprotonated, making a zwitterion.
questions.x: In water at neutral pH, the α-amino group (pKa ≈ 9.7) is protonated and the α-carboxyl (pKa ≈ 2.3) is deprotonated, giving the zwitterion ⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻. The fully uncharged form never dominates because the conditions that would neutralize one group charge the other.

questions.q: The α-COOH of an amino acid has pKa ≈ 2, far lower than acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8). What best explains this?
o: Resonance between the carboxyl and the side chain
The side chain is not conjugated with the carboxyl.
The nearby positively charged α-NH₃⁺ stabilizes the carboxylate
Correct: the electron-withdrawing ammonium favors loss of the proton.
Water hydrogen-bonds more strongly to the amino acid
Solvation alone does not explain a difference of nearly 3 pKa units.
The amino acid's larger size spreads the charge out
Size is not the cause; the inductive and electrostatic effect of NH₃⁺ is.
questions.x: An acid's strength rises when its conjugate base is stabilized. In an amino acid the positively charged α-NH₃⁺ sits on the adjacent carbon and stabilizes the carboxylate through inductive electron withdrawal and electrostatic attraction. That makes losing the carboxyl proton easier, lowering its pKa to about 2.

questions.q: A neighboring histidine lowers an active-site cysteine's thiol pKa from 8.3 to 6.5. What is the main effect at pH 7.4?
o: The cysteine is mostly protonated and unreactive
Lowering the pKa below 7.4 favors deprotonation.
The cysteine is mostly thiolate and a stronger nucleophile
Correct: pH above pKa favors S⁻, which is far more nucleophilic than SH.
The cysteine forms a disulfide bond with histidine
Histidine has no thiol, so no disulfide can form.
The cysteine gains a positive charge
Deprotonating a thiol gives a negative thiolate.
questions.x: Lowering a group's pKa means it deprotonates at lower pH. With pKa 6.5, at pH 7.4 the cysteine is about 90% thiolate (S⁻), which is a much stronger nucleophile than the neutral thiol. This is how cysteine proteases and similar enzymes activate their catalytic cysteine.

questions.q: Why is β-mercaptoethanol added to protein samples before SDS-PAGE?
o: To hydrolyze peptide bonds into smaller fragments
It is a reducing agent, not a protease.
To give each protein a uniform negative charge
That is the job of SDS.
To stabilize the native folded state
It is used to help fully denature the protein.
To reduce disulfide bonds so subunits separate
Correct: it breaks S–S bonds that SDS alone cannot.
questions.x: SDS denatures proteins and coats them with negative charge, but it cannot break covalent disulfide bonds. β-Mercaptoethanol is a reducing agent that converts S–S bonds to free SH groups, so disulfide-linked chains separate and loops open. Then each polypeptide runs according to its own mass.

questions.q: A protein runs as one 100 kDa band on SDS-PAGE without reducing agent and as one 50 kDa band with reducing agent. What is the best conclusion?
o: It has two identical 50 kDa subunits joined by disulfide bonds
Correct: only reduction splits the dimer, and the single band means the chains are the same size.
It is a noncovalent dimer of 50 kDa subunits
SDS alone would separate noncovalent subunits, giving 50 kDa without reducing agent.
It is a 100 kDa monomer that the reducing agent degrades
Reducing agents do not cut peptide bonds.
It has two different subunits of 60 and 40 kDa
That would show two bands under reducing conditions.
questions.x: SDS alone disrupts noncovalent interactions, so a band that shifts only after reduction must be held together by disulfide bonds. The 100 kDa unreduced species splitting into a single 50 kDa band means two disulfide-linked chains of the same size. A noncovalent dimer would already run at 50 kDa without reducing agent.

questions.q: Which residue is most likely buried in the core of a water-soluble globular protein?
o: Lysine
Charged lysine is usually on the surface, in contact with water.
Glutamate
Charged glutamate prefers the solvent-exposed surface.
Phenylalanine
Correct: nonpolar aromatic side chains are hidden from water.
Arginine
Arginine's charged guanidinium prefers the surface.
questions.x: The hydrophobic effect drives folding: nonpolar side chains cluster in the core, away from water, which increases solvent entropy. Phenylalanine's aromatic ring is nonpolar and is commonly buried. Charged residues like Lys, Glu and Arg are usually on the surface where they can be hydrated.

questions.q: A 20-residue segment is predicted to form a single membrane-spanning α-helix. Which residues should it be rich in?
o: Aspartate, glutamate and lysine
Charged residues are very unfavorable inside the bilayer.
Serine, asparagine and glutamine
These polar side chains prefer water.
Proline and glycine
These residues disfavor stable α-helices.
Leucine, isoleucine and valine
Correct: nonpolar side chains contact the hydrophobic lipid tails.
questions.x: The interior of a lipid bilayer is about 30 Å of hydrocarbon, which a helix of about 20 residues can span. Residues facing the lipid tails must be nonpolar, so transmembrane helices are rich in Leu, Ile, Val and similar side chains. Charged residues pay a large energy penalty when buried there, and Pro and Gly destabilize helices.

questions.q: Which standard amino acid has two stereocenters?
o: Serine
Serine's β-carbon (CH₂OH) has two identical H atoms.
Valine
Valine's β-carbon carries two identical methyl groups.
Threonine
Correct: both its α-carbon and β-carbon are chiral.
Leucine
Leucine's γ-carbon has two identical methyl groups, so only Cα is chiral.
questions.note: Thr and Ile each have two chiral centers.
questions.x: A carbon is a stereocenter only if it has four different substituents. Threonine's β-carbon carries OH, CH₃, H and the α-carbon, so threonine has two stereocenters (as does isoleucine). Serine, valine and leucine each have a side-chain carbon with two identical groups, so only their α-carbon is chiral.

questions.q: Which amino acid differs from phenylalanine only by a para-hydroxyl group on the ring?
o: Tryptophan
Tryptophan has a two-ring indole, not a hydroxylated phenyl.
Tyrosine
Correct: tyrosine is phenylalanine with an OH at the para position.
Histidine
Histidine has a five-membered imidazole ring.
Serine
Serine has a hydroxyl but no aromatic ring.
questions.x: Tyrosine is phenylalanine with a hydroxyl at the para position of the benzene ring; the body makes tyrosine by hydroxylating phenylalanine. This OH makes tyrosine more polar and a target for tyrosine kinases. Tryptophan and histidine are aromatic but have different ring systems.

questions.q: The N-terminal α-NH₃⁺ in a peptide has pKa ≈ 8, lower than in a free amino acid (≈ 9.6). Why?
o: There is no adjacent carboxylate to stabilize the protonated amine
Correct: in a free amino acid, the nearby COO⁻ helps hold the NH₃⁺ proton.
The peptide bond makes the amine a stronger base
A lower pKa means a weaker base, not a stronger one.
The N-terminal amine is part of the peptide bond
The N-terminal amine is free; only internal amines form peptide bonds.
Side chains donate electrons to the terminal amine
Donating electrons would raise the pKa, not lower it.
questions.x: In a free amino acid, the adjacent α-COO⁻ electrostatically stabilizes the protonated α-NH₃⁺, raising its pKa to about 9.6. In a peptide, the N-terminal residue's carboxyl is tied up in a neutral amide, so that stabilization is lost and the amine gives up its proton more easily. A lower pKa means a weaker base, not a stronger one.

questions.q: Amino acids can accept protons and also donate them. What is this property called?
o: Hydrophobic
Hydrophobicity describes how a molecule behaves in water, not acid-base behavior.
Chiral
Chirality is about handedness, not acid-base behavior.
Amphoteric
Correct: they act as both acids and bases.
Aromatic
Aromaticity describes ring electrons, not acid-base behavior.
questions.x: An amphoteric substance can act as either an acid or a base. Amino acids have a carboxyl group that can donate a proton and an amino group that can accept one. This is why they exist as zwitterions and can buffer at two or more pH ranges.

questions.q: Free histidine has pKa values of 1.8, 6.0 and 9.2. At which pH would it buffer best?
o: 3.9 is more than 2 units from any pKa, so buffering is poor.
Correct: buffering is strongest at a pKa, and 6.0 is the side-chain pKa.
7.6 is histidine's pI, an equivalence point with weak buffering.
11.0 is almost 2 units above the highest pKa, so little buffer remains.
questions.note: Trap: the pI is where buffering is weakest.
questions.x: A buffer resists pH change best when pH equals the pKa of a weak acid group, because acid and conjugate base are present in equal amounts. Histidine's pKa values are 1.8, 6.0 and 9.2, so 6.0 is a buffering point. Its pI, (6.0 + 9.2)/2 = 7.6, is an equivalence point where buffering is weakest.

questions.q: Trypsin cleaves on the C-terminal side of Lys and Arg (except before Pro). How many fragments does it make from Ala-Lys-Gly-Arg-Phe-Lys?
o: This misses one of the two internal cleavage sites.
Correct: cuts after Lys2 and Arg4 give Ala-Lys, Gly-Arg and Phe-Lys.
The final Lys is the C-terminus, so there is no bond after it to cut.
Trypsin does not cut after every residue.
questions.x: Trypsin hydrolyzes the peptide bond after the carbonyl of Lys or Arg, except when Pro follows. In Ala-Lys-Gly-Arg-Phe-Lys, bonds after Lys2 and Arg4 are cut, giving three fragments. The C-terminal Lys has no following peptide bond to cleave, so it adds no extra fragment.

questions.q: Glycine is common in tight turns and flexible loops. Which property of glycine explains this?
o: Its tiny side chain allows backbone angles that other residues cannot adopt
Correct: with only H as a side chain, glycine has the most φ/ψ freedom.
Its side chain forms strong hydrogen bonds
Glycine's side chain is only a hydrogen atom.
It cannot form peptide bonds on one side
Glycine forms normal peptide bonds.
It is charged at physiological pH
Its side chain is uncharged.
questions.x: Glycine's side chain is a single hydrogen, so it causes minimal steric clash and can adopt φ/ψ combinations forbidden to other residues. That flexibility makes it common in tight turns and loops. The same flexibility makes glycine a poor α-helix former, since the helix costs it more conformational entropy.

questions.q: Alanine (pKa values 2.3 and 9.7) is in a solution at pH 9.7. What is its average net charge?
o: Full −1 needs pH well above 9.7.
Correct: half the molecules are zwitterions (0) and half are anions (−1).
Zero is the average charge at the pI (6.0), not at pKa2.
+0.5 is the average charge at pKa1 (2.3).
questions.note: At any pKa, the group is half protonated.
questions.x: When pH equals a pKa, that group is half protonated. At pH 9.7 the carboxyl is fully deprotonated, and half of the amino groups have lost their protons. So half the molecules are zwitterions (0) and half are anions (−1), giving an average charge of −0.5.

questions.q: What does a protein's primary structure refer to?
o: Its α-helices and β-sheets
Those are secondary structures.
The overall 3D fold of one chain
That is tertiary structure.
How multiple subunits are arranged
That is quaternary structure.
Its amino acid sequence linked by peptide bonds
Correct: primary structure is the linear order of residues.
questions.x: Primary structure is the covalent sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, written N to C. It is the only level held together by covalent backbone bonds, and it ultimately determines the higher levels: secondary (local backbone H-bonded patterns), tertiary (the whole chain's fold) and quaternary (assembly of multiple chains).

questions.q: What chiefly stabilizes α-helices and β-sheets?
o: Ionic bonds between side chains
Side-chain interactions mainly stabilize tertiary structure.
Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups
Correct: secondary structure is defined by backbone hydrogen bonding.
Disulfide bonds between cysteines
Disulfides are covalent tertiary or quaternary links.
Peptide bonds between adjacent residues
Peptide bonds make up primary structure.
questions.x: Secondary structure is defined by hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl oxygens and amide N–H groups, which is why helices and sheets form in almost any sequence. Side-chain interactions such as salt bridges, hydrophobic packing and disulfides mainly stabilize tertiary and quaternary structure. Peptide bonds define primary structure.

questions.q: In an α-helix, the backbone C=O of residue n hydrogen-bonds to the N–H of which residue?
o: An i+2 bond would make a very tight turn, not an α-helix.
Correct: this i → i+4 pattern gives about 3.6 residues per turn.
Adjacent residues are too close to hydrogen-bond across the helix.
A residue on a neighboring strand
That describes a β-sheet.
questions.x: In an α-helix each backbone C=O of residue n accepts a hydrogen bond from the N–H of residue n + 4. Repeating this pattern down the chain yields a right-handed helix with about 3.6 residues per turn. Bonds between strands, rather than within one coil, describe β-sheets.

questions.q: How are side chains arranged in an α-helix?
o: They point into the center of the helix
The core of an α-helix is filled by backbone atoms.
They lie flat in a plane above and below
That alternating pattern describes β-strands.
They form the hydrogen bonds that hold the helix
The helix is held by backbone hydrogen bonds, not side chains.
They project outward from the helix axis
Correct: this keeps them away from the tightly packed backbone.
questions.x: The α-helix's interior is packed tightly with backbone atoms, and its hydrogen bonds run parallel to the axis between backbone groups. Side chains therefore project outward from the axis, like bristles on a brush. This lets them interact with solvent, membranes or other parts of the protein.

questions.q: What defines an antiparallel β-sheet?
o: Adjacent strands run in opposite N-to-C directions
Correct: antiparallel means neighboring strands point opposite ways.
Adjacent strands run in the same N-to-C direction
That is a parallel β-sheet.
Hydrogen bonds form within a single strand
β-sheet hydrogen bonds form between strands.
Side chains lie in the plane of the sheet
Side chains point above and below the sheet.
questions.x: β-sheets are classified by the direction of adjacent strands. In antiparallel sheets neighboring strands run in opposite N-to-C directions, giving well-aligned, straight hydrogen bonds; in parallel sheets they run the same way. In both, the hydrogen bonds link backbone groups on different strands.

questions.q: Along a single β-strand, how do successive side chains point?
o: All point to the same face of the sheet
Successive residues alternate sides.
They spiral around the strand every 3.6 residues
That describes an α-helix.
They alternate above and below the plane of the sheet
Correct: the pleated backbone flips each side chain to the opposite face.
They point toward the hydrogen-bonded neighboring strand
The backbone C=O and N–H groups face the neighbor strands, not the side chains.
questions.note: A sheet can have one hydrophobic face and one polar face.
questions.x: The β-strand backbone is extended and pleated, so consecutive residues point their side chains to alternate faces of the sheet. This lets a sheet have one hydrophobic face packed against the core and one polar face toward water when residues alternate nonpolar/polar. Spiraling every 3.6 residues describes an α-helix.

questions.q: Which two residues are especially common in β-turns?
o: Leucine and isoleucine
Bulky nonpolar residues favor helices and buried strands.
Lysine and arginine
Charge alone does not make a residue suited to turns.
Phenylalanine and tryptophan
Large aromatic residues are poorly suited to tight turns.
Glycine and proline
Correct: glycine's flexibility and proline's built-in kink suit tight turns.
questions.x: A β-turn reverses chain direction over about four residues, which requires unusual backbone angles. Glycine's tiny side chain allows those angles, and proline's ring imposes a fixed kink that fits turn geometry. Bulky residues like Leu or Trp clash in such tight conformations.

questions.q: What does a protein's tertiary structure describe?
o: The sequence of amino acids
That is primary structure.
Local helices and sheets only
That is secondary structure.
The overall three-dimensional fold of a single polypeptide
Correct: it is how the secondary elements pack together.
How two or more chains assemble
That is quaternary structure.
questions.x: Tertiary structure is the complete three-dimensional fold of one polypeptide, created by how its helices, sheets and loops pack together. It is stabilized mainly by side-chain interactions: the hydrophobic effect, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and disulfides. Assembly of separate chains is quaternary structure.

questions.q: Which protein has quaternary structure?
o: Myoglobin
Myoglobin is a single polypeptide chain.
Hemoglobin
Correct: it is an α₂β₂ tetramer of four polypeptide chains.
Ribonuclease A
RNase A is a single chain held by internal disulfides.
A 30-residue monomeric peptide
One chain cannot have quaternary structure.
questions.x: Quaternary structure exists only when a protein has two or more separate polypeptide chains. Hemoglobin is an α₂β₂ tetramer whose subunits interact, enabling cooperative O₂ binding. Myoglobin and RNase A are single chains, so their highest level is tertiary.

questions.q: What is the main driving force for a soluble protein to fold with nonpolar residues in its core?
o: Water gains entropy when nonpolar groups are buried
Correct: this is the hydrophobic effect, as ordered water around nonpolar surfaces is released.
Hydrogen bonds form between nonpolar side chains
Nonpolar side chains cannot form hydrogen bonds.
The polypeptide chain gains conformational entropy
Folding reduces the chain's own entropy.
Disulfide bonds form between all buried residues
Few residues are cysteines, and many proteins fold without disulfides.
questions.x: Water forms ordered cages around exposed nonpolar groups, which lowers its entropy. Burying nonpolar side chains in the core frees that water, increasing the solvent's entropy, and this hydrophobic effect is the main driving force for folding. The chain itself loses conformational entropy upon folding, so that cannot be the driver.

questions.q: Folded proteins are typically only about 20 to 60 kJ/mol more stable than the unfolded state, despite many favorable interactions. Why?
o: Folding has a positive ΔG that ATP hydrolysis overcomes
Most proteins fold spontaneously without ATP.
Noncovalent interactions contribute no energy
Each interaction is weak, but together they are large.
The chain's large loss of conformational entropy offsets most of those interactions
Correct: net stability is a small difference between large opposing terms.
Folded proteins are held only by covalent bonds
Folding relies mainly on noncovalent forces.
questions.x: Folding gains enthalpy from many weak interactions and entropy from released water, but the chain pays a large entropic cost by becoming fixed in one conformation. The net ΔG of folding is a small difference between large opposing terms, so proteins are only marginally stable. This marginal stability lets proteins be flexible and turned over.

questions.q: A small enzyme is unfolded with urea and a reducing agent. When both are removed slowly, it refolds and regains full activity. What does this show?
o: The amino acid sequence contains the information for the native fold
Correct: it refolds correctly with nothing but its sequence to guide it.
Chaperones are always needed for folding
No chaperones were present, yet the protein refolded.
Disulfide bonds determine the sequence
Sequence comes from the gene; disulfides form after folding.
Denaturation breaks peptide bonds
Recovery of activity shows the primary structure was intact.
questions.x: This is the logic of Anfinsen's classic RNase experiment: after complete denaturation and reduction, the enzyme refolded to its active form with only its sequence to guide it. So the information for the native fold is encoded in the primary structure. Chaperones help many proteins fold efficiently in cells but are not the source of that information.

questions.q: A denatured, reduced enzyme is reoxidized while still in 8 M urea, and then the urea is removed. Activity stays very low. Why?
o: Urea hydrolyzed peptide bonds during reoxidation
Urea disrupts noncovalent interactions but does not cleave peptide bonds.
Oxidation converted cysteine into methionine
Oxidizing cysteine thiols forms disulfides, not methionine.
The enzyme lost its primary structure
The sequence is unchanged; the problem is incorrect disulfide pairing.
Disulfides formed randomly in the unfolded chain, trapping non-native structures
Correct: oxidation before folding locks in mismatched cysteine pairs.
questions.x: If disulfides form while the chain is still unfolded in urea, cysteines pair randomly, and most of the possible pairings are wrong. Those incorrect covalent cross-links trap non-native structures that cannot reach the active fold even after urea is removed. The sequence is unchanged; the problem is the order of folding and oxidation.

questions.q: What do molecular chaperones mainly do?
o: Provide the structural information that specifies the native fold
The information for the fold is in the amino acid sequence.
Bind exposed hydrophobic regions to prevent misfolding and aggregation
Correct: they protect folding intermediates; the sequence still decides the final fold.
Form permanent covalent bonds with their client proteins
Chaperone binding is transient and noncovalent.
Catalyze peptide bond formation on the ribosome
That is done by the ribosome's peptidyl transferase.
questions.x: Chaperones such as Hsp70 and GroEL bind exposed hydrophobic surfaces on unfolded or partly folded chains. This prevents those surfaces from sticking to other proteins and aggregating, giving the chain more chances to fold correctly. They do not supply fold information; the sequence still specifies the native structure.

questions.q: How does a high concentration of urea denature proteins?
o: It hydrolyzes peptide bonds
Urea does not break covalent backbone bonds.
It disrupts hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions
Correct: it competes for hydrogen bonds and solvates nonpolar groups, leaving the primary structure intact.
It reduces disulfide bonds
Urea is not a reducing agent.
It permanently adds groups to side chains
Urea denaturation is usually reversible and noncovalent.
questions.x: Urea denatures by competing for hydrogen bonds and by making water a better solvent for nonpolar groups, which weakens the hydrophobic effect. These are noncovalent effects, so peptide bonds and disulfides survive and denaturation is usually reversible. Breaking disulfides requires a separate reducing agent.

questions.q: An enzyme solution is boiled for ten minutes. Which level of structure is most likely still intact?
o: Secondary
Backbone hydrogen bonds are disrupted by heat.
Tertiary
The native 3D fold is lost on boiling.
Quaternary
Subunit contacts are noncovalent and fall apart.
Primary
Correct: heat breaks noncovalent interactions but not peptide bonds.
questions.x: Heat adds enough energy to disrupt the noncovalent forces behind secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure. Peptide bonds are covalent and kinetically very stable, so boiling for minutes leaves the amino acid sequence intact. Denaturation destroys the shape, not the sequence.

questions.q: How do strongly acidic or basic conditions denature a protein?
o: They change side-chain ionization, disrupting salt bridges and hydrogen bonds
Correct: altered charges break the electrostatic interactions that hold the fold.
They break disulfide bonds by reduction
pH changes do not act as reducing agents.
They convert L-amino acids to D-amino acids instantly
Racemization is slow and is not how pH denatures proteins.
They remove water from the protein core
Changes in charge, not dehydration, drive acid or base denaturation.
questions.x: Extreme pH protonates or deprotonates ionizable side chains, changing their charges. That breaks salt bridges and hydrogen bonds and can create clusters of like charges that repel each other, unfolding the protein. pH changes are not reducing and do not break covalent backbone or disulfide bonds.

questions.q: In SDS-PAGE, what mainly determines how far a protein moves?
o: Its isoelectric point
pI is the basis of isoelectric focusing, not SDS-PAGE.
Its native three-dimensional shape
SDS unfolds proteins, removing differences in shape.
Its molecular mass
Correct: SDS denatures proteins and gives uniform charge per mass, so smaller chains move farther.
Its intrinsic net charge
SDS's negative charge swamps the protein's own charge.
questions.x: SDS unfolds proteins and binds in proportion to chain length, giving each a similar negative charge-to-mass ratio and a similar rod-like shape. Movement through the gel matrix then depends mainly on size, so smaller polypeptides travel farther. A protein's own charge and native shape no longer matter.

questions.q: Thermal unfolding shows a wild-type protein with a melting temperature (Tm) of 52 °C and a point mutant with Tm 44 °C. What is the best conclusion?
o: The mutation stabilizes the folded state
Stabilizing mutations raise the Tm.
The mutant has higher catalytic activity
Tm measures stability, not activity.
The mutant cannot fold at any temperature
It has a Tm, so it is folded below 44 °C.
The mutation destabilizes the folded state
Correct: a lower Tm means less heat is needed to unfold the protein.
questions.x: Tm is the temperature at which half the molecules are unfolded, so it reports thermodynamic stability. The mutant unfolds at 44 °C instead of 52 °C, meaning its folded state is less stable relative to the unfolded state. Tm says nothing directly about catalytic activity, and the mutant is clearly folded below its Tm.

questions.q: How do prions cause disease?
o: A small DNA genome encodes a toxic protein
Prions contain no nucleic acid.
Point mutations spread from cell to cell
Infectious prions copy a shape, not a sequence.
A misfolded, β-sheet-rich protein converts normally folded copies into the misfolded form
Correct: the misfolded conformation spreads without nucleic acid.
The prion protein is hydrolyzed into toxic peptides
Prions are notably resistant to breakdown.
questions.x: Prions are infectious proteins with no nucleic acid. The misfolded, β-sheet-rich form of the prion protein acts as a template that converts normally folded copies into the same misfolded shape, which aggregates into protease-resistant fibrils. What spreads is a conformation, not a sequence change.

questions.q: A region of a protein folds on its own into a compact unit and often has its own function. What is it called?
o: A subunit
A subunit is a separate polypeptide chain.
A domain
Correct: domains are independently folding parts of tertiary structure.
A primary sequence
Primary sequence describes the order of residues, not a folded unit.
A β-turn
A β-turn is a short reversal of chain direction, not a functional unit.
questions.x: A domain is a part of a single polypeptide that folds independently into a compact unit, often with its own function such as binding a ligand. Many proteins combine several domains. A subunit, in contrast, is a separate polypeptide chain in a quaternary assembly.

questions.q: Why are disulfide bonds much more common in secreted proteins than in cytosolic ones?
o: The cytosol is a reducing environment, while the ER lumen and extracellular space are oxidizing
Correct: reducing agents in the cytosol keep cysteines as thiols.
Cytosolic proteins contain no cysteine
Cytosolic proteins have cysteines, usually as free thiols.
Disulfides form only at low temperature
Temperature is not what controls disulfide formation.
Ribosomes in the cytosol cannot translate cysteine codons
All ribosomes translate cysteine codons.
questions.x: Disulfide formation is an oxidation, so it depends on the local redox environment. The cytosol is kept reducing by glutathione, which keeps cysteines as free thiols. Secretory proteins fold in the oxidizing ER lumen, where protein disulfide isomerase helps form disulfides that persist outside the cell.

questions.q: Adding 1 M NaCl most weakens which interaction in a folded protein?
o: Peptide bonds in the backbone
Covalent peptide bonds are not affected by salt.
Disulfide bonds
Disulfides are covalent and need a reducing agent to break.
Salt bridges between charged side chains
Correct: dissolved ions screen the attraction between opposite charges.
Hydrophobic packing in the core
Moderate salt tends to strengthen hydrophobic interactions, if anything.
questions.x: High concentrations of dissolved ions cluster around charged side chains, screening their electrostatic attraction. This weakens salt bridges between opposite charges. Covalent peptide and disulfide bonds are unaffected, and salt does not weaken, and may even strengthen, hydrophobic packing.

questions.q: What does a Ramachandran plot show?
o: Which combinations of φ and ψ backbone angles are sterically allowed
Correct: allowed regions match α-helix and β-sheet conformations.
How absorbance changes with wavelength
That is an absorption spectrum.
How reaction rate depends on substrate concentration
That is a Michaelis–Menten plot.
How net charge changes with pH
That is a titration curve.
questions.x: A Ramachandran plot graphs the backbone dihedral angles φ against ψ for each residue. Steric clashes make most combinations impossible, and the allowed regions correspond to α-helices and β-sheets. Glycine populates more of the plot because of its tiny side chain, and proline fewer.

questions.q: Adding high concentrations of ammonium sulfate makes a protein come out of solution. What is this called, and why does it happen?
o: Salting in; the salt shields charges and increases solubility
Salting in happens at low salt and increases solubility.
Denaturation; the salt breaks peptide bonds
Salting out is usually reversible and leaves the chain intact.
Reduction; sulfate breaks disulfide bonds
Sulfate is not a reducing agent.
Salting out; the salt ions take up water needed to solvate the protein
Correct: proteins then associate with each other and precipitate.
questions.x: At high concentrations, salts like ammonium sulfate bind so much water that too little is left to hydrate protein surfaces. The proteins then associate with each other and precipitate, which is salting out. It is usually reversible, so it is used to purify and concentrate proteins; salting in occurs at low salt.

questions.q: At what pH is a protein typically least soluble in water?
o: Two units below its pI
Here the protein is positively charged, and repulsion keeps it in solution.
At its isoelectric point
Correct: with no net charge, molecules do not repel each other and they aggregate.
Two units above its pI
Here net negative charge keeps molecules apart.
At pH 7 regardless of pI
Solubility depends on each protein's own pI.
questions.x: Proteins with a net charge repel one another and interact well with water, which keeps them in solution. At the pI the net charge is zero, so intermolecular repulsion is minimal and molecules aggregate and precipitate. Solubility is lowest at each protein's own pI, not at a fixed pH.

questions.q: In size-exclusion chromatography, which protein elutes first?
o: The smallest protein
Small proteins enter the pores and are delayed.
The largest protein
Correct: large proteins cannot enter the bead pores and take the shortest path.
The most positively charged protein
Size exclusion separates by size, not charge.
The protein with the lowest pI
pI matters in ion exchange, not size exclusion.
questions.x: Size-exclusion beads have pores that small molecules can enter, giving them a longer path through the column. Large proteins are excluded from the pores, travel only in the space between beads, and elute first. Charge and pI matter for ion exchange, not this method.

questions.q: How does native PAGE differ from SDS-PAGE in what it separates by?
o: Native PAGE separates by mass alone
Separation by mass alone needs SDS to remove charge and shape effects.
Native PAGE separates only by pI
That is isoelectric focusing.
Native PAGE always denatures the proteins
Native PAGE is designed to keep proteins folded.
Native PAGE separates by size, charge and shape
Correct: without SDS, proteins keep their own charge and folded shape.
questions.x: In SDS-PAGE, the detergent unfolds proteins and swamps their charge, so separation depends mainly on mass. Native PAGE omits SDS, so proteins keep their own charge and folded shape, and mobility depends on size, charge and shape together. This preserves activity and subunit interactions.

questions.q: A cation-exchange column has negatively charged beads. At pH 7, which protein binds most strongly?
o: A protein with pI 9.5
Correct: below its pI it is positively charged and sticks to the negative beads.
A protein with pI 4.5
It is negatively charged at pH 7 and is repelled.
A protein with pI 7.0
It is about neutral at pH 7 and binds weakly.
A protein with pI 5.5
It is negatively charged at pH 7 and passes through.
questions.x: A protein is positively charged when the buffer pH is below its pI. At pH 7, the protein with pI 9.5 is clearly positive and binds the negatively charged cation-exchange beads. Proteins with pI below 7 are negative and are repelled, and one with pI 7.0 is nearly neutral.

questions.q: Gel filtration gives a native mass of 150 kDa. SDS-PAGE shows one 50 kDa band whether or not reducing agent is added. What is the protein's structure?
o: A disulfide-linked trimer
Disulfide-linked subunits would stay together without reducing agent.
A 150 kDa monomer
A monomer would run near 150 kDa on SDS-PAGE.
A noncovalent trimer of 50 kDa subunits
Correct: 150 ÷ 50 = 3, and SDS alone separates the subunits, so they are not disulfide-linked.
A noncovalent dimer of 75 kDa subunits
Subunits of 75 kDa would run as a 75 kDa band, not 50 kDa, on SDS-PAGE.
questions.x: Gel filtration keeps proteins native, so it reports the mass of the whole assembly, while SDS-PAGE reports individual chains. The 150 kDa assembly made of 50 kDa chains must contain three subunits. Because the chains separate even without reducing agent, they are held together only by noncovalent forces, not disulfides.

questions.q: A protein is heated in 8 M urea with no reducing agent. Which bonds remain intact?
o: Hydrogen bonds only
Hydrogen bonds are the first to be lost.
Salt bridges and disulfide bonds
Salt bridges are noncovalent and are disrupted.
Hydrophobic interactions and peptide bonds
Urea and heat disrupt hydrophobic packing.
Peptide bonds and disulfide bonds
Correct: both are covalent; heat and urea disrupt only noncovalent forces.
questions.x: Heat and urea disrupt only noncovalent forces: hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and hydrophobic interactions. Peptide bonds and disulfide bonds are covalent, so they remain until hydrolysis or a reducing agent breaks them. This is why denaturing conditions plus a reducing agent are needed to fully unfold disulfide-containing proteins.

questions.q: An α-helix has leucines spaced every 3 to 4 residues and charged residues elsewhere. What is this helix likely to be?
o: Fully hydrophobic, able to span a membrane
Charged residues around most of the helix rule out a transmembrane helix.
Unable to form a helix
Leucine and charged residues are both compatible with helices.
Amphipathic, with one hydrophobic face
Correct: residues spaced by 3 to 4 line up along one side of a 3.6-residue helix.
A β-strand
The repeat spacing fits a helix; β-strands alternate every 2 residues.
questions.x: With about 3.6 residues per turn, residues spaced 3 to 4 apart line up along one face of an α-helix. Leucines at that spacing form a hydrophobic stripe while the charged residues occupy the other faces, making the helix amphipathic. Such helices often lie on membrane surfaces or pair with other helices, as in leucine zippers.

questions.q: Silk fibroin is built from repeating Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala segments arranged in β-sheets. Why does this sequence suit tightly stacked sheets?
o: Glycine and alanine form disulfide cross-links
Neither residue contains sulfur.
Small side chains let neighboring sheets pack closely together
Correct: H and CH₃ side chains fit tightly between stacked sheets.
Their charged side chains form salt bridges between sheets
Glycine and alanine side chains are uncharged.
These residues force the chain into an α-helix
The stated structure is a β-sheet, and small residues pack well in sheets.
questions.x: In a β-sheet, side chains of each strand alternate above and below the sheet. In fibroin, glycine (H) points to one face and alanine (CH₃) to the other, so both faces are very flat. This lets sheets stack tightly against each other, giving silk strength without disulfides or charged cross-links.

questions.q: How does ethanol denature proteins?
o: It solvates nonpolar side chains, weakening the hydrophobic effect
Correct: a less polar solvent reduces the drive to bury the hydrophobic core.
It hydrolyzes peptide bonds
Ethanol does not cleave the backbone.
It oxidizes cysteines to form extra disulfides
Ethanol is not an oxidizing agent here.
It removes all metal cofactors by chelation
Ethanol is not a chelator.
questions.x: Ethanol is less polar than water, so it can solvate nonpolar side chains. That reduces the energetic advantage of burying them in the core, weakening the hydrophobic effect and letting the protein unfold. Ethanol does not hydrolyze, oxidize or chelate under these conditions.

questions.q: Heavy metal ions such as Hg²⁺ and Pb²⁺ inactivate many proteins. What is the main mechanism?
o: They hydrolyze peptide bonds
Metal ions at these levels do not cut the backbone.
They convert lysine into arginine
Metals cannot change one amino acid into another.
They bind cysteine thiols and disrupt structure
Correct: soft metals bind sulfur tightly and distort the fold.
They raise the pH above 12
Metal salts do not create strongly basic conditions.
questions.x: Heavy metal ions like Hg²⁺ and Pb²⁺ are soft acids that bind strongly to soft sulfur atoms in cysteine thiols. This can block active sites, disrupt disulfides or metal-binding sites, and distort the native fold. They do not hydrolyze peptide bonds or interconvert amino acids.

questions.q: Cooked egg white stays solid after cooling and does not return to a clear liquid. Why?
o: Unfolded proteins aggregate through exposed hydrophobic regions
Correct: tangled aggregates cannot refold, so the change is irreversible.
Cooking hydrolyzes the proteins into free amino acids
Free amino acids would dissolve; peptide bonds survive cooking.
Heat converts the proteins into carbohydrates
Heat does not convert proteins into carbohydrates.
The proteins form new peptide bonds with each other
Heat does not create new peptide bonds between proteins.
questions.x: Heating egg white unfolds its proteins, exposing hydrophobic regions that are normally buried. These sticky surfaces bind other unfolded chains, forming a tangled aggregate network. On cooling, the chains are trapped and cannot refold, so this denaturation is irreversible even though the peptide bonds are intact.

questions.q: How do cells mark misfolded cytosolic proteins for destruction?
o: They phosphorylate them for export out of the cell
Phosphorylation is a regulatory signal, not a disposal tag.
They add mannose-6-phosphate to send them to mitochondria
Mannose-6-phosphate targets proteins to lysosomes, and it is added in the Golgi.
They glycosylate them in the cytosol
Glycosylation mainly occurs in the ER and Golgi.
They attach polyubiquitin chains for degradation by the proteasome
Correct: the ubiquitin–proteasome system removes faulty proteins.
questions.x: Misfolded cytosolic proteins are tagged by ubiquitin ligases with a chain of ubiquitin molecules linked through lysines. The polyubiquitin chain is recognized by the 26S proteasome, which unfolds the protein and cleaves it into short peptides. Mannose-6-phosphate is a Golgi tag that sends enzymes to lysosomes, not a cytosolic disposal signal.

questions.q: About how many residues make up one turn of an α-helix?
o: Two residues per repeat is typical of an extended β-strand.
Correct: the α-helix rises about 0.54 nm per 3.6-residue turn.
Close, but the i → i+4 hydrogen bond pattern gives 3.6 residues per turn.
That is about the number of base pairs per turn of B-DNA.
questions.x: The α-helix has about 3.6 residues per turn and rises about 0.15 nm per residue, giving a pitch of about 0.54 nm. Although hydrogen bonds link residue n to n + 4, that does not mean exactly four residues per turn. Ten units per turn is the value for B-DNA base pairs.

questions.q: How do the hydrogen bonds in a β-sheet differ from those in an α-helix?
o: They form between side chains rather than backbone groups
Both structures use backbone C=O and N–H hydrogen bonds.
They form between strands that may be far apart in sequence
Correct: sheet hydrogen bonds link separate strands, not nearby residues in one coil.
They are covalent bonds
Hydrogen bonds are noncovalent in both structures.
They form only between residues four apart
The i → i+4 pattern is the α-helix.
questions.x: Both α-helices and β-sheets use backbone C=O to N–H hydrogen bonds. In a helix those bonds link residues 4 apart in one continuous coil, while in a sheet they link adjacent strands, which may be far apart in sequence or even on different chains. That is why sheets can connect distant parts of a protein.

questions.q: A protein is rich in lysine and arginine and has few acidic residues. What is its pI most likely to be?
o: Well below 7
Acidic residues lower the pI; basic residues raise it.
Well above 7
Correct: many basic groups need a high pH before the net charge reaches zero.
Exactly 7
pI depends on composition and is not fixed at 7.
Impossible to estimate from composition
Composition gives a good estimate of pI.
questions.x: The pI is the pH where positive and negative charges balance. Lys and Arg side chains stay protonated up to high pH, so a protein rich in them stays positive until the pH is quite basic. Its pI is therefore well above 7, while proteins rich in Asp and Glu have low pI values.

questions.q: What is the net charge of a protein in a buffer whose pH is below the protein's pI?
o: Negative
Net negative charge occurs at pH above the pI.
Zero
Net zero charge occurs only at pH equal to the pI.
It depends only on the protein's mass
Charge depends on pH relative to pI, not mass.
Positive
Correct: pH below pI means excess protonation, so net positive.
questions.x: When pH is below a protein's pI, there are more protons available than needed for neutrality, so more groups are protonated and the protein is net positive. At pH equal to pI it is net zero, and above its pI it is net negative. This rule governs electrophoresis and ion-exchange behavior.

questions.q: What composition is typical of intrinsically disordered protein regions, which lack a stable fold?
o: High in charged and polar residues, low in bulky hydrophobic residues
Correct: without a hydrophobic core there is little drive to collapse and fold.
High in leucine, isoleucine and phenylalanine
Such residues usually drive formation of a folded core.
Many cysteines forming disulfides
Disulfides tend to stabilize folded structure.
Composed entirely of glycine
Disordered regions have mixed compositions, not pure glycine.
questions.x: Folding is driven largely by burying hydrophobic side chains. Intrinsically disordered regions have few bulky hydrophobic residues and many charged and polar ones, so there is little drive to collapse into a stable core, and like charges repel. Many become ordered only when they bind a partner.

questions.q: Why do cells make more heat shock proteins after a rise in temperature?
o: Heat shock proteins generate heat to restore body temperature
They help proteins fold; they do not produce heat.
Heat converts other proteins into heat shock proteins
Heat shock proteins are made from their own genes.
More proteins partly unfold and need chaperones to refold or avoid aggregation
Correct: heat shock proteins are chaperones that respond to unfolding stress.
They break down all heat-damaged DNA
Heat shock proteins act on proteins, not DNA.
questions.x: Heat partly unfolds proteins, exposing hydrophobic surfaces that can aggregate. Cells respond by inducing heat shock proteins, many of which are chaperones such as Hsp70 that bind unfolded chains, help them refold and prevent aggregation. They are made from their own genes and act on proteins, not DNA.

questions.q: Wild-type and mutant proteins are unfolded with urea. The midpoints of unfolding are 4.0 M urea for wild type and 2.0 M for the mutant. What does this show?
o: The mutant's folded state is more stable
A more stable protein needs more urea to unfold.
The mutant binds urea covalently
Urea acts through noncovalent effects.
The mutant has twice as many residues
Unfolding midpoints reflect stability, not chain length.
The mutant's folded state is less stable
Correct: less denaturant is needed to unfold half of the mutant molecules.
questions.x: The denaturant midpoint is the urea concentration at which half of the molecules are unfolded. A protein that unfolds at 2.0 M urea needs less denaturant than one that unfolds at 4.0 M, so its folded state is less stable. Midpoints reflect stability, not size or covalent urea binding.

questions.q: Which process changes a protein's primary structure?
o: Heat denaturation
Heat leaves peptide bonds intact.
Treatment with 6 M urea
Urea disrupts only noncovalent structure.
Proteolytic cleavage of a precursor
Correct: cutting peptide bonds changes the covalent sequence.
Shifting the pH from 7 to 3
Protonation changes charge, not sequence.
questions.x: Primary structure is the covalent amino acid sequence, so only processes that make or break peptide bonds alter it. Proteolytic cleavage, as when a zymogen or preprohormone is processed, cuts the chain and changes the sequence. Heat, urea and pH changes alter only noncovalent structure and charge.

questions.q: Many DNA-binding transcription factors contain a helix-turn-helix. What kind of structural element is it?
o: A primary sequence that is always identical
Motifs are defined by structure, and their sequences vary.
A supersecondary motif in which one helix fits into the DNA major groove
Correct: two helices joined by a turn form a recurring DNA-binding motif.
A quaternary arrangement of four subunits
It is formed within a single chain.
A covalent link between protein and DNA
Binding is noncovalent.
questions.x: A supersecondary structure, or motif, is a recurring arrangement of a few secondary elements. In the helix-turn-helix, two α-helices are joined by a short turn, and one, the recognition helix, inserts into the DNA major groove to read bases. It occurs within one chain and binds DNA noncovalently.

questions.q: What stabilizes the fold of a classic zinc-finger domain?
o: Zn²⁺ held by cysteine and histidine side chains
Correct: the metal ion holds a small fold together that has too little hydrophobic core on its own.
Zn²⁺ forming peptide bonds
Metal ions do not form peptide bonds.
A disulfide between two zinc atoms
Disulfides form between sulfur atoms of cysteines, not between metals.
Hydrophobic packing alone, with zinc acting only as a catalyst
Zinc here plays a structural role, not a catalytic one.
questions.x: Classic zinc fingers are too small to have a substantial hydrophobic core. A Zn²⁺ ion coordinated by two cysteines and two histidines acts as a structural cross-link that holds the small ββα fold together. Here zinc is structural rather than catalytic, and disulfides form only between cysteine sulfurs.

questions.q: How can phosphorylating a serine change a protein's conformation?
o: It changes serine's α-carbon configuration
Phosphorylation does not alter stereochemistry.
It breaks the peptide bond next to the serine
The backbone stays intact.
It adds a bulky negative charge that forms new electrostatic interactions
Correct: the phosphate's −2 charge can rearrange nearby contacts.
It adds a positive charge that attracts carboxylates
Phosphate groups are negatively charged.
questions.x: Phosphorylation adds a bulky phosphate group that carries about −2 charge at physiological pH. This new charge can form salt bridges with nearby Lys or Arg, repel nearby negative groups, or create binding sites, shifting the protein's conformation. The backbone and stereochemistry are unchanged.

questions.q: Which engineered change is most likely to raise a protein's thermal stability?
o: Adding a disulfide bond between two residues that are close in the native fold
Correct: a covalent cross-link lowers the entropy of the unfolded state and stabilizes the fold.
Replacing a buried leucine with aspartate
Burying a charge in the core is destabilizing.
Placing several glycines in the middle of an α-helix
Glycine's flexibility weakens helices.
Removing a surface salt bridge by mutating both residues to alanine
Losing a stabilizing interaction lowers stability.
questions.x: A disulfide between residues that are close in the native fold covalently links them, so the unfolded chain loses conformational freedom. Reducing the entropy of the unfolded state makes unfolding less favorable and raises thermal stability. Burying a charge, adding helix-breaking glycines or removing a salt bridge all destabilize a protein.

questions.q: Which residue binds the heme iron on its proximal side in myoglobin and hemoglobin?
o: Cysteine
Cysteine binds heme in cytochrome P450, not in globins.
Lysine
Lysine is not the proximal ligand in globins.
Glutamate
Glutamate is not the iron ligand in globins.
Histidine
Correct: an imidazole nitrogen binds Fe²⁺, the fifth coordination site.
questions.x: In myoglobin and hemoglobin, the heme iron (Fe²⁺) is bound by four porphyrin nitrogens plus the imidazole nitrogen of the proximal histidine, its fifth ligand. O₂ binds at the sixth site on the opposite face, near the distal histidine. Cysteine is the iron ligand in cytochrome P450, not in globins.

questions.q: Collagen has glycine at every third position (Gly-X-Y). Why is glycine needed there?
o: Glycine forms disulfide bonds between the three chains
Glycine has no sulfur.
Only glycine is small enough to fit in the crowded center of the triple helix
Correct: every third residue faces the helix axis, where only an H side chain fits.
Glycine's charged side chain forms salt bridges
Glycine's side chain is an uncharged H atom.
Glycine is the residue that becomes hydroxylated
Hydroxylation occurs on proline and lysine.
questions.x: Collagen's three chains wind into a tight triple helix in which every third residue faces the crowded central axis. Only glycine, with H as its side chain, is small enough to fit there, so substituting any other residue at those positions disrupts the helix, as in some forms of osteogenesis imperfecta. Hydroxylation affects proline and lysine, not glycine.

questions.q: Why does vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) weaken connective tissue?
o: Vitamin C is a structural residue within collagen chains
Vitamin C is a cofactor for an enzyme, not a building block of the protein.
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need ascorbate, so collagen triple helices are less stable
Correct: too little hydroxyproline weakens the helix and its cross-links.
Vitamin C is needed to form peptide bonds in collagen
Peptide bonds are made by ribosomes without vitamin C.
Vitamin C directly cross-links collagen fibrils
Fibril cross-linking is done by lysyl oxidase, not by ascorbate.
questions.x: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need ascorbate to keep their active-site iron reduced. Without vitamin C, collagen has too little hydroxyproline to hydrogen-bond and stabilize the triple helix, and too little hydroxylysine for normal cross-linking. The result is weak connective tissue, bleeding gums and poor wound healing.

questions.q: A permanent wave treatment for hair first reduces and then reoxidizes which bonds in α-keratin?
o: Peptide bonds
Reducing agents do not cut peptide bonds.
Hydrogen bonds only
Water alone can reset hydrogen bonds; perms work on covalent cross-links.
Glycosidic bonds
Keratin is a protein; glycosidic bonds join sugars.
Disulfide bonds
Correct: breaking and re-forming S–S bonds while the hair is curled fixes a new shape.
questions.x: α-Keratin in hair is rich in cysteine, and disulfide bonds between chains lock in its shape. A perm reduces these S–S bonds to SH groups, the hair is set around curlers, and an oxidizer forms new disulfides in the new positions.
