Hydrogen bonds reset with water alone, which is why a wet set is only temporary.

questions.q: Microfilaments of the cytoskeleton are polymers of which protein?
o: Actin
Correct: G-actin polymerizes into F-actin microfilaments.
Tubulin
Tubulin builds microtubules.
Keratin
Keratin forms intermediate filaments.
Collagen
Collagen is an extracellular fibrous protein.
questions.x: The three cytoskeletal filament types are built from different proteins: microfilaments from actin, microtubules from tubulin, and intermediate filaments from proteins such as keratin, vimentin and lamins. G-actin monomers bind ATP and polymerize into polar F-actin filaments. Collagen is outside the cell in the extracellular matrix.

questions.q: Microtubules are built from α/β-tubulin heterodimers. Which nucleotide do these dimers bind to support polymerization?
o: ATP
Actin, not tubulin, binds ATP.
cAMP
cAMP is a second messenger, not a cytoskeletal nucleotide.
GTP
Correct: GTP-bound tubulin adds to growing microtubules, and hydrolysis to GDP promotes disassembly.
NADH
NADH is an electron carrier.
questions.x: Tubulin dimers bind GTP, and GTP-tubulin adds to the plus end of microtubules. After incorporation, β-tubulin hydrolyzes GTP to GDP, which weakens the lattice; losing the GTP cap triggers rapid shrinkage, called dynamic instability. Actin, in contrast, uses ATP.

questions.q: Which motor protein carries cargo from axon terminals back toward the neuron cell body?
o: Kinesin
Most kinesins move toward the plus end, outward to the terminal.
Myosin II
Myosin II moves on actin and drives muscle contraction.
Tubulin
Tubulin is the track, not the motor.
Dynein
Correct: dynein walks toward the microtubule minus end, which faces the cell body.
questions.note: Kinesin goes out (+ end); dynein comes back (− end).
questions.x: Microtubules in axons are oriented with their plus ends toward the terminal and minus ends toward the cell body. Kinesins generally walk toward the plus end (anterograde transport), while cytoplasmic dynein walks toward the minus end (retrograde transport). So returning cargo to the soma requires dynein.

questions.q: In the cross-bridge cycle, what happens when ATP binds the myosin head?
o: Myosin performs the power stroke
The power stroke follows release of Pi, not ATP binding.
Troponin releases Ca²⁺
Ca²⁺ binding to troponin is set by sarcoplasmic reticulum release, not myosin.
Myosin detaches from actin
Correct: without ATP, heads stay locked to actin, which causes rigor mortis.
Actin depolymerizes
Thin filaments stay intact during contraction.
questions.x: In the cross-bridge cycle, a myosin head bound to actin stays attached until ATP binds, which lowers its actin affinity and releases it. Hydrolysis then re-cocks the head, and Pi release drives the power stroke. Without ATP after death, heads stay locked to actin, which causes rigor mortis.

questions.q: Which step in the myosin cycle is most closely linked to the power stroke?
o: Binding of ATP to the head
ATP binding causes detachment, not force.
Release of Pi after the head binds actin
Correct: Pi release triggers the conformational change that pulls the thin filament.
Hydrolysis of ATP while detached
Hydrolysis re-cocks the head into its high-energy position before binding.
Release of Ca²⁺ from troponin
That leads to relaxation, not the power stroke.
questions.x: The cycle is: ATP binding releases myosin from actin, ATP hydrolysis cocks the head, the head binds actin, and Pi release triggers the power stroke, followed by ADP release. Hydrolysis stores energy in the cocked head but does not itself move the filament. The force-generating step is coupled to Pi release after binding.

questions.q: Why is hemoglobin's O₂-binding curve sigmoidal while myoglobin's is hyperbolic?
o: Hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively among its four subunits
Correct: binding at one heme raises the affinity of the others.
Hemoglobin has a higher O₂ affinity at all pressures
Myoglobin actually has higher affinity.
Myoglobin contains no heme
Myoglobin has one heme group.
Hemoglobin binds O₂ covalently
O₂ binds iron reversibly in both proteins.
questions.x: Hemoglobin's four subunits interact: O₂ binding to one heme shifts the tetramer from the low-affinity T state toward the high-affinity R state, raising the affinity of the remaining sites. This positive cooperativity gives a sigmoidal curve. Single-chain myoglobin has one heme and no cooperativity, so its curve is hyperbolic.

questions.q: Which change in actively contracting muscle helps hemoglobin release more O₂?
o: A fall in temperature
Cooling raises O₂ affinity.
A fall in CO₂
Less CO₂ raises affinity, shifting the curve left.
A fall in pH
Correct: the Bohr effect; H⁺ stabilizes the low-affinity T state.
A fall in 2,3-BPG
Less 2,3-BPG raises affinity.
questions.x: Active muscle produces CO₂, H⁺ and heat. A lower pH (Bohr effect) protonates groups that stabilize hemoglobin's T state, lowering O₂ affinity and shifting the curve right, so more O₂ is unloaded. Falls in temperature, CO₂ or 2,3-BPG would do the opposite and increase affinity.

questions.q: Why does fetal hemoglobin (α₂γ₂) have a higher O₂ affinity than adult hemoglobin?
o: It binds 2,3-BPG less tightly
Correct: weaker binding of this allosteric inhibitor leaves HbF in the high-affinity state more often.
It contains twice as many hemes
Both are tetramers with four hemes.
It binds O₂ covalently
Binding is reversible in both.
It lacks cooperativity
HbF is still cooperative.
questions.x: 2,3-BPG binds the central cavity of deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the low-affinity T state. Fetal γ chains have fewer positive charges in that pocket than adult β chains, so HbF binds 2,3-BPG weakly and has higher O₂ affinity. This lets the fetus pull O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta.

questions.q: A mutant hemoglobin has a P50 of 12 mmHg, compared with 26 mmHg for normal hemoglobin. What does this mean?
o: It binds O₂ more weakly
Weaker binding would raise the P50.
It carries twice as much O₂ per molecule
P50 describes affinity, not capacity.
It has lost all cooperativity
P50 alone does not show the curve's shape.
It binds O₂ more tightly and unloads less in tissues
Correct: a lower P50 means half-saturation at lower pressure, a left shift.
questions.x: P50 is the O₂ partial pressure at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated. A lower P50 means half saturation is reached at lower pressure, so the curve is shifted left and affinity is higher. High affinity helps loading but means less O₂ is released at tissue pressures.

questions.q: A binding protein has a measured Hill coefficient of 1.0. What does this indicate?
o: Positive cooperativity
Positive cooperativity gives n > 1.
No cooperativity between binding sites
Correct: n = 1 gives a hyperbolic curve like myoglobin's.
Negative cooperativity
Negative cooperativity gives n < 1.
Exactly one binding site per molecule
n measures cooperativity, not the number of sites.
questions.x: The Hill coefficient n measures cooperativity in ligand binding. n = 1 means binding at one site does not affect the others, giving a hyperbolic curve; n > 1 indicates positive cooperativity, as in hemoglobin (n ≈ 2.8), and n < 1 negative. It is not a count of binding sites.

questions.q: Carbon monoxide occupies some hemes in hemoglobin. Why does it cut O₂ delivery more than the loss of those sites alone would?
o: CO oxidizes all iron to Fe³⁺
CO binds Fe²⁺; it does not cause methemoglobin.
The remaining hemes gain O₂ affinity and release less O₂ in tissues
Correct: CO pushes Hb toward the R state, shifting the curve left.
CO breaks hemoglobin into monomers
Hb stays tetrameric.
CO lowers O₂ affinity at the remaining hemes
Lower affinity would increase unloading, not reduce it.
questions.x: CO binds heme iron about 200 times more tightly than O₂, removing those sites from O₂ transport. CO-bound hemes also push hemoglobin toward the high-affinity R state, so the remaining hemes hold their O₂ more tightly and the curve shifts left. Less O₂ is released in tissues than the lost capacity alone would predict.

questions.q: Which parts of an antibody form its antigen-binding site?
o: The constant region of the heavy chains only
The Fc region interacts with immune cells and complement, not antigen.
The disulfide hinge region
The hinge gives flexibility; it does not bind antigen.
The light chain constant region only
Constant regions do not change to match each antigen.
The variable regions of the heavy and light chains
Correct: hypervariable loops at the tips of the arms fit the epitope.
questions.x: An antibody is made of two heavy and two light chains. The N-terminal variable domains of one heavy and one light chain together form each antigen-binding site, with hypervariable loops (CDRs) shaped to match a particular epitope. The constant (Fc) region does not bind antigen; it engages immune cells and complement.

questions.q: Antibodies coat a bacterium so that macrophages engulf it more readily. What is this process called?
o: Opsonization
Correct: phagocytes recognize the Fc regions of bound antibody.
Neutralization
Neutralization blocks a pathogen or toxin from binding host cells.
Agglutination
Agglutination is the clumping of antigens by antibodies.
Class switching
Class switching changes the antibody isotype made by B cells.
questions.x: Opsonization is the coating of a pathogen with antibodies or complement so that phagocytes, which have Fc receptors, recognize and engulf it more efficiently. Neutralization blocks a toxin or virus from binding host cells, and agglutination clumps antigens together. All use antigen binding, but only opsonization relies on Fc recognition by phagocytes.

questions.q: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor opens a cation pore when acetylcholine binds. What kind of protein is it?
o: A voltage-gated ion channel
Voltage-gated channels open in response to membrane potential.
A G protein-coupled receptor
Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are GPCRs; nicotinic receptors are channels.
A ligand-gated ion channel
Correct: binding a ligand directly opens the channel.
A receptor tyrosine kinase
Kinase receptors phosphorylate proteins and do not form pores.
questions.x: Ligand-gated ion channels open their pore directly when a chemical binds. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a pentamer whose pore opens to Na⁺ and K⁺ when acetylcholine binds, depolarizing the cell. Muscarinic receptors bind the same ligand but are GPCRs that act through G proteins.

questions.q: Which cell adhesion molecules need Ca²⁺ to bind identical molecules on neighboring cells?
o: Integrins
Integrins bind mainly extracellular matrix proteins.
Selectins
Selectins bind carbohydrates on other cells.
Aquaporins
Aquaporins are water channels, not adhesion molecules.
Cadherins
Correct: cadherins are Ca²⁺-dependent and bind like to like.
questions.x: Cadherins mediate homophilic adhesion: a cadherin on one cell binds the same type of cadherin on the neighboring cell, and Ca²⁺ ions rigidify their extracellular domains. They form adherens junctions and desmosomes. Integrins bind matrix proteins and selectins bind carbohydrates.

questions.q: Which transmembrane proteins link extracellular matrix proteins such as fibronectin to the actin cytoskeleton?
o: Cadherins
Cadherins mediate cell-to-cell adhesion.
Selectins
Selectins mediate transient binding to carbohydrates.
Integrins
Correct: they connect the matrix to cytoskeleton and can signal in both directions.
Connexins
Connexins form gap junction channels.
questions.x: Integrins are heterodimeric transmembrane receptors whose extracellular domains bind matrix proteins such as fibronectin and laminin, while their cytoplasmic tails link through adaptor proteins to actin. They signal in both directions, communicating matrix contact into the cell and vice versa. Cadherins link cell to cell, not cell to matrix.

questions.q: Leukocytes roll along blood vessel walls before leaving the blood. Which adhesion molecules bind carbohydrate ligands to make this rolling possible?
o: Cadherins
Cadherins join similar cells in tissues by binding each other.
Selectins
Correct: selectins are lectins that bind specific carbohydrate groups.
Integrins
Integrins mediate the later firm arrest, not carbohydrate-based rolling.
Collagens
Collagen is a structural matrix protein, not an adhesion receptor on cells.
questions.x: Selectins are lectins: they bind specific carbohydrate groups on glycoproteins. Endothelial selectins form weak, rapidly broken bonds with leukocyte sugars, which slows the cells into a rolling motion. Firm arrest and migration out of the vessel then depend on integrins.

questions.q: What happens when a growth factor binds a receptor tyrosine kinase?
o: The receptors dimerize and phosphorylate each other's tyrosines
Correct: the phosphotyrosines then recruit signaling proteins.
A heterotrimeric G protein swaps GDP for GTP
That is how GPCRs signal.
A pore opens to let Na⁺ into the cell
That describes a ligand-gated channel.
The receptor enters the nucleus to act as a transcription factor
That is typical of steroid hormone receptors.
questions.x: Receptor tyrosine kinases are activated when ligand binding brings two receptors together. Their cytoplasmic kinase domains then phosphorylate tyrosines on each other (autophosphorylation), and the phosphotyrosines serve as docking sites for signaling proteins such as Grb2, which leads to Ras. GDP/GTP exchange on a heterotrimeric G protein is the GPCR mechanism.

questions.q: How does an activated G protein-coupled receptor turn on its G protein?
o: It phosphorylates the G protein on tyrosine
GPCRs act as exchange factors, not kinases.
It hydrolyzes the G protein's GTP
Gα's own GTPase activity turns the signal off.
It promotes exchange of GDP for GTP on the Gα subunit
Correct: GTP-bound Gα separates from Gβγ and acts on effectors.
It cleaves the G protein into active fragments
Activation is not proteolytic.
questions.x: A ligand-bound GPCR acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor: it causes Gα to release GDP and bind GTP. GTP-bound Gα dissociates from Gβγ, and both can regulate effector enzymes or channels. The signal ends when Gα's own GTPase activity hydrolyzes GTP back to GDP.

questions.q: Activating a Gq-coupled receptor leads directly to which events?
o: Phospholipase C activation, producing IP₃ and DAG and releasing Ca²⁺
Correct: IP₃ releases ER Ca²⁺ and DAG activates PKC.
Adenylyl cyclase activation, raising cAMP
That is the Gs pathway.
Adenylyl cyclase inhibition, lowering cAMP
That is the Gi pathway.
Opening of a ligand-gated Na⁺ channel
Gq signals through enzymes, not by opening a channel directly.
questions.x: Gq activates phospholipase C, which cleaves PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ opens ER channels to release Ca²⁺, and DAG with Ca²⁺ activates protein kinase C. Gs and Gi instead raise or lower cAMP by stimulating or inhibiting adenylyl cyclase.

questions.q: Cholera toxin modifies Gαs so that it can no longer hydrolyze GTP. What happens in intestinal cells?
o: cAMP falls because adenylyl cyclase is inhibited
Gαs stimulates adenylyl cyclase; it does not inhibit it.
IP₃ stays high because phospholipase C stays on
Phospholipase C is the Gq effector, not the Gs effector.
The receptor can no longer bind its ligand
The toxin acts on the G protein, not on ligand binding.
cAMP stays high because adenylyl cyclase stays on
Correct: Gαs stuck in the GTP form keeps signaling.
questions.x: Gαs turns itself off by hydrolyzing its bound GTP. Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gαs, blocking this GTPase activity, so Gαs stays in its active GTP-bound form and adenylyl cyclase keeps making cAMP. High cAMP opens CFTR chloride channels, and water follows, causing severe watery diarrhea.

questions.q: What motor drives the bending of cilia and flagella in eukaryotic cells?
o: Myosin pulling on actin filaments
Actomyosin is not the axoneme motor.
Dynein sliding neighboring microtubule doublets past each other
Correct: dynein arms on the axoneme convert sliding into bending.
A rotary motor powered by a proton gradient
That describes bacterial flagella.
Kinesin walking toward the minus end
Most kinesins walk toward the plus end and do not drive axoneme bending.
questions.x: Eukaryotic cilia and flagella have a 9+2 axoneme of microtubule doublets. Dynein arms on one doublet walk along the next, but because the doublets are linked, the sliding becomes bending. Bacterial flagella are entirely different: rotary motors powered by a proton gradient.

questions.q: Which plasma protein is most responsible for oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure and also carries fatty acids and many drugs?
o: Hemoglobin
Hemoglobin stays inside red blood cells.
Albumin
Correct: it is the most abundant plasma protein and a general carrier.
Fibrinogen
Fibrinogen is a clotting factor at much lower concentration.
Immunoglobulin G
IgG functions in immunity, not as the main driver of oncotic pressure.
questions.x: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and, because capillary walls largely retain it, it creates most of the plasma oncotic pressure that draws fluid back into capillaries. It also binds and transports fatty acids, bilirubin, calcium and many drugs. Low albumin can therefore cause edema.

questions.q: How does calmodulin pass a rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺ on to target enzymes?
o: Calmodulin pumps Ca²⁺ out of the cell
Ca²⁺ pumps are separate ATPases.
Calmodulin phosphorylates its targets directly
Calmodulin activates kinases but is not itself a kinase.
Calmodulin hydrolyzes GTP to time the signal
That describes G proteins.
Ca²⁺ binding changes calmodulin's shape so it binds and activates target proteins
Correct: Ca²⁺-calmodulin acts as a switchable regulatory protein.
questions.x: Calmodulin has four Ca²⁺-binding EF-hand sites. When cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises, Ca²⁺ binding changes calmodulin's shape, exposing hydrophobic surfaces that wrap around target proteins such as CaM kinases and activate them. Calmodulin itself is not an enzyme; it is a Ca²⁺-sensing regulatory protein.

questions.q: How do enzymes speed up reactions?
o: They lower the activation energy by stabilizing the transition state
Correct: a lower barrier means more molecules react per second.
They make ΔG of the reaction more negative
Enzymes do not change the overall free energy change.
They raise the temperature of the solution
Enzymes work without changing temperature.
They shift the equilibrium toward products
Enzymes reach the same equilibrium faster.
questions.x: Enzymes bind and stabilize the transition state more tightly than the substrate, lowering the activation energy. With a lower barrier, more molecules have enough energy to react per second, so the rate rises. ΔG and the equilibrium constant are unchanged; enzymes affect only kinetics.

questions.q: An enzyme is added to a reaction mixture that is already at equilibrium. What happens?
o: More product forms
That would require Keq to change, which catalysts cannot do.
More reactant forms
Catalysts favor neither side.
The equilibrium concentrations do not change
Correct: catalysts speed forward and reverse reactions equally, so Keq is unchanged.
The reaction stops
Reactions keep running in both directions at equilibrium.
questions.x: At equilibrium, forward and reverse rates are equal. An enzyme lowers the activation barrier for both directions equally, so both rates increase by the same factor and remain equal. Equilibrium concentrations depend on ΔG°, which catalysts do not change.

questions.q: A stable compound is made to resemble an enzyme reaction's transition state. Compared with the substrate, how does it bind?
o: More weakly
Active sites are shaped to fit the transition state, not to fit it poorly.
With the same affinity
Enzymes bind the transition state more strongly than the substrate.
Only at an allosteric site
Transition-state analogs bind the active site.
More tightly
Correct: active sites bind the transition state most strongly, so transition-state analogs make potent inhibitors.
questions.x: An enzyme's active site is complementary to the transition state, so it binds the transition state much more tightly than the substrate. A stable molecule that mimics the transition state therefore binds more tightly than the substrate, often making a potent competitive inhibitor. This principle is used in drug design and in making catalytic antibodies.

questions.q: Crystal structures show an enzyme's active site changing shape when substrate binds. Which model does this support?
o: Lock and key
Lock and key assumes a rigid active site that already matches the substrate.
Concerted model
The concerted model describes how allosteric subunits switch together.
Induced fit
Correct: substrate binding causes a conformational change that improves the fit.
Fluid mosaic model
The fluid mosaic model describes membranes, not enzymes.
questions.x: The induced-fit model says that substrate binding causes a conformational change in the enzyme that brings catalytic groups into proper alignment. Observing an active site changing shape on binding supports this model. The lock-and-key model assumes a rigid site that already matches the substrate.

questions.q: Which enzyme class joins two molecules using energy from ATP hydrolysis?
o: Lyases
Lyases break or form bonds without ATP or water.
Ligases
Correct: ligases form bonds coupled to ATP hydrolysis, such as DNA ligase.
Hydrolases
Hydrolases split bonds with water.
Isomerases
Isomerases rearrange atoms within a molecule.
questions.x: Ligases join two molecules with a new covalent bond and couple this to hydrolysis of ATP or another nucleoside triphosphate; DNA ligase is an example. Lyases can also form or break bonds, but without ATP, hydrolysis or oxidation. Hydrolases use water to split bonds, and isomerases rearrange a single molecule.

questions.q: Hexokinase moves a phosphate from ATP to glucose. Which enzyme class does it belong to?
o: Transferases
Correct: kinases transfer a functional group (phosphate) between molecules.
Ligases
Using ATP does not make a kinase a ligase; no two molecules are joined.
Hydrolases
Water is not used to break a bond.
Oxidoreductases
No electrons are transferred.
questions.note: Trap: kinases are transferases even though they use ATP.
questions.x: Kinases are transferases: they move a phosphate group from ATP to a second molecule. Hexokinase transfers phosphate to glucose, forming glucose-6-phosphate and ADP. Although ATP is used, no two molecules are joined into one product, so it is not a ligase.

questions.q: Aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into two trioses without using water or a redox step. Which enzyme class does it belong to?
o: Hydrolases
Hydrolases need water to split bonds.
Oxidoreductases
No electrons move between substrates.
Lyases
Correct: lyases break bonds without hydrolysis or oxidation.
Ligases
Ligases join molecules; they do not split them.
questions.x: Lyases cleave bonds by mechanisms other than hydrolysis or oxidation, often forming a double bond or a new ring, and can work in reverse. Aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate without water or a redox step. Hydrolases always use water.

questions.q: Lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactate while oxidizing NADH to NAD⁺. Which enzyme class does it belong to?
o: Oxidoreductases
Correct: dehydrogenases transfer electrons (as hydride) between substrates.
Transferases
No functional group such as phosphate or amino is moved to a second substrate.
Isomerases
Pyruvate and lactate are not isomers; lactate has two more hydrogens.
Lyases
No bond is broken to form a double bond or ring.
questions.x: Oxidoreductases transfer electrons, and dehydrogenases do so as hydride ions to or from NAD⁺ or FAD. Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate's ketone to lactate's alcohol while oxidizing NADH to NAD⁺. Because pyruvate and lactate differ by two hydrogens, they are not isomers.

questions.q: Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ are inorganic ions that many enzymes need for activity. What are they called?
o: Coenzymes
Coenzymes are organic molecules, often derived from vitamins.
Substrates
Substrates are converted into products; these ions are not.
Zymogens
Zymogens are inactive enzyme precursors.
Cofactors
Correct: cofactors include metal ions; organic cofactors are called coenzymes.
questions.x: A cofactor is any non-protein helper an enzyme needs for activity. Inorganic ions like Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ are cofactors, while organic cofactors, often vitamin-derived, are called coenzymes. Cofactors are not consumed like substrates.

questions.q: The coenzyme NAD⁺ is made from which vitamin?
o: Riboflavin (B₂)
Riboflavin is used to make FAD and FMN.
Niacin (B₃)
Correct: niacin provides the nicotinamide ring of NAD⁺.
Thiamine (B₁)
Thiamine is used to make thiamine pyrophosphate.
Ascorbate (C)
Vitamin C is a reductant for hydroxylases, not part of NAD⁺.
questions.x: Many coenzymes are built from B vitamins. Niacin (B₃) supplies the nicotinamide ring of NAD⁺ and NADP⁺, riboflavin (B₂) makes FAD and FMN, and thiamine (B₁) makes thiamine pyrophosphate. Severe niacin deficiency causes pellagra.

questions.q: What is a cofactor called when it is tightly or covalently bound and stays with the enzyme throughout catalysis?
o: A cosubstrate
Cosubstrates such as NAD⁺ bind loosely and leave after each cycle.
A prosthetic group
Correct: examples include heme in cytochromes and covalently bound FAD.
An apoenzyme
An apoenzyme is an enzyme that lacks its cofactor.
An allosteric effector
Allosteric effectors regulate activity; they are not required groups.
questions.x: Coenzymes can be prosthetic groups or cosubstrates. A prosthetic group is bound tightly or covalently and stays with the enzyme through the catalytic cycle, like heme in cytochromes or FAD in succinate dehydrogenase. A cosubstrate such as NAD⁺ binds, is changed, and leaves each cycle.

questions.q: What is an enzyme called when it lacks a required cofactor and is therefore inactive?
o: A holoenzyme
A holoenzyme has its cofactor and is active.
A ribozyme
A ribozyme is a catalytic RNA.
An isozyme
Isozymes are different forms of an enzyme that catalyze the same reaction.
An apoenzyme
Correct: apoenzyme plus cofactor gives the active holoenzyme.
questions.x: An enzyme protein lacking its required cofactor is an apoenzyme and is inactive. When the cofactor binds, the complete active enzyme is called a holoenzyme. Isozymes are different proteins catalyzing the same reaction, and ribozymes are catalytic RNA.

questions.q: Thiamine deficiency impairs pyruvate dehydrogenase. Which coenzyme is missing?
o: Thiamine pyrophosphate
Correct: TPP, made from vitamin B₁, is required for decarboxylating pyruvate.
Biotin
Biotin is used by carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase.
Pyridoxal phosphate
PLP, from B₆, is used by transaminases.
Tetrahydrofolate
THF carries one-carbon units.
questions.x: Thiamine (B₁) is converted to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the coenzyme for decarboxylating α-keto acids. Pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase both need TPP, so B₁ deficiency impairs aerobic glucose metabolism and causes beriberi or Wernicke encephalopathy. Biotin serves carboxylases and PLP serves transaminases.

questions.q: What does histidine do in a serine protease catalytic triad (Ser-His-Asp)?
o: It forms a covalent acyl-enzyme bond with the substrate
Serine forms the acyl-enzyme bond.
It binds the substrate's side chain in the specificity pocket
Specificity comes from the S1 pocket, not the triad's histidine.
It acts as a general base, taking the proton from serine's hydroxyl
Correct: this makes serine a strong nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl.
It reduces a disulfide in the substrate
Proteases hydrolyze peptide bonds; they do not reduce disulfides.
questions.x: In the serine protease catalytic triad, aspartate orients and stabilizes histidine, and histidine acts as a general base that removes the proton from serine's hydroxyl. The activated serine alkoxide attacks the peptide carbonyl and forms the covalent acyl-enzyme intermediate. Substrate specificity comes from the separate S1 pocket.

questions.q: In carbonic anhydrase, a Zn²⁺ ion binds a water molecule. How does this help catalysis?
o: It reduces CO₂ to formate
The reaction is hydration, not reduction.
It forms a covalent bond to bicarbonate permanently
The product is released each cycle.
It changes the reaction's equilibrium constant
Catalysts never change Keq.
It lowers the water's pKa, giving a zinc-bound hydroxide that attacks CO₂
Correct: this is metal ion catalysis; the Lewis acid makes a strong nucleophile.
questions.x: Zn²⁺ is a Lewis acid. Binding water to Zn²⁺ lowers its pKa from about 15.7 to about 7, so at physiological pH much of it exists as zinc-bound hydroxide. That hydroxide is a strong nucleophile that attacks CO₂ to form bicarbonate, which is then released.

questions.q: An enzyme holds two substrates next to each other in the correct orientation. Why does this speed the reaction?
o: It makes the overall reaction more exergonic
ΔG of the reaction does not change.
It provides heat to the substrates
Enzymes do not supply thermal energy.
It reduces the entropy cost of bringing reactants together
Correct: this proximity and orientation effect raises the effective concentration.
It permanently fuses the two substrates to the enzyme
Products are released, and the enzyme is unchanged at the end.
questions.x: For two molecules to react they must meet in the correct orientation, which is unlikely in solution and carries an entropy cost. By binding both substrates side by side and aligned, an enzyme greatly raises their effective concentration. This proximity and orientation effect lowers the activation barrier without changing ΔG.

questions.q: Chymotrypsin cleaves after large aromatic residues such as phenylalanine. What explains this specificity?
o: Its catalytic triad uses a different nucleophile than trypsin
Trypsin and chymotrypsin share the same Ser-His-Asp triad.
A deep hydrophobic S1 pocket that fits aromatic side chains
Correct: the binding pocket's shape and polarity select the residue.
Phenylalanine's side chain is positively charged
Phenylalanine is nonpolar and uncharged.
It recognizes the substrate's disulfide bonds
Specificity depends on the residue beside the cleaved bond, not on disulfides.
questions.x: Serine proteases share the same Ser-His-Asp triad but differ in their S1 specificity pocket. Chymotrypsin's pocket is deep and hydrophobic, fitting large aromatic or bulky nonpolar side chains like Phe, Tyr and Trp. Trypsin's pocket has an Asp at the bottom that attracts positively charged Lys or Arg.

questions.q: An enzyme works in the lumen of the stomach. Near which pH is its activity most likely highest?
o: Correct: stomach enzymes such as pepsin are adapted to the acidic gastric pH.
7.4 is the pH of blood, not the stomach.
Pancreatic enzymes in the small intestine work near pH 8.
No digestive compartment is this basic.
questions.x: Enzymes have pH optima matched to where they act, because pH affects the ionization of active-site residues and the protein's fold. Pepsin works in gastric juice near pH 2, whereas pancreatic enzymes in the small intestine work near pH 8. Blood is about pH 7.4.

questions.q: An enzyme's activity rises with temperature up to a point and then drops sharply. Why?
o: Molecular motion first speeds catalysis, then heat denatures the enzyme
Correct: the peak is where faster kinetics are balanced against loss of structure.
Substrate molecules break down at high temperature
The sharp drop reflects the enzyme unfolding.
The reaction's ΔG reverses sign at high temperature
Changes in ΔG do not explain a loss of catalytic activity.
Enzymes need cold to bind substrate
Binding is not the reason activity rises at moderate temperatures.
questions.x: Raising temperature increases molecular motion and the fraction of molecules that can cross the activation barrier, so the rate rises. Beyond the optimum, thermal energy disrupts the noncovalent interactions that hold the enzyme's fold, and activity falls sharply as the enzyme denatures. The drop reflects loss of enzyme structure.

questions.q: An enzyme's activity is bell-shaped versus pH, falling below pH 6 and above pH 9. What most likely causes the drop below pH 6?
o: Deprotonation of a lysine that must be positive
Lysine deprotonates near pH 10, which fits the high-pH edge, not the low one.
Breaking of peptide bonds by acid
Mild acid does not hydrolyze the backbone.
Protonation of an active-site histidine that must be neutral to act as a base
Correct: histidine's pKa ≈ 6 matches the low-pH edge.
Loss of the enzyme's primary structure
pH 6 does not change the sequence.
questions.x: A bell-shaped pH profile often reflects two ionizable groups, each needed in a specific protonation state. The low-pH edge near 6 matches histidine's pKa: below pH 6 the imidazole is mostly protonated and cannot act as a general base. A lysine deprotonating near pH 10 would instead explain the high-pH edge.

questions.q: The active site residues of an enzyme are often far apart in its amino acid sequence. How do they come together?
o: Folding into tertiary structure brings them close
Correct: the active site is formed by the 3D fold.
Peptide bonds form between them after translation
Peptide bonds link only neighboring residues in the backbone.
The substrate pulls them together covalently
Substrate binding does not create covalent links between residues.
They are joined by disulfide bonds in every enzyme
Many enzymes have no disulfides.
questions.x: An active site is formed by the three-dimensional fold, not by sequence adjacency. Folding into tertiary structure brings residues that are far apart in the sequence close together in space, as in chymotrypsin's triad (His57, Asp102, Ser195). This is why denaturation destroys activity.

questions.q: An enzyme speeds up the forward reaction of A ⇌ B by 10⁶-fold. What happens to the rate of the reverse reaction?
o: It does not change
An unchanged reverse rate would shift the equilibrium.
It decreases 10⁶-fold
Catalysts never slow one direction.
It increases only once B accumulates
Rate enhancement applies whenever the enzyme is present.
It also increases 10⁶-fold
Correct: lowering the barrier affects both directions equally, so Keq is unchanged.
questions.x: A catalyst lowers the energy of the transition state, which is shared by the forward and reverse reactions. Both activation barriers fall by the same amount, so both rates increase by the same factor. The ratio of forward to reverse rate constants, Keq, therefore stays the same.

questions.q: Peptide bond formation in the ribosome is catalyzed by ribosomal RNA. What does this show?
o: All enzymes are made of RNA
Most enzymes are proteins.
Some biological catalysts are RNA molecules (ribozymes)
Correct: the peptidyl transferase center is made of rRNA.
Ribosomal proteins are not needed for translation
They help with structure and assembly, but the catalysis is done by RNA.
RNA catalysts change a reaction's equilibrium
No catalyst, RNA or protein, changes the equilibrium.
questions.x: In the ribosome, the peptidyl transferase center, which forms peptide bonds, is made of rRNA, so the ribosome is a ribozyme. This shows that biological catalysts need not be proteins. Like all catalysts, ribozymes speed reactions without changing their equilibrium.

questions.q: In Michaelis–Menten kinetics, how is Km defined experimentally?
o: The maximum rate the enzyme can reach
That is Vmax.
The substrate concentration at which v = Vmax/2
Correct: setting [S] = Km in the equation gives half of Vmax.
The number of substrate molecules converted per second per active site
That is kcat, the turnover number.
The substrate concentration at which v = Vmax
v only approaches Vmax as [S] keeps rising and never exactly reaches it.
questions.x: Km is defined operationally as the substrate concentration that gives half the maximal rate: substituting [S] = Km into v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) gives v = Vmax/2. Vmax is only approached asymptotically, so no finite [S] gives v = Vmax. Km has concentration units, unlike kcat, which is a rate constant.

questions.q: An enzyme has Km = 2 mM and Vmax = 100 μmol/min. What is the initial rate at [S] = 6 mM?
o: 33 μmol/min
This computes Vmax × Km/[S] instead of Vmax × [S]/(Km + [S]).
50 μmol/min
50 is the rate at [S] = Km = 2 mM.
75 μmol/min
300 μmol/min
v can never exceed Vmax.
questions.x: Use v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). With [S] = 6 mM = 3 Km, v = 100 × 6/8 = 75 μmol/min, three-quarters of Vmax. A handy check is that v must lie between Vmax/2 (at [S] = Km) and Vmax, which rules out 33 and 300.

questions.q: What substrate concentration is needed for an enzyme to reach 90% of Vmax?
o: At [S] = 0.9 Km, v is only about 47% of Vmax.
9 × Km
Correct: 0.9 = [S]/(Km + [S]) gives [S] = 9 Km.
10 × Km
At 10 Km, v ≈ 91% of Vmax, slightly more than asked.
90 × Km
At 90 Km, v ≈ 99% of Vmax.
questions.x: Set v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]) = 0.9. Then [S] = 0.9 Km + 0.9[S], so 0.1[S] = 0.9 Km and [S] = 9 Km. Saturation is approached slowly: 9 Km gives 90%, and even 90 Km gives only about 99%, which is why Vmax is estimated rather than measured directly.

questions.q: At a substrate concentration of one-third of Km, what fraction of Vmax does an enzyme reach?
o: This ignores the Km term in the denominator.
Half of Vmax requires [S] = Km.
0.75 Vmax requires [S] = 3 Km.
questions.x: Write [S] as a multiple of Km: v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]). With [S] = Km/3, this is (1/3)/(1 + 1/3) = 1/4. Forgetting the [S] term in the denominator gives 1/3, which is only approximately right when [S] is far below Km.

questions.q: When [S] is far above Km, what is the order of the enzyme reaction with respect to substrate?
o: First order
First-order behavior happens when [S] is far below Km.
Second order
Michaelis–Menten kinetics is never second order in substrate.
Negative first order
Adding substrate does not slow an enzyme that follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics.
Zero order
Correct: the enzyme is saturated, so v ≈ Vmax regardless of [S].
questions.x: When [S] ≫ Km, the denominator Km + [S] ≈ [S], so v ≈ Vmax. Nearly every active site is occupied, and adding substrate no longer raises the rate, so the reaction is zero order in substrate. It remains first order in enzyme, since more enzyme raises Vmax.

questions.q: When [S] is far below Km, the Michaelis–Menten equation reduces to which form?
o: v ≈ (Vmax/Km)[S]
Correct: Km + [S] ≈ Km, so the rate is proportional to [S].
v ≈ Vmax
That is the high-[S] limit.
v ≈ Vmax/2
That holds only when [S] = Km.
v ≈ Km/[S]
Rate cannot rise as substrate falls.
questions.x: When [S] ≪ Km, Km + [S] ≈ Km, and the equation becomes v ≈ (Vmax/Km)[S], so the rate is first order in substrate. Most active sites are empty, so doubling substrate doubles the rate. Expressed per enzyme, this slope is kcat/Km, the catalytic efficiency.

questions.q: An enzyme solution with 2 × 10⁻⁸ M active sites gives Vmax = 2 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. What is kcat?
o: 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹
This inverts the division.
4 × 10⁻¹² s⁻¹
This multiplies the values instead of dividing.
10⁴ s⁻¹
Correct: kcat = Vmax/[E]T = (2 × 10⁻⁴)/(2 × 10⁻⁸).
10¹² s⁻¹
This mishandles the exponents; −4 − (−8) = +4.
questions.x: kcat = Vmax/[E]T, the number of substrate molecules each active site converts per second at saturation. Here (2 × 10⁻⁴ M/s)/(2 × 10⁻⁸ M) = 10⁴ s⁻¹. When dividing powers of ten, subtract exponents: −4 − (−8) = +4.

questions.q: Which enzyme has the highest catalytic efficiency?
o: kcat = 100 s⁻¹, Km = 10⁻⁵ M
kcat/Km = 10⁷ M⁻¹s⁻¹.
kcat = 1000 s⁻¹, Km = 10⁻³ M
kcat/Km = 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹; a high kcat alone is not efficiency.
kcat = 10⁴ s⁻¹, Km = 10⁻² M
kcat/Km = 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹; the high Km offsets the fast turnover.
kcat = 10 s⁻¹, Km = 10⁻⁷ M
Correct: kcat/Km = 10⁸ M⁻¹s⁻¹, the highest of the four.
questions.note: Efficiency is kcat/Km, not kcat alone.
questions.x: Catalytic efficiency is kcat/Km, the rate constant for free enzyme plus substrate at low [S]. Dividing gives 10⁷, 10⁶, 10⁶ and 10⁸ M⁻¹s⁻¹, so the enzyme with kcat = 10 s⁻¹ and Km = 10⁻⁷ M wins. A large kcat alone is misleading if the enzyme binds substrate poorly (high Km).

questions.q: Enzyme X has Km = 0.1 mM and enzyme Y has Km = 10 mM for the same substrate. At [S] = 5 mM, about what fraction of its Vmax does enzyme Y reach?
o: Half of Vmax would require [S] = 10 mM.
This uses Km/(Km + [S]) instead of [S]/(Km + [S]).
98% is enzyme X's fraction: 5/5.1.
questions.x: The fraction of Vmax is [S]/(Km + [S]). For enzyme Y, 5/(10 + 5) = 1/3 ≈ 33%, while enzyme X with its low Km is about 98% saturated at the same [S]. A low Km means an enzyme reaches near-saturation at much lower substrate concentrations.

questions.q: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v vs 1/[S]), what does the x-intercept equal?
o: 1/Vmax
1/Vmax is the y-intercept.
Km/Vmax
Km/Vmax is the slope.
−1/Km
Correct: setting 1/v = 0 gives 1/[S] = −1/Km.
−Vmax
Vmax is never read directly from the x-axis.
questions.x: The Lineweaver–Burk equation is 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. The y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the slope is Km/Vmax. Setting 1/v = 0 gives the x-intercept 1/[S] = −1/Km.

questions.q: A Lineweaver–Burk plot has a y-intercept of 0.02 min/μM and an x-intercept of −0.25 μM⁻¹. What are Vmax and Km?
o: Vmax = 0.02 μM/min, Km = 0.25 μM
The intercepts are reciprocals and must be inverted.
Vmax = 50 μM/min, Km = 4 μM
Correct: Vmax = 1/0.02 and Km = 1/0.25.
Vmax = 50 μM/min, Km = 0.25 μM
Km must be inverted too: −1/Km = −0.25.
Vmax = 4 μM/min, Km = 50 μM
This swaps the two intercepts.
questions.x: On a double-reciprocal plot, the y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is −1/Km. So Vmax = 1/0.02 = 50 μM/min and Km = 1/0.25 = 4 μM. The common mistake is reading the intercepts as Vmax and Km themselves instead of inverting them.

questions.q: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, lines with and without an inhibitor cross on the x-axis. Which type of inhibition is this?
o: Pure noncompetitive
Correct: Km is unchanged (same x-intercept) while 1/Vmax rises.
Competitive
Competitive lines cross on the y-axis.
Uncompetitive
Uncompetitive lines are parallel.
Mixed, binding E more tightly than ES
Mixed inhibition lines cross to the left of the y-axis but not on the x-axis.
questions.x: Lines on a Lineweaver–Burk plot share an x-intercept when Km is unchanged, since that intercept is −1/Km. A higher y-intercept with the same x-intercept means Vmax fell while Km stayed the same, the signature of pure noncompetitive inhibition. Competitive inhibition instead shares the y-intercept, and uncompetitive gives parallel lines.

questions.q: Why does a pure noncompetitive inhibitor lower Vmax but leave Km unchanged?
o: It binds the active site and blocks substrate
That is competitive inhibition, which raises Km.
It binds only the ES complex
Binding only ES is uncompetitive inhibition, which lowers Km.
It binds free enzyme and the ES complex with equal affinity
Correct: equal binding removes active enzyme without changing apparent substrate affinity.
It permanently destroys substrate
Inhibitors act on the enzyme, not on substrate.
questions.x: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor binds an allosteric site on both E and ES with the same affinity. Because it does not favor either form, it does not change how readily substrate binds, so apparent Km is unchanged. But inhibitor-bound enzyme cannot turn over, so effectively less active enzyme is present and Vmax falls.

questions.q: An inhibitor binds only to the enzyme–substrate complex. How do the apparent Km and Vmax change?
o: Both decrease
Correct: this is uncompetitive inhibition; pulling ES away lowers both by the same factor.
Km increases; Vmax unchanged
That pattern is competitive inhibition.
Km unchanged; Vmax decreases
That pattern is pure noncompetitive inhibition.
Km increases; Vmax decreases
That pattern is mixed inhibition favoring free enzyme.
questions.x: An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only ES, forming an inactive ESI complex. Removing ES lowers Vmax, and by Le Châtelier pulling more E + S into ES, which increases the apparent affinity and lowers Km by the same factor. On a Lineweaver–Burk plot this gives parallel lines.

questions.q: A mixed inhibitor binds free enzyme much more tightly than the ES complex. How does it change the kinetic parameters?
o: Km decreases and Vmax decreases
That happens when the mixed inhibitor favors ES.
Km increases and Vmax is unchanged
An unchanged Vmax is the purely competitive case, where the inhibitor cannot bind ES.
Km and Vmax are both unchanged
An inhibitor that binds both E and ES must change Vmax.
Km increases and Vmax decreases
Correct: favoring free E lowers apparent affinity, and binding to ES as well lowers Vmax.
questions.x: A mixed inhibitor binds both E and ES. Because it can bind ES, it always lowers Vmax. The direction of the Km change depends on preference: favoring free enzyme competes with substrate and raises Km, while favoring ES lowers Km. Only binding exclusively to free E, the competitive case, leaves Vmax unchanged.

questions.q: Methanol poisoning can be treated with ethanol, which is a substrate of the same alcohol dehydrogenase. Why does this work?
o: Ethanol irreversibly destroys the enzyme
Ethanol is a substrate, not a covalent inactivator.
Ethanol competes for the active site and slows the formation of toxic methanol products
Correct: a high level of a competing substrate acts as a competitive inhibitor.
Ethanol converts methanol back into harmless glucose
No such reaction occurs.
Ethanol binds an allosteric site and raises Vmax
Raising Vmax would make poisoning worse.
questions.x: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts methanol into formaldehyde, which is then oxidized to toxic formic acid. Ethanol is a better substrate for the same active site, so at high levels it outcompetes methanol, slowing toxic product formation while methanol is excreted unchanged. This is competitive substrate inhibition; fomepizole works the same way.

questions.q: An irreversible inhibitor permanently inactivates half of the enzyme molecules in a sample. How do the kinetic parameters of the sample change?
o: Km doubles and Vmax is unchanged
That is the pattern of competitive inhibition.
Vmax is halved and Km is unchanged
Correct: fewer working enzymes means lower Vmax, but the remaining ones bind substrate normally.
Both Km and Vmax are halved
That is the uncompetitive pattern.
Neither parameter changes
Removing active enzyme must lower Vmax.
questions.x: An irreversible inhibitor removes enzyme molecules from action, which is like lowering [E]T. Since Vmax = kcat[E]T, Vmax falls by half. The surviving enzymes are unaltered, so they bind substrate normally and Km stays the same, mimicking noncompetitive kinetics.

questions.q: Rates (μM/s) without and with inhibitor: [S] = 1 μM: 33 vs 17; [S] = 10 μM: 83 vs 67; [S] = 100 μM: 98 vs 95. What type of inhibition is this?
o: Pure noncompetitive
Noncompetitive inhibition would lower the rate by the same fraction even at high [S].
Uncompetitive
Uncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax and is not overcome by high [S].
Irreversible
Losing active enzyme would lower the rate at high [S] too.
Competitive
Correct: the inhibitor matters at low [S] but is overcome at high [S], so Vmax is unchanged.
questions.x: Compare the inhibitor's effect at low versus high [S]. At 1 μM the rate is halved, but at 100 μM it is nearly normal (95 vs 98), so excess substrate overcomes the inhibitor and Vmax is unchanged. That is competitive inhibition; noncompetitive or irreversible inhibition would still lower the rate at saturating [S].

questions.q: With an inhibitor present, an enzyme's apparent Km rises from 2 to 5 μM and its Vmax falls from 100 to 60 μM/s. What type of inhibition is this?
o: Mixed
Correct: both parameters change, with Km rising, so the inhibitor favors free enzyme.
Competitive
Competitive inhibition does not change Vmax.
Uncompetitive
Uncompetitive inhibition lowers Km.
Pure noncompetitive
Pure noncompetitive inhibition leaves Km unchanged.
questions.x: Each inhibition type has a fingerprint: competitive raises Km with Vmax unchanged, uncompetitive lowers both, and pure noncompetitive lowers Vmax with Km unchanged. Here Km rises (2→5 μM) and Vmax falls (100→60 μM/s), which only mixed inhibition can do. Rising Km shows the inhibitor binds free enzyme more tightly than ES.

questions.q: An enzyme has Km = 3 μM. A competitive inhibitor is added at a concentration equal to 2 Ki. What is the apparent Km?
o: 1 μM
Dividing by the factor gives the wrong direction; affinity appears lower.
3 μM
Competitive inhibitors do raise the apparent Km.
6 μM
This uses a factor of 2 instead of 1 + 2 = 3.
9 μM
Correct: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki) = 3 × (1 + 2) = 9.
questions.x: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km by the factor α = 1 + [I]/Ki. With [I] = 2Ki, α = 3, so Km,app = 3 × 3 = 9 μM, while Vmax is unchanged. Using only [I]/Ki = 2 as the factor forgets the 1, which represents the uninhibited enzyme.

questions.q: How does a plot of v versus [S] for an allosteric enzyme with cooperative subunits differ from a Michaelis–Menten plot?
o: It is a straight line through the origin
A linear plot would mean the enzyme never saturates.
It decreases as [S] increases
Activity still rises with substrate.
It is sigmoidal instead of hyperbolic
Correct: cooperative binding gives an S-shaped curve.
It is identical to the hyperbolic plot
Cooperativity changes the curve's shape.
questions.x: Cooperative allosteric enzymes have multiple subunits whose substrate binding affects one another. At low [S] activity rises slowly, then increases steeply as binding shifts subunits to the high-affinity state, and finally plateaus, giving a sigmoidal curve. Michaelis–Menten enzymes with independent sites give a hyperbola.

questions.q: What does an allosteric activator do to a cooperative enzyme?
o: It binds the active site and is converted into product
Allosteric activators bind elsewhere and are not converted.
It shifts the equilibrium toward T, moving the curve right
That is what an allosteric inhibitor does.
It changes the reaction's ΔG
Regulators alter rates, not thermodynamics.
It shifts the T ⇌ R equilibrium toward R, moving the v vs [S] curve left
Correct: the high-affinity R state is favored, so less substrate is needed.
questions.x: Allosteric enzymes switch between a low-activity T state and a high-activity R state. An activator binds a regulatory site and stabilizes R, so less substrate is needed for a given rate, shifting the sigmoidal curve left (lower apparent K0.5). An inhibitor stabilizes T and shifts the curve right; neither changes ΔG.

questions.q: The final product of a biosynthetic pathway inhibits the enzyme for the pathway's first committed step. What is this called?
o: Feedforward activation
Feedforward activation is when an early metabolite activates a later enzyme.
Zymogen activation
That is activation of a precursor by cleavage.
Feedback inhibition
Correct: the product signals that enough has been made.
Substrate-level phosphorylation
That is a way of making ATP, not a regulatory mechanism.
questions.x: In feedback inhibition, the end product of a pathway binds an allosteric site on the enzyme catalyzing the first committed step and reduces its activity. When enough product accumulates, the pathway slows, avoiding waste of intermediates and energy. Feedforward activation runs the other direction, from an early metabolite to a later enzyme.

questions.q: In the concerted (MWC) model of allostery, how do the subunits change state?
o: Each subunit changes state one at a time as it binds ligand
That is the sequential (KNF) model.
All subunits switch between T and R together, so mixed states do not exist
Correct: symmetry is preserved; binding shifts the whole-molecule equilibrium.
Subunits never change conformation
Both models involve conformational change.
Only the catalytic subunit changes, never the regulatory subunit
The concerted model does not separate subunits this way.
questions.x: The concerted (MWC) model holds that all subunits of an allosteric protein are in the same state at once, either all T or all R. Ligand binding shifts the equilibrium between these two symmetric forms. In contrast, the sequential (KNF) model lets subunits change one by one, allowing mixed states.

questions.q: When a substrate binding to one active site increases binding at other active sites of the same enzyme, what is this effect called?
o: A homotropic allosteric effect
Correct: the effector is the substrate itself.
A heterotropic allosteric effect
Heterotropic effectors are molecules other than the substrate.
Competitive inhibition
Here binding at one site helps binding at others; it does not block it.
Covalent modification
No covalent bond is formed or broken.
questions.x: A homotropic allosteric effect is one in which the regulating molecule is the same as the substrate or ligand. Substrate binding at one active site enhances binding at others, which is positive cooperativity, like O₂ binding to hemoglobin. Heterotropic effectors are different molecules, such as 2,3-BPG for hemoglobin.

questions.q: Why does the pancreas secrete its proteases as inactive zymogens?
o: Because zymogens digest proteins faster
Zymogens are inactive until cleaved.
To keep them from being denatured by stomach acid
Pancreatic secretions go to the duodenum, not the stomach.
To prevent the proteases from digesting the pancreas itself
Correct: activation happens only once they reach the small intestine.
Because the proteases need a coenzyme only found in the gut
Activation is by cleavage, not by adding a coenzyme.
questions.x: Pancreatic proteases like trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase would digest the pancreas's own proteins if active there. They are therefore made as zymogens (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen and so on) and activated by proteolytic cleavage only in the small intestine. Premature activation within the pancreas causes pancreatitis.

questions.q: Enteropeptidase in the duodenum activates trypsinogen. Why does this one step activate many digestive proteases?
o: Trypsin cleaves and activates the other pancreatic zymogens
Correct: trypsin activation sets off a cascade.
Enteropeptidase activates each zymogen separately
Enteropeptidase specifically activates trypsinogen.
Trypsin acts as an allosteric activator of the other proteases
Activation occurs by cleaving peptide bonds, not by allostery.
The zymogens activate themselves in acidic conditions
That describes pepsinogen in the stomach, not the pancreatic zymogens.
questions.x: Enteropeptidase, made by the duodenal mucosa, cleaves trypsinogen to active trypsin. Trypsin then cleaves the other pancreatic zymogens, including chymotrypsinogen, proelastase and more trypsinogen, setting off a cascade. A single localized trigger therefore activates the whole digestive enzyme set where it is needed.

questions.q: Which form of enzyme regulation is irreversible?
o: Phosphorylation by a kinase
Phosphatases can remove the phosphate.
Binding of an allosteric inhibitor
Allosteric effectors bind noncovalently and come off.
Competitive inhibition by a substrate analog
Reversible inhibitors can be displaced.
Proteolytic activation of a zymogen
Correct: a cleaved peptide bond cannot be re-formed to inactivate the enzyme.
questions.x: Zymogen activation cuts peptide bonds, and the cell has no mechanism for rejoining them, so the active enzyme must be inhibited or degraded to stop its activity. Phosphorylation is reversed by phosphatases, and allosteric and competitive inhibitors bind noncovalently and dissociate. Irreversible activation suits one-way processes like digestion and blood clotting.

questions.q: Two isozymes catalyze the same reaction in different tissues. How do they usually differ?
o: In the reaction they catalyze
By definition, isozymes catalyze the same reaction.
In amino acid sequence and kinetic or regulatory properties
Correct: isozymes are distinct proteins tuned to each tissue's needs.
In the equilibrium constant they produce
No enzyme changes Keq.
In nothing; they are identical molecules
Identical molecules would not be called isozymes.
questions.x: Isozymes catalyze the same reaction but are encoded by different genes or splice variants, so they differ in sequence. These differences tune Km, Vmax and regulation to each tissue; for example, liver glucokinase has a much higher Km for glucose than muscle hexokinase. Like all enzymes, they cannot change Keq.

questions.q: Which assumption is central to the steady-state derivation of the Michaelis–Menten equation?
o: Enzyme concentration greatly exceeds substrate concentration
The usual assumption is the opposite: [S] ≫ [E].
[ES] stays roughly constant during the initial-rate period
Correct: d[ES]/dt ≈ 0 because ES forms as fast as it breaks down.
The reaction has reached chemical equilibrium
Initial rates are measured far from equilibrium.
The product rapidly converts back into ES
Reverse reaction from product is assumed negligible.
questions.x: The steady-state approximation assumes that during the initial rate period [ES] stays roughly constant, because ES forms as fast as it breaks down (d[ES]/dt ≈ 0). This holds when substrate greatly exceeds enzyme and product is too low to react in reverse. Solving for [ES] then gives the Michaelis–Menten equation.

questions.q: Km equals (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁. When is Km a good approximation of the substrate's dissociation constant (Kd)?
o: When kcat is much larger than k₋₁
Then Km is dominated by kcat and overstates Kd.
When k₁ is zero
Then no ES would form at all.
Always, by definition
Km and Kd differ whenever kcat is significant.
When kcat is much smaller than k₋₁
Correct: then Km ≈ k₋₁/k₁ = Kd.
questions.note: Low Km means high affinity only roughly.
questions.x: Km = (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁, while Kd = k₋₁/k₁. If kcat ≪ k₋₁, ES dissociates back to E + S much faster than it reacts, so Km ≈ Kd and a low Km truly reflects tight binding. If kcat is large, Km exceeds Kd and overstates the dissociation constant.

questions.q: Why are enzyme kinetics measured as initial rates?
o: Substrate is nearly at its starting level and product has not built up
Correct: this avoids substrate depletion, the reverse reaction and product inhibition.
Enzymes are only active for the first few seconds
Enzymes keep working; the issue is changing concentrations.
Vmax can be measured only at time zero
Vmax comes from many initial rates over a range of [S].
The enzyme has not yet bound any substrate
Binding happens within milliseconds of mixing.
questions.x: Initial rates are measured in the first moments after mixing, when [S] is still essentially its starting value and product concentration is near zero. This avoids substrate depletion, reverse reaction and product inhibition, all of which would distort the relationship between rate and [S]. Measuring v₀ at many [S] values gives Km and Vmax.

questions.q: Raising [S] from 10 mM to 20 mM leaves an enzyme's initial rate unchanged. What can be concluded?
o: The enzyme is denatured
A denatured enzyme would show essentially no activity, not a steady maximal rate.
[S] is well below Km
Below Km, doubling [S] nearly doubles the rate.
The enzyme is saturated, with [S] well above Km
Correct: at saturation, extra substrate cannot raise the rate.
A competitive inhibitor must be present
Competitive inhibition can be overcome by raising [S].
questions.x: In Michaelis–Menten kinetics, doubling [S] raises the rate substantially unless the enzyme is nearly saturated. A rate that does not change between 10 and 20 mM means nearly all active sites are already filled, so [S] is well above Km and v ≈ Vmax. A denatured enzyme would show essentially no activity.

questions.q: An enzyme has kcat/Km ≈ 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹. What does this suggest?
o: It binds substrate very weakly
A very high kcat/Km means efficient capture and turnover.
Its reaction has a large positive ΔG
kcat/Km reflects kinetics, not thermodynamics.
Its rate is limited by how fast substrate diffuses to it
Correct: values near 10⁸ to 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ approach the diffusion limit.
It must be allosterically regulated
Efficiency does not show whether an enzyme is regulated.
questions.x: kcat/Km is the second-order rate constant for enzyme meeting free substrate. Its ceiling is set by how fast molecules diffuse together in water, about 10⁸ to 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹. An enzyme at this value, such as triose phosphate isomerase, converts nearly every substrate molecule it encounters, so diffusion limits the rate.

questions.q: Protein kinase A is a tetramer of two regulatory and two catalytic subunits. How does cAMP activate it?
o: cAMP phosphorylates the catalytic subunits
cAMP is a second messenger, not a phosphate donor.
cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, releasing active catalytic subunits
Correct: losing the regulatory subunits frees the kinase.
cAMP cleaves the regulatory subunits
Activation is reversible binding, not proteolysis.
cAMP binds the active site as a substrate
cAMP acts as an allosteric effector.
questions.x: In inactive PKA, two regulatory subunits bind and block two catalytic subunits. cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, changing their shape so they release the catalytic subunits. The freed catalytic subunits then phosphorylate target proteins on serine and threonine; activation is reversed when cAMP is degraded.

questions.q: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, an inhibitor increases the slope without changing the y-intercept. What is most likely true of the inhibitor?
o: It resembles the substrate and binds the active site
Correct: this is competitive inhibition, so Vmax is unchanged and Km rises.
It binds only the enzyme–substrate complex
That gives parallel lines.
It covalently destroys enzyme molecules
Losing enzyme raises the y-intercept, since Vmax falls.
It binds an allosteric site on E and ES equally
That gives lines crossing on the x-axis.
questions.x: A higher slope (Km/Vmax) with an unchanged y-intercept (1/Vmax) means Vmax is the same but Km is higher. That is competitive inhibition, typically by a substrate-like molecule competing for the active site. High [S] outcompetes it, which is why Vmax is unchanged.

questions.q: A suicide (mechanism-based) inhibitor works by which mechanism?
o: It binds reversibly at an allosteric site
That describes an allosteric inhibitor.
It competes with substrate and is easily displaced
That describes a reversible competitive inhibitor.
The enzyme converts it into a reactive form that covalently inactivates the enzyme
Correct: the enzyme's own catalysis creates the reactive group.
It denatures the enzyme by raising the temperature
Inhibitors act chemically, not by heating.
questions.x: A suicide, or mechanism-based, inhibitor is an unreactive compound that the enzyme recognizes as a substrate. During normal catalysis, the enzyme converts it into a reactive intermediate that covalently bonds to the active site, permanently inactivating that enzyme. Because the enzyme activates it, it is very specific.

questions.q: Which way of regulating enzyme activity usually takes longest to take effect?
o: Changing transcription of the enzyme's gene
Correct: making new enzyme takes hours, while other controls act in seconds to minutes.
Allosteric inhibition by a metabolite
Allosteric binding acts within milliseconds.
Phosphorylation by an existing kinase
Covalent modification of existing enzyme acts within seconds to minutes.
Competitive inhibition by an existing molecule
Binding is nearly instantaneous.
questions.x: Allosteric binding and competitive inhibition work in milliseconds, and phosphorylation by existing kinases acts within seconds to minutes. Changing gene expression requires transcription, translation and folding of new enzyme, or degradation of old enzyme, which takes hours. So transcriptional control is the slowest form.

questions.q: An enzyme has Km = 2 μM and Vmax = 90 μM/s. A competitive inhibitor is present at [I] = Ki. What is v at [S] = 4 μM?
o: 30 μM/s
This treats the inhibitor as noncompetitive, halving Vmax instead of doubling Km.
45 μM/s
Correct: Km,app = 4 μM, so v = 90 × 4/(4 + 4) = 45.
60 μM/s
60 is the uninhibited rate: 90 × 4/6.
90 μM/s
v reaches Vmax only at saturating [S].
questions.x: A competitive inhibitor changes only Km: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki) = 2 × 2 = 4 μM, and Vmax stays 90 μM/s. At [S] = 4 μM, which now equals Km,app, v = Vmax/2 = 45 μM/s. Halving Vmax instead treats the inhibitor as noncompetitive, giving 30.

questions.q: An enzyme has Vmax = 120 μM/s. A pure noncompetitive inhibitor is added at [I] = Ki. What is v at [S] = Km?
o: 30 μM/s
Correct: Vmax,app = 120/2 = 60, and at [S] = Km, v = 60/2 = 30.
40 μM/s
This treats the inhibitor as raising Km instead of lowering Vmax.
60 μM/s
60 is either Vmax,app or the uninhibited v at Km, not both together.
120 μM/s
This ignores both the inhibitor and the [S] = Km condition.
questions.x: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax by the factor 1 + [I]/Ki and leaves Km unchanged. With [I] = Ki, Vmax,app = 120/2 = 60 μM/s. At [S] = Km, v is half of that, 30 μM/s; applying the factor of 2 to Km instead would give 40.

questions.q: More enzyme is added to an assay. How does its Lineweaver–Burk line change?
o: The x-intercept moves and the y-intercept stays the same
That pattern means Km changed, as with a competitive inhibitor.
The line shifts parallel to itself
A parallel shift is the uncompetitive pattern.
Nothing changes
Vmax depends on enzyme concentration.
The y-intercept falls and the x-intercept stays the same
Correct: Vmax rises (1/Vmax falls) while Km stays the same.
questions.x: Vmax = kcat[E]T, so adding enzyme raises Vmax proportionally, lowering the y-intercept 1/Vmax. Km is a property of the enzyme–substrate pair and does not depend on enzyme amount, so the x-intercept −1/Km stays fixed. The line pivots around its x-intercept, becoming less steep.

questions.q: Substrates A (kcat/Km = 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹) and B (kcat/Km = 10⁴ M⁻¹s⁻¹) are present at equal, low concentrations with one enzyme. What is the ratio of their rates, A : B?
o: Equal concentrations do not mean equal rates.
Correct: when substrates compete, the rate ratio equals the ratio of kcat/Km values times concentrations.
This compares exponents (6 vs 4) instead of values.
questions.x: When two substrates compete for one enzyme, each rate is v = (kcat/Km)[E][S], and the free enzyme term is shared. The rate ratio is therefore (kcat/Km)A[A] divided by (kcat/Km)B[B]. With equal concentrations, the ratio is 10⁶/10⁴ = 100, which is why kcat/Km defines substrate specificity.

questions.q: Most kinases actually use a complex of ATP with which ion as their substrate?
o: Na⁺
Na⁺ is not the usual ATP partner in kinases.
Mg²⁺
Correct: Mg²⁺ shields the phosphate negative charges and positions ATP.
Cl⁻
An anion cannot neutralize the phosphate charges.
Fe³⁺
Iron is a redox cofactor, not the usual partner of ATP.
questions.x: ATP in cells exists mostly as a Mg²⁺–ATP complex. Mg²⁺ coordinates the phosphate oxygens, partially neutralizing their negative charge and holding ATP in a conformation the kinase can use, which makes the γ-phosphate easier to attack. This is why kinases and many other ATP-using enzymes require Mg²⁺.

questions.q: What is an allosteric site?
o: The site where substrate is converted to product
That is the active site.
The site where a protease cleaves a zymogen
That is a cleavage site.
The DNA sequence that controls the enzyme's expression
That is a promoter or enhancer.
A regulatory binding site separate from the active site
Correct: binding there changes the enzyme's conformation and activity.
questions.x: An allosteric site is a regulatory binding site distinct from the active site. When an effector binds there, it changes the enzyme's conformation and thus its activity, either increasing or decreasing it. The effector is not converted to product, unlike a substrate at the active site.

questions.q: Phosphofructokinase-1 is inhibited by ATP and activated by AMP. What does a high AMP level signal to it?
o: The cell is low on energy, so glycolysis should speed up
Correct: AMP builds up when ATP is depleted and allosterically activates PFK-1.
The cell has plenty of energy, so glycolysis should slow down
High ATP, not AMP, signals plenty of energy.
AMP is PFK-1's main substrate
PFK-1 phosphorylates fructose-6-phosphate using ATP.
Glycolysis should be replaced by gluconeogenesis
Low energy favors making ATP, not using it to make glucose.
questions.x: PFK-1 catalyzes the committed step of glycolysis and senses the cell's energy charge. When ATP is used faster than it is made, AMP rises, binds an allosteric site and activates PFK-1, speeding glycolysis to make more ATP. High ATP binds an inhibitory site and slows it, so ATP is both substrate and inhibitor.

questions.q: Why does the reaction rate level off at high substrate concentrations?
o: The substrate becomes a competitive inhibitor
Typical enzymes do not show substrate inhibition.
The equilibrium constant decreases
Keq is independent of [S].
Nearly all active sites are occupied
Correct: once enzymes are saturated, extra substrate has no free enzyme to bind.
The enzyme is denatured by substrate
Saturation is not the same as denaturation.
questions.x: Rate depends on how many enzyme molecules are in the ES complex. At low [S], more substrate fills more active sites and the rate rises. At high [S] nearly all sites are occupied, so adding substrate has no free enzyme to bind and the rate plateaus at Vmax. The enzyme is saturated, not denatured.

questions.q: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme assay. What happens to the enzyme's apparent kcat/Km?
o: It increases
An inhibitor cannot make the enzyme more efficient.
It is unchanged
An unchanged kcat/Km is the uncompetitive case, where both terms fall together.
It becomes zero
Partial inhibition leaves some activity.
It decreases
Correct: apparent kcat falls with Vmax while Km stays the same, so kcat/Km falls.
questions.x: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor lowers apparent kcat (since Vmax falls) but leaves Km unchanged, so kcat/Km falls. This means the inhibitor reduces activity even at low [S]. An uncompetitive inhibitor lowers kcat and Km by the same factor, leaving kcat/Km unchanged.

questions.q: During an enzyme purification, total protein falls from 500 mg to 5 mg while total activity falls only from 1000 to 500 units. What happens to specific activity?
o: It falls by half
That is the change in total activity, not activity per mg of protein.
It rises 100-fold
That is the change in total protein alone, ignoring the lost activity.
It rises 50-fold, from 2 to 100 units/mg
Correct: 1000/500 = 2 and 500/5 = 100, because contaminating proteins were removed.
It stays the same
Removing other proteins concentrates the enzyme relative to total protein.
questions.x: Specific activity is enzyme activity divided by total protein, and it tracks purity. Before: 1000 units/500 mg = 2 units/mg; after: 500 units/5 mg = 100 units/mg, a 50-fold purification. Some enzyme was lost (yield 50%), but contaminating proteins were removed much faster.

questions.q: After mild treatment with a mercury compound, an allosteric enzyme gives a hyperbolic v vs [S] curve, still catalyzes, and no longer responds to its allosteric inhibitor. What most likely happened?
o: The active site was destroyed
The enzyme still catalyzes, so the active site is intact.
Catalytic subunits separated from regulatory subunits
Correct: free catalytic subunits keep activity but lose cooperativity and regulation.
The enzyme's primary structure was hydrolyzed
Mild mercurial treatment does not break peptide bonds.
The inhibitor became covalently attached to the active site
That would block catalysis, not remove regulation.
questions.x: Some allosteric enzymes, like aspartate transcarbamoylase, have separate catalytic and regulatory subunits. Mercurials react with cysteine thiols and can dissociate them. Free catalytic subunits keep their activity but lose cooperativity (hyperbolic curve) and no longer respond to effectors that bind the regulatory subunits.

questions.q: Mendel's law of segregation is best explained by which meiotic event?
o: Separation of sister chromatids in anaphase II
Sister chromatids are copies of one homolog; the allele pair splits when homologs separate.
Crossing over during prophase I
Crossing over recombines linked alleles; it does not separate an allele pair.
Cytokinesis after telophase II
Cytokinesis divides cytoplasm; the alleles were already separated earlier.
Separation of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I
Correct: each homolog carries one allele, so allele pairs part when homologs separate.
questions.note: Segregation = homologs part in meiosis I.
questions.x: Each homolog in a pair carries one allele of a gene, so when homologs are pulled to opposite poles in anaphase I, the two alleles end up in different cells. That is the physical basis of segregation. Sister chromatids are replicated copies of a single homolog and carry the same allele (barring crossing over), so splitting them in anaphase II does not separate an allele pair.

questions.q: Two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder have two children. What is the probability that exactly one child is affected?
o: Correct: 2 birth orders × (1/4)(3/4) = 6/16 = 3/8.
Counts only one birth order; affected-first and affected-second both qualify.
That is the chance for a single child to be affected.
Treats affected and unaffected as equally likely outcomes.
questions.note: Exactly one of n: multiply by the number of orders.
questions.x: Each child is affected with probability 1/4 and unaffected with 3/4. 'Exactly one affected' can happen two ways (affected then unaffected, or unaffected then affected), each with probability 3/16, so the total is 2 × 3/16 = 3/8. Forgetting to count both orders gives 3/16, the most common error in binomial-type questions.

questions.q: An unaffected woman whose brother has an autosomal recessive disease (parents unaffected) has a child with a man who is a known carrier. What is the probability the child is affected?
o: Uses 1/2 as her carrier probability instead of 2/3.
Assumes she is definitely a carrier.
Correct: P(she is carrier) 2/3 × P(aa from two carriers) 1/4 = 1/6.
Adds an extra factor of 1/2; the 1/4 already includes both parents' transmission.
questions.x: First find her carrier probability: her parents must both be carriers, and since she is unaffected she is a carrier with probability 2/3. If she is a carrier, two carriers have an affected child 1/4 of the time. Multiply the independent steps: 2/3 × 1/4 = 1/6. Using 1/2 for her carrier status gives 1/8, the classic mistake.

questions.q: Mendel's law of independent assortment applies most strictly to genes that are:
o: Tightly linked on the same chromosome
Linked genes tend to be inherited together and violate independent assortment.
Alternative alleles of the same gene
Alleles of one gene segregate; assortment concerns different genes.
Found only on the X chromosome
Being X-linked does not make two genes assort independently.
Located on different nonhomologous chromosomes
Correct: nonhomologous chromosomes orient independently at metaphase I.
questions.x: Independent assortment arises because each pair of homologs lines up at metaphase I without regard to how other pairs line up. Genes on different chromosomes therefore sort independently, giving equal frequencies of all gamete combinations. Genes close together on one chromosome are physically tied and travel together unless a crossover separates them, so linkage violates this law.

questions.q: Of 100 people with a genotype for an autosomal dominant disease, 80 show signs of the disease and 20 show none. This describes:
o: 80% expressivity
Expressivity is the degree of severity among those who express it.
Codominance
Codominance concerns two alleles both being expressed in a heterozygote.
A 20% mutation rate
Carriers who show no signs still have the mutant genotype.
80% penetrance
Correct: penetrance is the fraction of carriers of a genotype who express the phenotype.
questions.note: Penetrance = whether; expressivity = how much.
questions.x: Penetrance is the percentage of individuals with a given genotype who show the phenotype at all; here 80 of 100 do, so penetrance is 80%. Expressivity is a different idea: it describes how severely the trait appears among those who do express it. The 20 unaffected people still carry the allele, so they are not explained by a lack of mutation.

questions.q: A woman with normal vision has a color-blind father (X-linked recessive). She has a child with a man with normal vision. What is the probability their first child is a color-blind son?
o: That is the risk for a son once you know the child is male.
Correct: she is an obligate carrier; P(son) 1/2 × P(mutant X) 1/2 = 1/4.
Treats her carrier status as 1/2; her father gave her his mutant X for sure.
She must carry the allele from her father and can pass it on.
questions.x: Her color-blind father had only one X, carrying the mutant allele, and he must have given it to her, so she is an obligate carrier. A child is a son with probability 1/2, and a son gets her mutant X with probability 1/2, so a color-blind son has probability 1/4. Answering 1/2 answers a different question: the risk once you already know the child is a son.

questions.q: Siblings born to a mother with a mitochondrial DNA mutation vary widely in severity of the resulting disease. The best explanation is that:
o: Each oocyte received a different proportion of mutant mitochondria
Correct: heteroplasmy plus random partitioning gives each egg a different mutant load.
Paternal mitochondria compensate in some children
Paternal mitochondria are essentially not transmitted.
mtDNA recombines with nuclear DNA during meiosis
mtDNA does not cross over with nuclear chromosomes.
X-inactivation differs between siblings
X-inactivation is unrelated to mitochondrial genes.
questions.note: Heteroplasmy explains variable severity in mitochondrial disease.
questions.x: A cell can contain a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA (heteroplasmy). When oocytes form, mitochondria are distributed randomly, so different eggs get different mutant fractions, and symptoms appear only above a threshold load. This explains why siblings from the same mother differ in severity; paternal mitochondria do not contribute to make up the difference.

questions.q: Deleting the same region of chromosome 15 causes one syndrome when inherited from the father and a different syndrome when inherited from the mother. This best illustrates:
o: X-inactivation
Chromosome 15 is an autosome; X-inactivation silences an X.
Mitochondrial inheritance
The defect is in a nuclear chromosome, passed by either parent.
Incomplete dominance
That concerns blending of allele effects, not parent of origin.
Genomic imprinting
Correct: some genes are silenced depending on parent of origin, so the active copy differs.
questions.x: In genomic imprinting, certain genes are epigenetically silenced depending on which parent transmitted them, so only one parental copy is active. Losing the 15q region from the father removes the active paternal genes (Prader-Willi syndrome), while losing it from the mother removes active maternal genes (Angelman syndrome). The key clue is that the outcome depends on parent of origin, not the DNA change itself.

questions.q: Two genes show a recombination frequency of 50% in testcrosses. This indicates that the genes:
o: Assort independently, as if unlinked
Correct: 50% recombinants is the maximum and matches independent assortment.
