Are adjacent on the same chromosome
Adjacent genes would show near 0% recombination.
Are exactly 100 map units apart
Observed RF cannot exceed 50%, so it cannot measure 100 units.
Are linked in the repulsion phase
Phase changes which classes are recombinant, not the RF value.
questions.x: Recombination frequency maxes out at 50%, because even if a crossover always occurs between two loci, only half the chromatids involved are recombinant. An RF of 50% gives equal parental and recombinant classes, exactly as for genes on different chromosomes. Such genes may be far apart on one chromosome or on different chromosomes, but in either case they behave as unlinked.

questions.q: In a three-point testcross, the parental classes are ABC and abc, and the two rarest classes are AbC and aBc. Which gene is in the middle?
o: A
A stays with C as in parentals in the rarest classes, so it is not in the middle.
C
C keeps its parental partner A in the rarest classes.
B
Correct: double crossovers swap only the middle gene relative to the parental arrangement.
It cannot be determined without map distances
The rarest (double crossover) class alone reveals the middle gene.
questions.note: Rarest class = double crossover; the swapped gene is in the middle.
questions.x: In a three-point testcross, the parental classes are the most common and the double-crossover classes are the rarest. A double crossover swaps only the middle gene relative to its flanking neighbors. Comparing ABC with AbC, only B has changed, so B is in the middle. No map distances are needed for this step.

questions.q: A dihybrid with genes linked in repulsion (Ab/aB) and little recombination is testcrossed to ab/ab. Which progeny classes are most frequent?
o: AB and ab (recombinant types)
Those are recombinant classes when the parent is in repulsion.
All four classes equally
That happens only with independent assortment.
AB only
A testcross reveals all gametes the dihybrid makes.
Ab and aB (parental types)
Correct: parental chromosomes are Ab and aB, so those classes dominate.
questions.x: The parental (non-recombinant) classes are always the allele combinations on the dihybrid's own chromosomes. In repulsion (Ab/aB), those are Ab and aB, so with little recombination they dominate the testcross. AB and ab arise only by crossing over here, so they are the rare recombinants. Which classes count as parental depends on phase.

questions.q: Genes A and B are 20 cM apart. Two dihybrids with coupling-phase chromosomes (AB/ab) are crossed. What fraction of offspring are ab/ab?
o: Correct: each parent makes ab gametes at (1 − 0.20)/2 = 0.40; 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.16.
That is 1/16, the value for unlinked genes.
Assumes complete linkage, so ab gametes would be 50%.
Squares a recombinant gamete frequency (0.10); ab is a parental gamete here.
questions.note: Linked genes: parental gametes = (1 − RF)/2 each; recombinant = RF/2 each.
questions.x: With 20% recombination, the dihybrid makes 80% parental gametes split equally (40% AB, 40% ab) and 20% recombinant gametes (10% Ab, 10% aB). An ab/ab offspring needs an ab gamete from each parent: 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.16. Treating ab as a recombinant gamete (0.10) would apply only to repulsion-phase parents.

questions.q: Recombination frequencies between distant genes underestimate their true map distance mainly because:
o: Distant genes are never separated by crossing over
Distant genes are separated most often.
Even numbers of crossovers between them restore parental combinations
Correct: double crossovers go undetected, so RF levels off near 50%.
Crossover frequency decreases toward chromosome ends
That is not the general reason RF saturates.
Recombinant gametes fail to fertilize eggs
Recombinant gametes are fully viable.
questions.note: Map from short intervals added together, not one long measurement.
questions.x: A single crossover between two loci produces a recombinant, but a second crossover in the same interval switches the alleles back to the parental arrangement. For distant genes, multiple crossovers are common and many go undetected, so the measured RF underestimates true distance and plateaus near 50%. Accurate maps add up distances measured over short intervals.

questions.q: A child with trisomy 21 has two different maternal alleles at a marker very close to the chromosome 21 centromere. Nondisjunction most likely occurred in:
o: Maternal meiosis II
Sister chromatids would give two identical maternal alleles near the centromere.
Paternal meiosis I
The extra copies are maternal in origin.
Maternal meiosis I
Correct: two different maternal alleles means both homologs entered the egg.
Mitosis after fertilization
Post-zygotic error would duplicate one existing allele, not add a second different one.
questions.note: Different homologs = MI error; identical copies = MII error.
questions.x: Near the centromere, crossing over rarely separates the alleles, so markers there reflect which centromeres went into the egg. Two different maternal alleles mean both maternal homologs entered the egg, which happens when homologs fail to separate in meiosis I. In a meiosis II error, the egg would get two sister chromatids carrying identical alleles near the centromere.

questions.q: A normal egg is fertilized by sperm produced after nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes in paternal meiosis I. What karyotypes can result?
o: 47,XYY or 45,X
YY sperm come from nondisjunction in meiosis II.
47,XXY or 45,X
Correct: MI nondisjunction gives XY or no-sex-chromosome sperm.
47,XXX or 45,X
XX sperm come from meiosis II nondisjunction.
47,XXY only
The other daughter cell lacks a sex chromosome, giving 45,X.
questions.x: In the father, meiosis I normally separates X from Y. If they fail to separate, one secondary spermatocyte gets both X and Y and the other gets neither, so sperm are XY or carry no sex chromosome. Fertilizing a normal X egg gives 47,XXY or 45,X. XX or YY sperm arise only from meiosis II nondisjunction, after X and Y have already separated.

questions.q: A compound causes reversion in the Ames test only when rat liver extract is added; extract alone causes no reversion. The best interpretation is:
o: Liver extract itself is the mutagen
Extract alone caused no reversion, so it is not the mutagen.
The compound is mutagenic only to mammals
The bacteria do mutate once the compound is activated.
Liver enzymes convert it into a mutagenic metabolite
Correct: metabolic activation makes some procarcinogens mutagenic.
Liver enzymes repair the bacterial DNA
Repair would reduce, not increase, revertants.
questions.x: Many compounds are not mutagenic themselves but are converted by liver enzymes such as cytochrome P450s into reactive, DNA-damaging metabolites. Adding rat liver extract to the Ames test mimics this metabolic activation. Since the extract alone causes no reversion, the extract is not the mutagen; the activated compound is.

questions.q: A cytosine in a C–G base pair is deaminated to uracil and not repaired. After two rounds of replication, one descendant DNA molecule will carry what at that site?
o: A G–C pair, no change
The original G strand gives normal products, but the U strand does not.
A T–A pair, a C→T transition
Correct: U pairs with A, and A then pairs with T.
A G–T mismatch
Mismatches are resolved by replication into full base pairs.
An A–T transversion from purine to pyrimidine
C→T is pyrimidine to pyrimidine, a transition.
questions.x: Uracil pairs with adenine. In the first replication, the U strand templates an A, giving a U–A pair; in the next round, that A templates a T, giving a T–A pair. The net effect is C–G → T–A, a transition (pyrimidine to pyrimidine). This is why cells remove uracil from DNA with uracil-DNA glycosylase before replication.

questions.q: In a population at equilibrium, ABO allele frequencies are Iᴬ = 0.3, Iᴮ = 0.1 and i = 0.6. What fraction of people have type A blood?
o: Counts only IᴬIᴬ; Iᴬi people are type A too.
Counts only Iᴬi (or confuses with type O, i² = 0.36).
That is the allele frequency, not the phenotype frequency.
questions.x: Type A blood comes from two genotypes, IᴬIᴬ and Iᴬi, because Iᴬ is dominant to i. Their frequencies are 0.3² = 0.09 and 2(0.3)(0.6) = 0.36, totaling 0.45. With multiple alleles, Hardy–Weinberg still applies: each homozygote is the allele frequency squared and each heterozygote is twice the product of the two allele frequencies.

questions.q: In a population with strong positive assortative mating for a trait controlled by one gene, what happens over generations without other forces?
o: Allele frequencies shift toward the dominant allele
Mating pattern alone does not change allele frequencies.
Homozygotes increase and heterozygotes decrease, with allele frequencies unchanged
Correct: like-with-like mating shifts genotypes, not allele counts.
Heterozygotes increase
Similar mates produce more homozygotes.
Genotype frequencies remain at Hardy–Weinberg values
Nonrandom mating violates HW.
questions.x: In positive assortative mating, individuals choose mates with the same phenotype, so like genotypes tend to mate together. This raises the proportion of homozygotes and reduces heterozygotes each generation. Because no alleles are added or removed, allele frequencies stay the same; only genotype frequencies depart from Hardy–Weinberg proportions.

questions.q: Two unaffected parents with no family history have two children with the same fully penetrant autosomal dominant disorder. The best explanation is:
o: Two independent new mutations
Possible but extremely unlikely in the same gene twice.
Both parents are carriers of a recessive allele
The disorder is dominant with full penetrance.
Incomplete penetrance in both children
The children are affected; penetrance is full.
Germline mosaicism in one parent
Correct: a mutation in part of one parent's germline can reach several children.
questions.x: Germline mosaicism occurs when a mutation arises in a parent's germ-cell lineage during development, so some of that parent's gametes carry it while their body cells do not. The parent is unaffected yet can pass the dominant allele to more than one child. Two separate new mutations in the same gene in one family would be extremely improbable.

questions.q: A phenotypically normal woman's brother has hemophilia A (X-linked recessive); her parents are unaffected. If she has a son with an unaffected man, what is the probability the son has hemophilia?
o: Assumes she is definitely a carrier.
Multiplies an extra 1/2 for the child's sex; the child is known to be a son.
Correct: her mother is a carrier, so she is a carrier with 1/2; then 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Uses the autosomal 2/3 carrier logic, which does not apply to X-linked traits.
questions.x: An affected brother with unaffected parents means their mother is a carrier (X-linked recessive alleles in sons come from the mother). So the woman inherited the mutant X from her mother with probability 1/2. If she is a carrier, a son has a 1/2 chance of getting her mutant X: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The 2/3 rule is for autosomal recessive cases, not X-linked.

questions.q: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 9% of people show a recessive phenotype. What fraction of people with the dominant phenotype are heterozygous?
o: That is heterozygotes as a fraction of the whole population.
That is p², the homozygous dominant fraction.
That is pq without the factor of 2.
Correct: q = 0.3, 2pq = 0.42, dominant phenotype = 0.91; 0.42/0.91 = 6/13.
questions.note: Conditional: divide by the dominant phenotype frequency, 1 − q².
questions.x: q² = 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 0.7. Heterozygotes make up 2pq = 0.42 of the population, and the dominant phenotype is 1 − q² = 0.91. Among dominant-phenotype people, the heterozygous fraction is 0.42/0.91 = 6/13 ≈ 0.46. The trap is answering 0.42, which forgets to restrict the denominator to dominant-phenotype individuals.

questions.q: In a diploid population of N individuals, what is the probability that a single new neutral mutation will eventually become fixed by genetic drift?
o: A single copy among 2N is far more likely to be lost.
Zero, since neutral alleles never fix
Drift can fix neutral alleles by chance.
1/(2N), its starting frequency
Correct: a neutral allele's fixation probability equals its initial frequency.
1/N²
The starting frequency is 1/(2N), not 1/N².
questions.x: A diploid population of N individuals has 2N copies of each gene, so a new mutation starts at a frequency of 1/(2N). For a neutral allele, drift is equally likely to favor any copy, so the chance that this particular copy's descendants eventually replace all the others equals its starting frequency, 1/(2N). Most new neutral mutations are lost.

questions.q: A tetraploid plant arises from a diploid ancestor. It cannot produce fertile offspring with the diploid because:
o: Tetraploid pollen cannot fertilize diploid ovules
Fertilization can occur; hybrid sterility is the barrier.
The tetraploid has different genes than the diploid
It has the same genes, just doubled.
Their triploid hybrids have unpaired chromosomes in meiosis and are sterile
Correct: odd ploidy disrupts homolog pairing, so few balanced gametes form.
Tetraploids reproduce only asexually
Many polyploid plants reproduce sexually.
questions.note: Polyploidy can create a new species in a single generation.
questions.x: A tetraploid makes diploid gametes and a diploid makes haploid gametes, so their hybrid is triploid. In triploid meiosis, three copies of each chromosome cannot pair evenly, so most gametes get unbalanced chromosome sets and are not viable. This hybrid sterility isolates the tetraploid reproductively from its parent species in a single generation, a common way plants speciate.

questions.q: Certain flowers and their specific pollinators show matching adaptations, each having evolved in response to the other. This is:
o: Convergent evolution
That involves unrelated species independently evolving similar traits.
Coevolution
Correct: reciprocal evolutionary change between interacting species.
Genetic drift
The matching traits are adaptive.
Allopatric speciation
No geographic separation or speciation is described.
questions.x: Coevolution is reciprocal evolutionary change between interacting species, where adaptations in one create selective pressure on the other. Flower shapes that fit specific pollinators, and pollinator mouthparts that fit specific flowers, are classic examples, as are predator–prey and host–parasite arms races. Convergence involves unrelated species evolving similar traits independently, not in response to each other.

questions.q: Guppies moved from a stream with many predators to a stream with few predators evolve brighter-colored males over several generations. The best interpretation is that:
o: Bright color was caused by the new stream's diet in each fish
Change over generations indicates heritable evolution.
Reduced predation let sexual selection for bright males outweigh natural selection against them
Correct: the balance of selective pressures shifted once predators were rare.
Predators prefer bright guppies, so color increased
Fewer predators means less selection against bright males, not more.
Genetic drift produced the same change by chance
A consistent, directional change matches altered selection.
questions.x: Male guppy coloration is under two opposing pressures: sexual selection (females prefer bright males) and natural selection (predators spot bright males). Where predators are rare, the cost of brightness falls, so sexual selection dominates and brighter males leave more offspring. A consistent, directional change over generations points to selection, not drift or diet.

questions.q: Where two closely related species meet, their hybrids have low fitness, and over time mating preferences that avoid hybridization become stronger. This process is called:
o: Reinforcement
Correct: selection against hybrids strengthens prezygotic isolation.
Gene flow
Gene flow would blend the species.
Hybrid vigor
Here the hybrids are less fit, not more.
Genetic drift
The change is driven by selection against hybrids.
questions.x: Reinforcement occurs when two diverging populations meet again and their hybrids have low fitness. Individuals who mate with their own type leave more fit offspring, so selection strengthens prezygotic isolating mechanisms such as mating preferences. This completes speciation. Gene flow, by contrast, would merge the two populations.

questions.q: In a fish species, individuals with the rarer of two mouth shapes always have higher feeding success. Over many generations this will most likely:
o: Fix the more common form
The common form is at a disadvantage.
Eliminate both forms
Selection favors one or the other, not neither.
Fix whichever form is rare now
As it becomes common it loses its advantage.
Keep both forms present near a stable intermediate frequency
Correct: negative frequency-dependent selection favors whichever is rare.
questions.x: In negative frequency-dependent selection, a phenotype's fitness is higher when it is rare. As the rare form becomes common it loses its advantage, while the formerly common form becomes rare and gains it. This pushes both forms toward a stable balance, maintaining polymorphism. Neither form can become fixed, because each is disfavored once it predominates.

questions.q: A neutral allele tightly linked to a strongly favored allele rises in frequency along with it. The best explanation is:
o: The neutral allele is itself favored
By definition it has no fitness effect.
Independent assortment
Tightly linked genes do not assort independently.
Mutation repeatedly creates the neutral allele
Mutation is far too slow to cause this rise.
Genetic hitchhiking, since linkage keeps the two alleles together
Correct: little recombination lets the neutral allele ride the selective sweep.
questions.x: Genetic hitchhiking occurs when a neutral allele rises in frequency because it is tightly linked to a beneficial allele under strong selection. With little recombination between them, the neutral allele is carried along during the selective sweep. This reduces variation near selected genes. The neutral allele itself has no fitness effect; linkage, not selection on it, drives its rise.

questions.q: A population has 10 breeding males and 90 breeding females. Using Nₑ = 4(Nm)(Nf)/(Nm + Nf), what is its effective population size?
o: That is the census number of breeders, not Nₑ.
Averages the two sexes; Nₑ depends on their product, so the rarer sex dominates.
Uses twice the number of males.
questions.note: A skewed sex ratio lowers Nₑ and strengthens drift.
questions.x: Effective population size (Nₑ) is the size of an idealized population that would show the same amount of drift. With unequal sex ratios, Nₑ is dominated by the rarer sex because half of each offspring's genes come from it: 4(10)(90)/(10 + 90) = 3600/100 = 36. That is far below the census count of 100, so drift is stronger than headcount suggests.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane?
o: Two continuous protein sheets sandwich a central lipid layer
That is the older Davson–Danielli model, disproved by freeze-fracture images.
Phospholipids flip freely and rapidly between the two leaflets
Flip-flop is slow without flippases; lateral movement is the fast motion.
Proteins are locked in fixed positions by a rigid lipid lattice
The bilayer is fluid; FRAP shows many proteins move laterally.
Lipids and many proteins diffuse laterally within a phospholipid bilayer
Correct: the bilayer is a two-dimensional fluid in which proteins float and move sideways.
questions.note: Fast: lateral diffusion. Slow: flip-flop between leaflets.
questions.x: The fluid mosaic model treats the bilayer as a two-dimensional liquid: lipids and many proteins drift sideways within their own leaflet, while proteins are scattered through it like a mosaic. The tempting idea of free flip-flop fails because moving a polar head group through the hydrophobic core is very costly, so transverse movement is slow unless an enzyme such as a flippase catalyzes it.

questions.q: How does cholesterol affect an animal cell membrane at low temperature?
o: It makes the membrane even more rigid than it would be without it
That describes its effect at high temperature, where it restrains motion.
It greatly raises the bilayer's permeability to ions
Cholesterol actually lowers permeability to small polar solutes and ions.
It catalyzes rapid flip-flop of phospholipids
Cholesterol is not an enzyme; flippases catalyze flip-flop.
It disrupts tight packing of acyl tails, helping keep the membrane fluid
Correct: its rigid ring wedges between tails and prevents them from crystallizing.
questions.note: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer: less fluid when hot, more fluid when cold.
questions.x: Cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity. In the cold, its rigid ring system wedges between phospholipid tails and keeps them from packing into a gel, so the membrane stays more fluid than it would be without it. At high temperature the same ring restrains tail motion and reduces fluidity, which is the effect the most tempting distractor wrongly applies to low temperature.

questions.q: Why is spontaneous flip-flop of a phospholipid from one leaflet to the other very slow?
o: Its polar head group would have to pass through the hydrophobic core
Correct: dragging a charged head through the nonpolar interior is energetically costly.
Phospholipids are covalently bonded to neighboring membrane proteins
Most phospholipids are not covalently bound to proteins.
Lateral diffusion is equally slow, so all lipid motion is slow
Lateral diffusion is fast, about a micrometer per second.
The cytoskeleton anchors every phospholipid in place
The cytoskeleton anchors some proteins, not individual lipids.
questions.x: Flip-flop requires the hydrated, polar or charged head group to cross the roughly 3 nm nonpolar core of the bilayer, a large energy barrier, so it happens on a scale of hours to days unless flippases catalyze it. Lateral diffusion is the opposite case: the lipid stays within its leaflet with its head group in water, so it is very fast. That is why slow flip-flop cannot be explained by all lipid motion being slow.

questions.q: Uptake of solute X rises with external [X] but levels off at high [X], is unaffected by blocking ATP synthesis, and never builds [X] inside above outside. X enters by:
o: Simple diffusion through the bilayer
Simple diffusion rises linearly and does not saturate.
Primary active transport
That would depend on ATP and could concentrate X inside.
Secondary active transport
That could concentrate X against its gradient using an ion gradient.
Facilitated diffusion through a carrier
Correct: saturable, needs no energy, and only moves down the gradient.
questions.note: Saturation means a protein is involved; no uphill movement means no energy.
questions.x: Saturation at high [X] means a limited number of protein binding sites, which rules out simple diffusion. Indifference to ATP depletion, together with the fact that X never builds up above its outside concentration, shows movement only down the gradient. That combination defines facilitated diffusion. Secondary active transport also uses a carrier, but it can concentrate X uphill and fails when the ion gradients powered by ATP collapse.

questions.q: Red blood cells (about 300 mOsm inside) are placed in a 300 mM urea solution. Urea crosses the membrane readily. What happens?
o: Nothing, because the solution is isosmotic
Isosmotic is not isotonic when the solute can cross the membrane.
The cells shrink and crenate
Crenation needs an impermeant solute at higher osmolarity outside.
The cells swell and lyse
Correct: urea enters freely, so it adds no lasting osmotic force; water follows it in.
The cells shrink briefly, then stay smaller
Urea does not stay outside, so it cannot hold water out of the cell.
questions.note: Tonicity counts only solutes that cannot cross the membrane.
questions.x: Tonicity depends only on solutes that cannot cross the membrane. Urea enters red cells freely, so its concentration evens out across the membrane and it exerts no lasting osmotic force. The cell's own impermeant solutes then draw water in, and the cell swells and lyses. The solution is isosmotic but hypotonic, so the trap answer of no change fails.

questions.q: Intestinal cells absorb glucose against its gradient through a Na⁺–glucose symporter. What is the immediate energy source for this step?
o: The Na⁺ electrochemical gradient across the apical membrane
Correct: Na⁺ moving downhill drives glucose uphill (secondary active transport).
ATP hydrolysis by the symporter itself
The symporter has no ATPase activity; that would be primary active transport.
The glucose concentration gradient
Glucose is moving against its own gradient here.
The proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
That gradient drives ATP synthase, not plasma membrane symport.
questions.note: ATP is spent indirectly by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
questions.x: SGLT1 couples glucose entry to Na⁺ entry. Na⁺ moving down its steep electrochemical gradient releases enough free energy to carry glucose up its own gradient. This is secondary active transport: the symporter hydrolyzes no ATP itself, but the gradient it uses is kept up by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. That is why ATP hydrolysis by the symporter is wrong even though ATP is consumed indirectly.

questions.q: A vesicular transporter loads neurotransmitter into synaptic vesicles while H⁺ leaves the vesicle. This transporter is best described as a(n):
o: Symporter performing primary active transport
The substances move in opposite directions, and no ATP is used directly.
Uniporter performing facilitated diffusion
It moves two substances, and transmitter is concentrated uphill.
Antiporter performing secondary active transport
Correct: two substances move in opposite directions, powered by the H⁺ gradient.
ATP-driven pump
The H⁺ gradient, not ATP hydrolysis by this protein, provides the energy.
questions.x: Classify a transporter by two questions: which way do the substances move, and what supplies the energy. Here transmitter enters the vesicle while H⁺ leaves it, so they move in opposite directions: an antiporter. The energy comes from the H⁺ gradient set up earlier by a V-type ATPase, which makes this secondary active transport. It is not a pump, because this protein does not hydrolyze ATP itself.

questions.q: A toxin makes a resting cell's membrane far more permeable to Na⁺ than to any other ion. The membrane potential will move toward:
o: 0 mV, where no ions move
0 mV is not an equilibrium for Na⁺, given its gradient.
About −90 mV, near E_K
K⁺ is no longer the dominant permeant ion.
−70 mV, because the pump fixes Vm
The pump cannot hold Vm when permeabilities change drastically.
About +60 mV, near E_Na
Correct: Vm approaches the equilibrium potential of the most permeant ion.
questions.note: Goldman logic: Vm is a weighted average set by relative permeability.
questions.x: Vm always moves toward the equilibrium potential of the ion the membrane is most permeable to. If Na⁺ permeability dominates, Vm approaches E_Na, about +60 mV, which is what happens briefly at the peak of an action potential. Staying near E_K would require K⁺ to remain the main permeant ion, and 0 mV is not an equilibrium for any ion with a gradient.

questions.q: During a single action potential in a large neuron, intracellular [Na⁺]:
o: Roughly doubles and must be restored before the next spike
Bulk concentrations change negligibly per spike.
Barely changes, because very few ions must cross to change Vm
Correct: membrane capacitance is small, so a tiny ion flux changes voltage a lot.
Becomes equal to extracellular [Na⁺]
The gradient is essentially preserved; thousands of spikes can occur without the pump.
Falls, because Na⁺ leaves during depolarization
Na⁺ enters, not leaves, during depolarization.
questions.x: Membrane capacitance is small, so only a tiny charge has to cross to change Vm by about 100 mV. During one spike, the Na⁺ that enters changes intracellular [Na⁺] by a negligible fraction in a large neuron. Gradients are therefore essentially unchanged after each spike, and many action potentials can fire even with the pump blocked. The pump restores gradients over the long term rather than after every spike.

questions.q: A membrane protein is released into solution by a high-salt wash, with no detergent needed. It is most likely a(n):
o: Multipass transmembrane protein
Transmembrane proteins need detergent to be pulled from the bilayer.
Peripheral protein held by ionic interactions
Correct: high salt disrupts electrostatic attachment to lipids or other proteins.
Protein with a covalent lipid anchor
The lipid anchor stays in the bilayer; detergent is needed.
Single-pass transmembrane receptor
Its hydrophobic helix keeps it in the bilayer despite salt.
questions.note: Salt or pH strips peripheral proteins; integral proteins need detergent.
questions.x: Peripheral proteins attach to the membrane surface through ionic and hydrogen bonds to lipid head groups or to integral proteins. High salt or a change in pH breaks those electrostatic contacts and releases them without disturbing the bilayer. Integral and lipid-anchored proteins have hydrophobic parts buried in the core, so only a detergent that dissolves the bilayer can free them.

questions.q: A small fluorescent dye injected into one cardiac muscle cell quickly appears in neighboring cells. Which junction allows this?
o: Tight junctions
Tight junctions seal the space between cells; they do not join cytoplasms.
Desmosomes
Desmosomes give mechanical adhesion, not cytoplasmic continuity.
Hemidesmosomes
Hemidesmosomes attach cells to the basement membrane.
Gap junctions
Correct: connexon channels link cytoplasms and pass ions and small molecules.
questions.x: Gap junctions are built from connexons, connexin channels that line up between neighboring cells and connect their cytoplasms directly. Ions and small molecules up to about 1 kDa pass through them. This is how a small dye spreads from cell to cell and how action potentials spread through heart muscle. Tight junctions also join cells, but they seal the space between them instead of opening a path between cytoplasms.

questions.q: In a photobleaching experiment, protein X recovers 90% of its fluorescence but protein Y recovers only 30%. The best explanation is that Y:
o: Is a peripheral protein, not an integral one
Peripheral proteins are often quite mobile.
Is in a more fluid region of the membrane
More fluidity would speed and increase recovery.
Is smaller than X
Smaller size would tend to speed diffusion, not lower recovery.
Is largely anchored to the cytoskeleton
Correct: a tethered, immobile fraction cannot refill the bleached area.
questions.x: In FRAP, the plateau level of recovery measures the mobile fraction, and the speed of recovery reflects the diffusion rate. Only 30% recovery for Y means most Y molecules cannot move, typically because they are tethered to the cytoskeleton or to other fixed structures. A more fluid membrane or a smaller protein would increase mobility and recovery, not reduce them.

questions.q: K⁺ channels conduct K⁺ about 1000 times better than the smaller Na⁺ ion because:
o: The pore is too narrow for Na⁺ to fit
Na⁺ is smaller than K⁺, so size exclusion cannot explain it.
Na⁺ carries a larger charge than K⁺
Both carry a +1 charge.
Carbonyl oxygens in the filter fit dehydrated K⁺ but are too far apart for Na⁺
Correct: Na⁺ cannot shed its water shell favorably in a filter sized for K⁺.
K⁺ channels use ATP to reject Na⁺
Channels are passive; selectivity is structural.
questions.x: In water, both ions are surrounded by a hydration shell. The K⁺ selectivity filter is lined with backbone carbonyl oxygens spaced to replace that shell exactly for K⁺, so shedding water costs K⁺ almost nothing. Na⁺ is smaller and cannot contact all those oxygens at once, so dehydrating it inside the filter is unfavorable. Selectivity therefore comes from precise energetic fit, not from a pore that is too narrow.

questions.q: After receptor-mediated endocytosis, LDL separates from its receptor in the endosome mainly because:
o: Lysosomal enzymes digest the receptor
The receptor is recycled, not digested, in normal cycling.
The endosome's acidic pH lowers receptor binding affinity
Correct: low pH releases the LDL, and the receptor recycles to the surface.
The clathrin coat pulls the LDL away
The clathrin coat falls off soon after the vesicle forms.
The endosome is more alkaline than the blood
Endosomes are acidic, not alkaline.
questions.x: LDL receptors bind LDL tightly at the neutral pH of blood. After endocytosis, the endosome is acidified by V-type H⁺ pumps, and the low pH changes the receptor's shape so it lets go of its cargo. LDL continues on to lysosomes while the empty receptor returns to the surface for reuse. Digesting the receptor would waste it, which the cell avoids in normal cycling.

questions.q: Clathrin knockdown sharply reduces transferrin uptake but leaves uptake of a fluid-phase dye by macropinocytosis unchanged. This suggests that:
o: Transferrin enters by clathrin-mediated endocytosis
Correct: only the clathrin-dependent pathway was disrupted.
Transferrin enters by simple diffusion
A large protein cannot diffuse across the bilayer, and uptake fell with clathrin loss.
Macropinocytosis requires clathrin
Dye uptake was unaffected, so it does not.
All endocytosis requires clathrin
The fluid-phase pathway continued without clathrin.
questions.x: Knocking down clathrin is a selective test: any pathway that needs clathrin should fail, while others continue. Transferrin uptake fell, so it uses clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Fluid-phase uptake by macropinocytosis was unchanged, so that actin-driven pathway does not need clathrin. The result shows cells have more than one endocytic route, which rules out the idea that all endocytosis depends on clathrin.

questions.q: Inside-out vesicles containing Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase are prepared in a buffer with Na⁺ and K⁺, and ATP is then added to the outside medium. The pump will move:
o: Na⁺ out of the vesicle and K⁺ into it
That would be true for right-side-out vesicles with ATP inside.
Both ions into the vesicle
The pump is an antiporter; the ions move in opposite directions.
Nothing, because ATP cannot reach the pump
ATP binds the cytosolic face, which is exposed to the medium.
Na⁺ into the vesicle and K⁺ out into the medium
Correct: the cytosolic face, with its Na⁺ and ATP sites, now faces the medium.
questions.note: Track which face of the pump touches the ATP.
questions.x: The pump's cytosolic face binds Na⁺ and ATP and releases K⁺; its extracellular face releases Na⁺ and binds K⁺. In inside-out vesicles, the cytosolic face points toward the medium, so only externally added ATP can drive it. Na⁺ is pumped from the medium into the vesicle and K⁺ from the vesicle out to the medium. The rule is to ask which side the ATP-binding face is on.

questions.q: Replacing most extracellular Na⁺ with impermeant choline barely changes a neuron's resting potential. This indicates that:
o: Resting membrane permeability to Na⁺ is low
Correct: if Na⁺ barely contributes to Vm at rest, removing it changes little.
Choline is highly permeant at rest
The stem says choline is impermeant.
Na⁺ is the main determinant of resting potential
Then removing Na⁺ would hyperpolarize the cell noticeably.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump stops at low Na⁺
Pump changes would not explain a stable potential.
questions.x: The Goldman equation weights each ion by its membrane permeability. If removing most extracellular Na⁺ barely changes the resting potential, Na⁺ must contribute little to it, meaning resting Na⁺ permeability is low compared with K⁺. If Na⁺ were the main determinant, removing it would make the cell much more negative. Choline acts only as an impermeant stand-in to keep osmolarity steady.

questions.q: A protein reconstituted into liposomes moves glucose into them only when the outside has more Na⁺ than the inside. The protein is most likely a:
o: GLUT uniporter
A uniporter would move glucose without any Na⁺ gradient.
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
The pump does not carry glucose.
Na⁺–glucose symporter
Correct: glucose transport needs an inward Na⁺ gradient moving the same way.
Glucose-gated ion channel
Ion channels do not carry glucose into the lumen.
questions.x: A reconstitution experiment strips away everything except the protein, so the requirement for an inward Na⁺ gradient must come from the protein itself. Glucose moving in only when Na⁺ can also move in means the two are coupled in the same direction: a Na⁺–glucose symporter such as SGLT. A GLUT uniporter would carry glucose down its own gradient whether Na⁺ were present or not.

questions.q: A 90-kDa cytosolic protein moves into the nucleus after a short stretch of basic residues (PKKKRKV) is added to it. This stretch acts as a:
o: Signal sequence for the ER
ER signal sequences are hydrophobic stretches, usually at the N-terminus.
Nuclear localization signal
Correct: importins recognize basic NLS motifs and carry cargo through nuclear pores.
Mitochondrial targeting sequence
These are amphipathic helices with basic and hydrophobic residues, not a short basic motif.
Nuclear export signal
An export signal would move the protein out of the nucleus.
questions.note: Proteins too large to diffuse through the pore need an NLS.
questions.x: Large proteins (above about 40–60 kDa) cannot diffuse through nuclear pores and need a nuclear localization signal. A classic NLS is a short stretch of basic lysine and arginine residues, as in PKKKRKV from the SV40 large T antigen. Importins recognize it and carry the cargo through the pore, powered by the Ran-GTP gradient. ER signal sequences differ: they are hydrophobic, not basic.

questions.q: Cells unable to add mannose-6-phosphate to lysosomal enzymes would most likely:
o: Retain the enzymes in the rough ER
The enzymes leave the ER normally; the Golgi sorting step fails.
Send the enzymes into the nucleus
Mannose-6-phosphate is not involved in nuclear import.
Secrete the enzymes, leaving lysosomes full of undigested material
Correct: without the tag, enzymes follow the default secretory path.
Degrade the enzymes in proteasomes immediately
The untagged enzymes are folded and simply mis-sorted.
questions.note: This is I-cell disease: high lysosomal enzyme levels in the blood.
questions.x: In the cis Golgi, lysosomal enzymes receive a mannose-6-phosphate tag. M6P receptors in the trans Golgi then sort them into vesicles bound for lysosomes. Without the tag, the enzymes follow the default secretory route and are released from the cell, so lysosomes fill with undigested material while enzyme levels in the blood rise: I-cell disease. The enzymes still leave the ER normally.

questions.q: Bafilomycin A1 inhibits the V-type H⁺-ATPase. Treated cells would most likely show:
o: Lower lysosomal pH and faster digestion
Blocking the H⁺ pump cannot acidify lysosomes.
Loss of ATP synthesis in mitochondria
Mitochondria use F-type ATP synthase, not V-type pumps.
Higher lysosomal pH and slower breakdown of endocytosed proteins
Correct: without H⁺ pumping, lysosomes cannot stay acidic and hydrolases slow.
Faster mannose-6-phosphate tagging in the Golgi
Tagging does not depend on lysosomal pH.
questions.note: V-type pumps acidify lysosomes and endosomes.
questions.x: V-type H⁺-ATPases use ATP to pump H⁺ into lysosomes and endosomes, keeping them near pH 5. Bafilomycin blocks these pumps, so the lumen becomes more alkaline, acid hydrolases slow down, and receptors cannot release their ligands in endosomes. Mitochondria make ATP with F-type ATP synthase, a related but distinct enzyme, so their ATP production is not the direct target.

questions.q: A secretory protein's N-terminal signal sequence is deleted. The protein will most likely:
o: Be secreted faster than normal
Without the signal, it cannot enter the secretory pathway.
Be sent to the lysosome
Lysosomal targeting also depends on first entering the ER.
Stay in the cytosol, made on free ribosomes
Correct: without a signal for SRP, translation never moves to the ER.
Insert into the plasma membrane
Membrane insertion also requires ER targeting.
questions.x: As the N-terminal signal sequence emerges from the ribosome, SRP binds it and brings the ribosome to the ER, where the protein is threaded into the lumen. Without that signal, translation finishes on a free ribosome and the protein stays in the cytosol. Every route into the secretory pathway, including secretion, lysosomes and the plasma membrane, starts with entry into the ER.

questions.q: N-linked glycosylation of a secreted protein begins in the:
o: Lumen of the rough ER
Correct: a preformed oligosaccharide is added to asparagine as the protein enters the ER.
Golgi apparatus
The Golgi trims N-linked sugars and adds O-linked sugars.
Cytosol
Secreted protein glycosylation happens in the lumen, not the cytosol.
Lysosome
Lysosomes break down sugars; they do not add them.
questions.x: N-linked glycosylation begins in the rough ER lumen. Oligosaccharyltransferase moves a premade 14-sugar oligosaccharide from dolichol onto asparagine in Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequences, often while the chain is still being translated. The Golgi then trims and remodels these sugars and adds O-linked sugars. Because the Golgi modifies N-linked sugars, it is a tempting answer, but it does not start them.

questions.q: An ER-resident chaperone loses its C-terminal KDEL retrieval sequence. It will most likely:
o: Stay in the ER, unaffected
KDEL is needed to retrieve proteins that escape to the Golgi.
Move into the nucleus
KDEL loss does not create a nuclear signal.
Be secreted from the cell
Correct: without KDEL, it is not brought back from the Golgi and follows the default secretory route.
Be degraded in the cytosol right after synthesis
The protein still enters the ER through its signal sequence.
questions.note: Secretion is the default for lumenal proteins with no other signal.
questions.x: Soluble ER residents such as BiP carry a C-terminal KDEL sequence. When they escape to the cis Golgi, KDEL receptors bind them and return them to the ER in COPI vesicles. Without KDEL, the protein is not retrieved and follows the default route for soluble lumenal proteins, secretion. KDEL does not keep proteins in the ER to begin with; it retrieves the ones that leak out.

questions.q: Most proteins inside mitochondria are:
o: Encoded by nuclear genes, made in the cytosol and then imported
Correct: mtDNA encodes only a few proteins; the rest come through TOM/TIM complexes.
Encoded by mitochondrial DNA and made in the matrix
mtDNA encodes only about a dozen proteins in humans.
Made on the rough ER and delivered by vesicles
Mitochondria do not receive proteins by vesicles from the ER.
Taken up from the blood by endocytosis
Mitochondrial proteins are made inside the cell.
questions.x: Human mtDNA encodes only 13 proteins, all parts of the respiratory chain, along with rRNAs and tRNAs. The roughly 1,000 other mitochondrial proteins are encoded in the nucleus, made on free cytosolic ribosomes, and imported through the TOM and TIM complexes, often guided by an N-terminal amphipathic targeting sequence. Mitochondria are not part of the vesicle-based secretory pathway.

questions.q: In hepatocytes, the final step that releases free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate occurs in the:
o: Mitochondrial matrix
Gluconeogenesis starts there with pyruvate carboxylase, but not the final step.
Cytosol, by a soluble phosphatase
Glucose-6-phosphate must be moved into the ER to be dephosphorylated.
Lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum
Correct: glucose-6-phosphatase sits in the ER membrane with its active site in the lumen.
Peroxisome
Peroxisomes do not handle glucose release.
questions.x: Glucose-6-phosphatase is an integral ER membrane enzyme with its active site facing the lumen. G6P is moved into the ER by a transporter, dephosphorylated, and free glucose leaves through the secretory system and GLUT2. This location lets the liver release glucose while keeping G6P in the cytosol for other uses. Mitochondria start gluconeogenesis with pyruvate carboxylase but do not finish it.

questions.q: Brown fat produces heat because its mitochondria contain a protein that:
o: Blocks electron transport at complex IV
Blocking electron flow would stop heat and ATP production.
Lets H⁺ flow back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase
Correct: thermogenin uncouples the gradient from ATP synthesis, releasing heat.
Speeds ATP synthase to make extra ATP
Uncoupling lowers ATP output; the energy is released as heat.
Pumps H⁺ out of the intermembrane space using ATP
Heat comes from H⁺ leaking back in, not from pumping.
questions.x: Brown fat mitochondria contain thermogenin (UCP1), a channel that lets H⁺ return to the matrix without going through ATP synthase. The proton gradient then drives no ATP synthesis, and the energy from electron transport is released as heat. Electron transport actually speeds up under uncoupling, because nothing restrains it, so blocking it would stop heat production.

questions.q: Unlike microtubules and actin filaments, intermediate filaments:
o: Lack polarity and are not used as tracks by motor proteins
Correct: their antiparallel subunits produce a nonpolar rope-like filament.
Are built from globular subunits that bind GTP
That describes tubulin.
Turn over rapidly by dynamic instability
Intermediate filaments are the most stable cytoskeletal fibers.
Drive cell crawling by polymerizing at the leading edge
Actin polymerization drives crawling.
questions.x: Intermediate filament subunits pair into dimers, and the dimers line up antiparallel in tetramers. The two ends of the filament are therefore the same, so there is no plus or minus end for a motor to recognize. They also bind no nucleotide and are very stable, acting like ropes that resist tension. Dynamic instability and GTP binding describe microtubules, and ATP binding describes actin.

questions.q: Paclitaxel (Taxol) stabilizes microtubules and prevents them from shrinking. It blocks cell division mainly because:
o: It prevents tubulin from polymerizing at all
That is how colchicine works, not paclitaxel.
It breaks down actin in the contractile ring
Paclitaxel targets tubulin, not actin.
Spindle microtubules must shorten to pull sister chromatids apart
Correct: the spindle depends on dynamic instability; frozen microtubules cannot segregate chromosomes.
It stops DNA replication in S phase
Its block is in mitosis, not S phase.
questions.x: Chromosome segregation requires spindle microtubules that can both grow and shrink. Kinetochore microtubules shorten to pull sister chromatids to the poles in anaphase. Paclitaxel stabilizes microtubules so they cannot depolymerize, and cells stay arrested in mitosis. Colchicine and vinca alkaloids do the opposite, blocking polymerization, but both kinds of drug arrest mitosis.

questions.q: Plant cells lack centrioles yet still build working mitotic spindles. This shows that:
o: Plant spindles are made of actin
Plant spindles are made of microtubules too.
Plant cells separate chromosomes without microtubules
Plant mitosis still uses a microtubule spindle.
Centrioles are needed only in prokaryotes
Prokaryotes do not have centrioles.
Centrioles are not required to nucleate spindle microtubules
Correct: other microtubule-organizing centers can nucleate microtubules.
questions.x: Higher plant cells have no centrioles but still assemble microtubule spindles, nucleated by γ-tubulin at other microtubule-organizing centers such as the nuclear surface. This shows that centrioles are not needed to make a spindle. Even in animal cells, spindles can form after centrioles are removed. The spindle is made of microtubules in plants as well as animals.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts bacterial flagella with sperm flagella?
o: Both are built from tubulin in a 9 + 2 arrangement
Bacterial flagella are made of flagellin, not tubulin.
Sperm flagella rotate; bacterial flagella whip back and forth
This reverses the two mechanisms.
Bacterial flagella rotate using a H⁺ gradient; sperm flagella bend using dynein and ATP
Correct: the bacterial base is a rotary motor; the eukaryotic axoneme bends.
Both are powered directly by ATP hydrolysis at the base
The bacterial motor runs on the proton-motive force.
questions.x: Bacterial and eukaryotic flagella evolved separately. A bacterial flagellum is a rigid helical filament of flagellin turned by a rotary motor at its base, powered by H⁺ (or sometimes Na⁺) flowing into the cell. A sperm flagellum is a 9 + 2 microtubule axoneme that bends in waves as dynein uses ATP to slide neighboring doublets. They share a name, not a structure or mechanism.

questions.q: Mutations in keratins 5 and 14 cause basal skin cells to tear apart with minor friction. This shows that intermediate filaments mainly:
o: Give cells tensile strength against mechanical stress
Correct: keratin networks linked to desmosomes spread out mechanical force.
Move vesicles to the cell surface
Motor proteins on microtubules move vesicles.
Form the contractile ring in cytokinesis
The contractile ring is actin and myosin.
Seal the paracellular space
Tight junction proteins seal the paracellular space.
questions.x: Intermediate filaments are the cell's tension-bearing ropes. In basal keratinocytes, keratins 5 and 14 connect to desmosomes and hemidesmosomes to spread mechanical stress across the epithelium. When they are mutated, as in epidermolysis bullosa simplex, cells break open from minor friction. Moving vesicles is a job for motors on microtubules, not intermediate filaments.

questions.q: Carcinoma cells that lose E-cadherin expression are more likely to metastasize mainly because:
o: They detach more easily from neighboring cells
Correct: E-cadherin anchors adherens junctions that hold epithelial cells together.
They stop dividing
Losing cadherin does not stop proliferation.
They lose all integrins
E-cadherin loss does not remove integrins.
They form more gap junctions
Gap junctions are not what limits cell escape.
questions.x: E-cadherin is the main adhesion molecule of adherens junctions, linking neighboring epithelial cells and connecting to actin inside through catenins. Losing it is a key step in the epithelial–mesenchymal transition: cells loosen from one another, become motile, and can invade and spread. Losing cadherin does not slow growth, and integrins, which bind the matrix, are a separate adhesion system.

questions.q: In kidney tubule cells, the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is located mainly on which surface?
o: Basolateral membrane
Correct: pumping Na⁺ into the interstitium keeps cell Na⁺ low for apical uptake.
Apical membrane
Pumps on the apical side would push Na⁺ back into the urine.
Tight junctions
Junctions seal the space between cells and hold no pumps.
Nuclear envelope
The pump works at the plasma membrane.
questions.x: In polarized transport epithelia, the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase sits on the basolateral membrane. Pumping Na⁺ out into the interstitium keeps cell [Na⁺] low, creating the inward gradient that apical channels and symporters use to bring Na⁺ in from the tubular fluid. The result is net reabsorption from lumen to blood. A pump on the apical side would send Na⁺ back into the urine.

questions.q: Glycine must occupy every third position in a collagen chain because:
o: It forms the disulfide bonds that link the chains
Glycine has no sulfur; cysteine forms disulfides.
It is the residue that vitamin C hydroxylates
Proline and lysine are hydroxylated.
Its tiny side chain fits in the crowded center of the triple helix
Correct: any larger residue there would block tight winding of the three chains.
Its charged side chain binds water
Glycine's side chain is a single uncharged hydrogen.
questions.x: Collagen has a Gly-X-Y repeat, often with proline and hydroxyproline in the X and Y positions. In the triple helix, every third residue faces the crowded central axis where the three chains meet, and only glycine, whose side chain is a single hydrogen, fits there. A point mutation that replaces one of these glycines disrupts the helix and causes osteogenesis imperfecta.

questions.q: Tumor cells that overexpress matrix metalloproteinases tend to be more invasive because they:
o: Make more collagen to wall themselves off
MMPs break down collagen; they do not make it.
Degrade the basement membrane and surrounding matrix
Correct: breaking down matrix barriers lets cells move into nearby tissue.
Strengthen their own adherens junctions
MMPs act on the matrix, and stronger adhesion would limit invasion.
Speed up DNA repair
MMPs are extracellular proteases, not repair enzymes.
questions.x: Matrix metalloproteinases are zinc-dependent proteases that break down collagen, including type IV collagen in basement membranes, and other matrix proteins. Carcinoma cells must break through the basement membrane to invade, so high MMP activity helps them invade and spread. Stronger adhesion or more matrix would hold tumor cells in place rather than help them escape.

questions.q: Which part of a typical neuron is specialized mainly for receiving synaptic input from other cells?
o: Dendrites
Correct: dendrites carry most postsynaptic receptors and collect incoming signals.
Axon terminals
Axon terminals release neurotransmitter; they are the output end.
Axon hillock
The hillock integrates input and initiates the action potential, but it is not the main receiving surface.
Nodes of Ranvier
Nodes are gaps in myelin along the axon where action potentials are regenerated.
questions.x: Neurons are polarized: input arrives on dendrites (and the soma), is integrated at the axon hillock, and leaves through the axon terminals. Dendrites are branched to provide a large surface packed with postsynaptic receptors. The hillock is tempting because it handles integration, but it is the trigger zone, not the main receiving surface.

questions.q: A neuron receives many small excitatory and inhibitory inputs. Where is the decision to fire an action potential normally made?
o: At each dendritic spine independently
Spines generate graded local potentials, not the all-or-none firing decision.
At the axon hillock/initial segment, which has a high density of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Correct: summed potentials reaching threshold here trigger the action potential.
At the axon terminal, where Ca²⁺ channels open
Terminals respond to an action potential that already fired; they do not initiate it.
At the nucleus, which controls membrane voltage
The nucleus controls gene expression, not moment-to-moment electrical integration.
questions.note: Trap: the soma integrates, but the trigger zone is the axon hillock.
questions.x: Graded postsynaptic potentials from dendrites and soma spread passively and sum at the axon initial segment. This region has the lowest threshold because voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are densest there, so it is where an all-or-none spike begins. Individual spines only produce small local potentials; the firing decision depends on the summed signal at the trigger zone.

questions.q: The extracellular K⁺ concentration around a neuron is experimentally raised. What happens to the resting membrane potential?
o: It becomes more negative (hyperpolarizes)
More outside K⁺ reduces K⁺ efflux, which shifts Vm upward, not downward.
It does not change because the pump compensates
The pump cannot offset the change in the K⁺ equilibrium potential.
It becomes less negative (depolarizes)
Correct: a smaller K⁺ gradient makes EK less negative, and Vm follows EK at rest.
It reverses to about +60 mV
That value is ENa; the cell would still be dominated by K⁺ permeability.
questions.note: EK shifts with [K⁺]out, so resting Vm tracks extracellular K⁺.
questions.x: Resting Vm tracks EK because K⁺ dominates resting permeability. Raising extracellular K⁺ shrinks the K⁺ concentration gradient, making EK less negative by the Nernst equation, so the cell depolarizes. This is why hyperkalemia makes excitable tissue such as the heart dangerously unstable. The pump cannot cancel this shift because it does not change the equilibrium potential.

questions.q: During the absolute refractory period, no second action potential can be fired no matter how strong the stimulus. What is the cause?
o: The neuron has run out of releasable neurotransmitter
Transmitter depletion affects the synapse, not the axon's ability to fire.
The Na⁺ concentration gradient has been abolished
A single spike moves very few ions; the gradient is essentially unchanged.
Voltage-gated K⁺ channels are inactivated and closed
K⁺ channels are open during this phase; that drives repolarization.
Most voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen yet
Correct: inactivation gates must reset at negative voltage before Na⁺ channels can open again.
questions.x: After opening, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels enter an inactivated state that cannot be reopened until the membrane repolarizes and the inactivation gate resets. While most channels are inactivated, no stimulus can generate a new spike: the absolute refractory period. The ion gradients are essentially unchanged by one spike, so depletion is not the explanation.

questions.q: A stimulus applied during the relative refractory period can trigger an action potential only if it is larger than normal. Why?
o: All Na⁺ channels are inactivated, so a larger stimulus forces them open
If all were inactivated, no stimulus would work; that describes the absolute period.
The membrane is hyperpolarized and extra K⁺ channels are still open, so more depolarization is needed
Correct: open K⁺ channels oppose depolarization, and some Na⁺ channels are still inactivated.
The threshold voltage rises to about +30 mV
Threshold rises only slightly; it does not approach the peak voltage.
Myelin temporarily blocks current at that site
Myelin does not change during the refractory period.
questions.x: During the relative refractory period, some Na⁺ channels have recovered from inactivation, but many K⁺ channels are still open and the cell is often hyperpolarized. Extra K⁺ conductance opposes depolarization, so a stronger stimulus is needed to reach threshold. If all Na⁺ channels were still inactivated, no stimulus could work; that defines the absolute refractory period.

questions.q: Many neurons briefly become more negative than resting potential right after an action potential. What causes this afterhyperpolarization?
o: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels close slowly, so K⁺ permeability stays elevated
Correct: extra K⁺ efflux briefly drives Vm closer to EK than at rest.
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 K⁺ into the cell per cycle
The pump moves 2 K⁺ in and 3 Na⁺ out, and it is not the main cause.
Na⁺ channels open a second time
Na⁺ entry would depolarize, not hyperpolarize.
Cl⁻ is pumped out of the cell
Cl⁻ efflux would depolarize, and it is not the mechanism of afterhyperpolarization.
questions.x: Delayed-rectifier K⁺ channels open late and close slowly, so for a few milliseconds after the spike K⁺ permeability is even higher than at rest. That pulls Vm closer to EK, below the normal resting value, producing the afterhyperpolarization. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is a tempting answer, but its electrogenic effect is small and slow and it moves only 2 K⁺ in per cycle.

questions.q: Two unmyelinated axons differ only in diameter. Why does the wider axon conduct action potentials faster?
o: It has a more negative resting potential
Diameter does not set resting potential.
It has a higher threshold, so it fires less often
Threshold does not determine conduction speed.
It contains more mitochondria to power the spike
ATP does not directly drive the propagating spike; ion gradients do.
Its larger cross-section lowers internal resistance, so current spreads farther along the axon
Correct: lower axial resistance lets depolarization reach more distant membrane quickly.
questions.note: Speed up conduction two ways: wider axon or myelin.
questions.x: Conduction speed depends on how far local current spreads before it decays. Axial (internal) resistance falls with cross-sectional area, so a wider axon passes current farther down its length and depolarizes distant membrane to threshold sooner. Resting potential and threshold are not set by diameter, and the spike is powered by ion gradients rather than ATP directly.

questions.q: A neuromuscular preparation is bathed in Ca²⁺-free solution, and the motor nerve is stimulated. Nerve action potentials are recorded normally. What happens at the muscle?
o: It contracts more strongly because Ca²⁺ normally inhibits release
Ca²⁺ is required for release, not inhibitory.
It contracts normally because the nerve still fires
Firing alone cannot release transmitter without Ca²⁺ entry.
It fails to contract because acetylcholine is not released
Correct: transmitter release requires extracellular Ca²⁺ entering the terminal.
It contracts continuously because acetylcholinesterase is inactive
Acetylcholinesterase does not require extracellular Ca²⁺.
questions.note: The nerve fires, but the synapse fails without Ca²⁺.
questions.x: Nerve conduction uses Na⁺ and K⁺ channels, so the motor axon still fires in Ca²⁺-free solution. However, release of acetylcholine requires Ca²⁺ influx through voltage-gated channels at the terminal. With no extracellular Ca²⁺, no transmitter is released and the muscle never gets depolarized, showing that synaptic transmission, not axonal conduction, is Ca²⁺-dependent.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter do most postganglionic sympathetic neurons release onto their target organs?
o: Acetylcholine
Preganglionic fibers release ACh; most sympathetic postganglionic fibers do not.
Norepinephrine
Correct: most sympathetic postganglionic fibers are adrenergic.
Epinephrine
Epinephrine is released mainly by the adrenal medulla as a hormone.
Dopamine
Dopamine is a precursor of norepinephrine, not the main released transmitter.
questions.note: Exception: sympathetic fibers to sweat glands release ACh.
questions.x: In the sympathetic division, preganglionic neurons release ACh onto nicotinic receptors in ganglia, and most postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine onto adrenergic receptors. Epinephrine is tempting, but it is secreted as a hormone mainly by the adrenal medulla, which acts like a modified sympathetic ganglion. Sympathetic fibers to sweat glands are the cholinergic exception.

questions.q: Acetylcholine excites skeletal muscle but inhibits cardiac pacemaker cells. What best explains these opposite effects?
o: Acetylcholine is converted to norepinephrine in the heart
ACh is hydrolyzed to choline and acetate, not converted to norepinephrine.
The heart releases more acetylcholinesterase
Breakdown rate would change duration, not reverse the sign of the response.
Skeletal muscle has a more negative resting potential
Resting Vm does not explain excitation versus inhibition here.
The two tissues express different receptor types linked to different responses
Correct: the receptor, not the transmitter, determines the effect.
questions.x: A transmitter has no inherent excitatory or inhibitory effect; the response depends on the receptor and its signaling pathway. Skeletal muscle has nicotinic receptors, ligand-gated cation channels that depolarize the cell, while pacemaker cells have M2 muscarinic receptors that open K⁺ channels via Gi and slow firing. Changing ACh breakdown would alter duration, not reverse the sign.

questions.q: Ouabain irreversibly blocks the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Over the next several hours, what happens to an isolated neuron's resting potential?
o: It immediately becomes strongly positive
The pump's direct electrogenic contribution is only a few millivolts.
It hyperpolarizes as Na⁺ accumulates outside
Without the pump, Na⁺ accumulates inside, not outside.
It slowly depolarizes as the Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients run down
Correct: leak continues without the pump, so the K⁺ gradient and EK gradually collapse.
It stays exactly the same because leak channels set Vm
Leak channels need gradients, which the pump maintains.
questions.note: The pump's main role is keeping gradients, not directly setting Vm.
questions.x: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump contributes only a few millivolts directly; its main role is maintaining ion gradients. When it is blocked, Na⁺ and K⁺ keep leaking down their gradients, so intracellular K⁺ falls and Na⁺ rises. EK becomes less negative and the cell slowly depolarizes. The resting potential does not collapse instantly because the existing gradients take time to dissipate.

questions.q: Chloride is about 10 times more concentrated outside a neuron than inside. Using the Nernst equation (61 mV per decade), what is ECl?
o: About +61 mV
This forgets that Cl⁻ is negatively charged.
About −61 mV
Correct: for an anion, z = −1 flips the sign, so E = −61 log(10) = −61 mV.
About −6 mV
The log of 10 is 1, so the value is 61 mV, not 6.1 mV.
About +122 mV
This doubles the magnitude and ignores the negative charge; a 10-fold ratio of a monovalent ion gives 61 mV.
questions.note: Anion higher outside → negative equilibrium potential.
questions.x: In the Nernst equation E = (61/z) log([out]/[in]), the valence z carries a sign. For Cl⁻, z = −1, so a 10-fold higher outside concentration gives E = −61 × log 10 = −61 mV. Intuitively, a negative interior is what repels further Cl⁻ entry and balances its inward diffusion. Forgetting the charge sign gives +61 mV.

questions.q: In a voltage-clamp experiment, a depolarizing step produces an early inward current followed by a sustained outward current. Adding tetraethylammonium (TEA) abolishes only the outward current. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: The outward current is carried by K⁺ through voltage-gated channels
Correct: TEA is a K⁺ channel blocker, so the late outward current is K⁺ efflux.
The inward current is carried by K⁺
The early inward current survived TEA; in neurons it is carried by Na⁺ entering, not K⁺.
TEA blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
The early inward Na⁺ current was unaffected.
The outward current is caused by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
Pump currents are tiny and not blocked by TEA.
questions.x: In a classic voltage clamp, depolarization first opens Na⁺ channels (early inward current) and then delayed K⁺ channels (late outward current). TEA blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels, so losing only the outward current identifies it as K⁺ efflux. The inward current survived TEA; it is blocked by tetrodotoxin, which identifies it as Na⁺ current.

questions.q: Myelin increases conduction velocity partly because it changes the electrical properties of the internodal membrane. Which change is correct?
o: Membrane resistance decreases and capacitance increases
That would make the internode leakier and slower to charge.
Both resistance and capacitance increase
Thicker insulation lowers capacitance, like moving capacitor plates apart.
Membrane resistance increases and capacitance decreases
Correct: less current leaks out and less charge is needed to change voltage, so current spreads farther.
Internal axial resistance increases
Myelin does not change axoplasm resistance; that depends on diameter.
questions.x: Myelin adds many layers of membrane, which raises transmembrane resistance (less current leaks out) and lowers capacitance (thicker insulation stores less charge per volt, like widening a capacitor gap). Both effects let local current travel farther and charge the next node faster. Axial resistance depends on axon diameter, not on myelin.

questions.q: In the stretch reflex, the quadriceps contracts while the hamstrings relax. How does the hamstring motor neuron become inhibited?
o: The spindle afferent releases GABA directly onto the hamstring motor neuron
Primary afferents are excitatory (glutamate); an interneuron provides inhibition.
The quadriceps motor neuron releases glycine onto the hamstrings
Motor neurons release ACh onto muscle.
The brain sends a voluntary relaxation command
Reciprocal inhibition is a spinal reflex.
The spindle afferent excites an inhibitory interneuron that synapses on the hamstring motor neuron
Correct: reciprocal inhibition uses one inhibitory interneuron.
questions.note: An afferent can't inhibit directly; it needs an inhibitory interneuron.
questions.x: Sensory afferents are excitatory, releasing glutamate. To inhibit the antagonist muscle, the spindle afferent excites an inhibitory interneuron in the spinal cord, which releases glycine onto the hamstring motor neuron. This reciprocal inhibition lets the quadriceps contract without opposition. A direct afferent-to-motor neuron synapse can only excite.

questions.q: Sympathetic fibers to eccrine sweat glands are an exception to the usual autonomic pattern. What is unusual about them?
o: Their postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors
Correct: they are sympathetic in origin but cholinergic at the target.
They have no preganglionic neuron
They still use a two-neuron chain.
They release epinephrine directly into sweat
Glands are activated by transmitter, not hormone secretion into sweat.
They originate from the sacral spinal cord
They arise from thoracolumbar segments like other sympathetic fibers.
questions.x: Most sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine, but those to eccrine sweat glands release ACh onto muscarinic receptors. They are still sympathetic anatomically, arising from thoracolumbar outflow through a two-neuron chain. This is why anticholinergic drugs such as atropine reduce sweating and can cause overheating.

questions.q: Pressing on a closed eye can make a person "see" flashes of light even though no light enters. What principle does this illustrate?
o: The perceived modality depends on which pathway is activated, not on the stimulus type
Correct: labeled-line coding interprets any optic signal as light.
Photoreceptors respond only to pressure
Photoreceptors respond best to light; pressure is an atypical stimulus.
Sensory adaptation
Adaptation is reduced response to a sustained stimulus.
Mechanoreceptors in the eye convert pressure to light
No receptor produces light; perception is interpreted by the brain.
questions.x: Labeled-line coding means the brain interprets activity in a particular pathway as a particular sensation, regardless of what activated it. Mechanical pressure that excites retinal cells is perceived as light (phosphenes) because the signal arrives via the optic pathway. No receptor generates light; the experience is created by the brain's interpretation of the active line.

questions.q: After a complete spinal cord transection at the mid-thoracic level and recovery from spinal shock, what is expected for the legs?
o: Voluntary movement and sensation are lost, but spinal stretch reflexes still occur
Correct: reflex arcs below the lesion remain intact without brain input.
Voluntary movement returns but reflexes are lost
Descending motor tracts are severed, so voluntary control is lost.
Both reflexes and voluntary movement remain normal
Voluntary movement requires the severed tracts.
Arm movement is lost but leg movement is preserved
A thoracic lesion spares the arms.
questions.x: A complete thoracic transection cuts ascending sensory tracts and descending motor tracts, so the legs lose sensation and voluntary control. The spinal reflex arcs below the lesion are intact, so after spinal shock resolves, stretch reflexes return and are often exaggerated because descending inhibition is lost. Arm function is spared because its segments are above the lesion.

questions.q: A patient has weakness, muscle atrophy and absent reflexes in one arm. Damage to which structure best explains this pattern?
o: Upper motor neurons in the motor cortex
Upper motor neuron lesions typically produce spasticity and hyperreflexia.
The cerebellum
Cerebellar damage causes incoordination, not atrophy and areflexia.
Lower motor neurons in the ventral horn or their axons
Correct: losing the final motor pathway causes flaccid weakness, atrophy and areflexia.
Dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons only
Loss of sensation alone would not cause weakness and atrophy.
questions.x: Lower motor neurons in the ventral horn are the final pathway to skeletal muscle. Their loss causes flaccid weakness, atrophy from denervation, fasciculations and absent reflexes because the reflex arc's efferent limb is broken. Upper motor neuron lesions instead cause spasticity and hyperreflexia, because the lower motor neurons survive without descending inhibition.

questions.q: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies reduce the number of functional nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Why do acetylcholinesterase inhibitors improve strength?
o: They let acetylcholine persist longer, increasing binding to the remaining receptors
Correct: more ACh per receptor compensates for fewer receptors.
They create new nicotinic receptors
They do not change receptor number.
They remove the antibodies from the end plate
They act on the enzyme, not the immune response.
They block muscarinic receptors on skeletal muscle
Skeletal muscle uses nicotinic receptors.
questions.x: In myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies block and remove nicotinic receptors, so the end-plate potential may fail to reach threshold, especially with repeated use. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as pyridostigmine slow ACh breakdown, so each ACh molecule can bind receptors repeatedly, strengthening the end-plate potential. They treat symptoms but do not change receptor number or the immune attack.

questions.q: Most organs receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic input. Which target is controlled mainly by the sympathetic division alone?
o: The heart
The heart receives both vagal and sympathetic fibers.
Most systemic blood vessels
Correct: vascular tone is set by varying sympathetic firing, with little parasympathetic input.
The iris of the eye
The iris has both dilator (sympathetic) and sphincter (parasympathetic) muscles.
The salivary glands
Salivary glands receive both divisions.
questions.x: Most systemic arterioles and veins receive sympathetic but little or no parasympathetic innervation. Vascular tone is adjusted by raising or lowering sympathetic firing onto α1 receptors: more firing constricts, less firing allows dilation. The heart, iris and salivary glands all receive dual innervation from both divisions.

questions.q: In untreated type 1 diabetes, ketone bodies accumulate in the blood. What is the reason?
o: High insulin drives fat synthesis into ketones
Insulin is absent, and it suppresses ketogenesis.
Glucose is converted directly into ketones
Ketones come from fatty acid breakdown.
Without insulin, lipolysis and hepatic fatty-acid oxidation increase, producing excess acetyl-CoA that becomes ketones
Correct: low insulin with high glucagon drives ketogenesis.
The kidney stops excreting ketones
Ketones are excreted; overproduction is the problem.
questions.x: Insulin normally suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis. Without insulin, and with glucagon high, adipose tissue releases large amounts of fatty acids, which the liver oxidizes to acetyl-CoA faster than the citric acid cycle can use it. The excess acetyl-CoA is converted to acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate, causing ketoacidosis. Glucose itself is not converted into ketones.

questions.q: A patient makes large volumes of dilute urine. After injection of desmopressin (an ADH analog), urine becomes concentrated. Where is the defect most likely?
o: In kidney ADH receptors
Nephrogenic DI would not respond to desmopressin.
In ADH production or release from the hypothalamus–posterior pituitary
Correct: this is central diabetes insipidus.
In pancreatic β cells
β-cell failure causes diabetes mellitus with glucose in urine.
In the adrenal cortex
Adrenal defects do not produce desmopressin-responsive dilute urine.
questions.note: Response to ADH analog = central DI; no response = nephrogenic DI.
questions.x: Diabetes insipidus causes large volumes of dilute urine. If the kidney concentrates urine after a synthetic ADH analog, its receptors and aquaporin machinery work, so the problem is lack of ADH from the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary: central DI. In nephrogenic DI, the kidney fails to respond to ADH, so desmopressin would have little effect.

questions.q: A pituitary tumor compresses the stalk and blocks hypothalamic signals to the anterior pituitary. Which hormone level is most likely to RISE?
o: Prolactin
Correct: dopamine from the hypothalamus normally inhibits prolactin, so blocking it raises prolactin.
ACTH
ACTH depends on stimulatory CRH, so it falls.
TSH
TSH depends on stimulatory TRH, so it falls.
GH
GH depends mainly on stimulatory GHRH, so it falls.
questions.note: Prolactin is the one anterior pituitary hormone under tonic inhibition.
questions.x: Most anterior pituitary hormones depend on stimulatory hypothalamic hormones (CRH, TRH, GHRH, GnRH) carried in portal blood, so cutting the stalk lowers them. Prolactin is different: it is under tonic inhibition by hypothalamic dopamine. Interrupting dopamine delivery removes this brake, so prolactin rises even as the other anterior pituitary hormones fall.

questions.q: A patient with high cortisol and high ACTH is given high-dose dexamethasone. Cortisol falls substantially. What is the most likely source of excess ACTH?
o: An ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor in the lung
Ectopic sources usually do not suppress with dexamethasone.
A pituitary adenoma
Correct: pituitary adenomas usually retain partial feedback sensitivity to high-dose dexamethasone.
An adrenal tumor secreting cortisol
Adrenal tumors cause low ACTH.
Primary adrenal insufficiency
That causes low cortisol.
questions.x: Dexamethasone is a potent synthetic glucocorticoid that suppresses ACTH through negative feedback. Pituitary adenomas are only partly resistant to feedback, so a high dose still lowers their ACTH and therefore cortisol. Ectopic ACTH tumors usually ignore glucocorticoid feedback, and adrenal tumors already have suppressed ACTH, so neither shows this suppression.

questions.q: A male athlete uses high doses of anabolic steroids for a year. What changes in his testes are expected?
o: Shrinkage and reduced sperm production due to suppressed LH and FSH
Correct: exogenous androgens feed back to lower GnRH, LH and FSH.
Enlargement due to increased LH
LH falls, not rises.
Increased sperm production due to more testosterone
Intratesticular testosterone falls when LH is suppressed.
No change because the testes ignore feedback
The testes depend on gonadotropins.
questions.x: Exogenous androgens are sensed by the hypothalamus and pituitary as high testosterone, so GnRH, LH and FSH fall. Without LH, Leydig cells stop making testosterone, so testosterone inside the testes drops even though blood androgen is high. Without FSH and local testosterone, spermatogenesis falls and the testes shrink. High blood testosterone does not substitute for intratesticular androgen.

questions.q: A hormone's effect is blocked by an antibody that cannot cross membranes but binds the hormone's receptor. What does this suggest?
o: The receptor is in the nucleus
An impermeant antibody could not reach nuclear receptors.
The hormone is a steroid that acts on DNA
Steroid receptors are typically intracellular.
The receptor is on the cell surface
Correct: an impermeant antibody can reach only extracellular receptor sites.
The hormone acts without any receptor
Blocking with a receptor antibody shows a receptor is needed.
